latestRelease.notes:
# Hermes Agent v0.20.4 (v2026.8.18)

**Release Date:** August 18, 2026

> Patch release. This tag rolls up the ~74 PRs merged since v0.20.3 into a stable tagged release for downstream consumers (Docker images, hosted deployments, fresh installs).

---

## About this release

Since v0.20.3 (v2026.8.16.2, tagged August 17), this window landed **~146 commits** across **~265 files** (+21,697 / −2,217) — **~74 merged PRs** including the desktop glass/translucency surface work (matte glass, frost picker, macOS pre-select), the tabbed SESSIONS|BOTS sidebar with per-bot hide/unhide, Bot Mode group-chat fixes (long-running member turns, Markdown rendering, cross-machine routing), NVIDIA SkillEvaluator Tier 1 advisory scanning on skill installs (license + security checks), cron media-send hardening (configurable timeout, manual-run attachments, missed-fire surfacing), SessionDB event-loop-thread and contention fixes, `hermes update` parked-branch honesty, and kanban native OS notifications.

**Full curated release notes for this window will ship with v0.21.0**, which will document everything from v0.20.0 onward — highlights, feature areas, and complete contributor credits. Nothing in this window is skipped.

## Updating

- `hermes update` from an existing install
- Fresh install: `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/main/scripts/install.sh | bash`

**Full Changelog**: https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/compare/v2026.8.16.2...v2026.8.18

signals.title: [Bug]: Desktop message age ("8m ago") stops advancing without a re-render
signals.text: ### Bug Description Hermes Desktop can leave an assistant message's relative age frozen indefinitely. In one observed session, the message footer still displayed `8m ago` at 18:38:41 even though the persisted assistant message timestamp was 17:09:23. The actual elapsed time was 1 hour 29 minutes, and `hermes sessions list` correctly reported the session as `1h ago`. The underlying timestamp is correct. Only the rendered relative-age label is stale. This can mislead the operator about whether a response or background activity happened recently. Suggested priority: P3. This is a UI correctness issue with a simple workaround and no observed data loss. ### Steps to Reproduce 1. Open a completed chat in Hermes Desktop. 2. Hover an assistant response so its action bar displays a relative age such as `8m ago`. 3. Leave the same chat open long enough to cross one or more minute/hour boundaries, without switching sessions or otherwise triggering a React re-render. 4. Hover or continue hovering the response again. 5. Observe that the label can remain at its old value. 6. Switch to another chat and back, or reload Desktop. 7. Observe that the age is recalculated. ### Expected Behavior The visible relative age should advance as time passes, for example: - `8m ago` → `9m ago` - `59m ago` → `1h ago` It should not require unrelated UI state changes, session navigation, or a reload. ### Actual Behavior The label samples the current time during a render and can then remain frozen until an unrelated render occurs. Observed evidence: - Persisted assistant timestamp: `2026-07-30 17:09:23 +02:00` - Screenshot capture time: `2026-07-30 18:38:41 +02:00` - Displayed label: `8m ago` - Actual elapsed time: approximately 1h 29m - Native CLI session age: `1h ago` ### Affected Component Other — Hermes Desktop, in-thread assistant message footer (`MessageAge`). ### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related) Not applicable — Desktop UI. ### Debug Report ```shell Not uploaded: this is a deterministic renderer-state bug with no crash, traceback, or relevant log signature. Sanitized local checks confirmed that the persisted timestamp and CLI-derived age were correct; only the Desktop label was stale. ``` ### Operating System Windows 11 Pro, version 10.0.26200, build 26200, 64-bit. ### Python Version Hermes runtime: Python 3.11.15 Shell `python --version`: Python 3.14.6 ### Hermes Version Observed on Hermes Agent v0.19.0 (2026.7.20). The installed runtime reports that it is behind current upstream. However, the same causal code path was inspected on the current `main` branch on 2026-07-30 and is still present there. ### Additional Logs / Traceback (optional) ```shell No error or crash was emitted. The stored session data contains the correct timestamp. ``` ### Root Cause Analysis (optional) On current `main`, `apps/desktop/src/components/assistant-ui/thread/assistant-message.tsx` implements `MessageAge` by: 1. subscribing only to `s.message.createdAt`, which is stable after message creation; and 2. calling `formatAgo(date.getTime(), t.agents)` directly during render. `formatAgo` defaults its `nowMs` argument to `Date.now()`, but `MessageAge` has no reactive clock, interval, scheduled invalidation, or changing state. Consequently, `Date.now()` is sampled only when React happens to render the component. CSS hover visibility does not itself cause another React render. Current code: https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/main/apps/desktop/src/components/assistant-ui/thread/assistant-message.tsx#L296-L312 This was also confirmed in the packaged Windows bundle used during the incident. ### Proposed Fix (optional) Make the displayed age depend on a reactive notion of `now`. To avoid creating one permanent timer for every message in a long transcript, prefer either: 1. a shared coarse clock for message-age consumers; or 2. subscribing/scheduling updates only while the age control is visible or focused, with the next update scheduled at the next `coarseElapsed` display boundary. Add a fake-timer regression test demonstrating that the label advances from `8m ago` to `9m ago` and then to `1h ago` without any unrelated state update. ### Workaround Switching away from the chat and back, or reloading Desktop, forces the label to be recalculated. This is containment, not a permanent solution. ### Related Issues and Pull Requests - #70450 is related but not a duplicate. It concerns making exact timestamps discoverable through reliable tooltips: https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/70450 - #70487 implements those tooltip and accessibility changes, but its `MessageAge` replacement still calculates `formatAgo()` only during render and does not introduce a reactive clock: https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/70487 The affected surface overlaps, but the trigger, causal mechanism, acceptance criteria, and required fix are different.

signals.title: hermes config set: list-of-strings values written as stringified JSON literal instead of YAML list
signals.text: # Bug: `hermes config set` silently stringifies list-of-strings values ## Summary `hermes config set <key> '<JSON literal>'` writes the entire literal as a **quoted string** into `~/.hermes/config.yaml` instead of a real YAML list. Downstream consumers that call `_coerce_allow_set` (or any other "accept list-or-comma-string" parser) get a single-element set containing the stringified JSON, which silently breaks allowlist matching — including security-relevant allowlists like `gateway.platforms.telegram.group_allowed_chats`. ## Reproduction ```bash # Setup: pick any list-typed key hermes config set gateway.platforms.telegram.group_allowed_chats '["-5488240624"]' # Inspect raw YAML — appears to be a quoted string, not a list grep -n -A1 'group_allowed_chats' ~/.hermes/config.yaml # Actual: group_allowed_chats: '["-5488240624"]' # Expected: group_allowed_chats: # - "-5488240624" # Confirm parsed type with PyYAML python3 -c 'import yaml; print(type(yaml.safe_load(open("$HOME/.hermes/config.yaml"))["gateway"]["platforms"]["telegram"]["group_allowed_chats"]).__name__)' # Actual: str # Expected: list ``` ## Impact - **Severity:** High — silently breaks authorization allowlists. No warning, no validation error. - **Surface area:** all list-typed config keys consumed by `_coerce_allow_set` in `gateway/authz_mixin.py:46-58`. Includes (verified by `search_files`): - `gateway.platforms.telegram.group_allowed_chats` - `gateway.platforms.telegram.group_allow_from` - Plus all `*_allow_from` / `*_allowed_users` / `*_allowed_chats` keys that pass through `_coerce_allow_set` - **Real-world consequence encountered:** Telegram group `user_id=8763334778` in chat `-5488240624` repeatedly logged `Blocked unauthorized user` despite being in a group explicitly added to the allowlist. Setting `require_mention=false` and `group_allow_from: ["*"]` had no effect until the value was rewritten as a YAML scalar. - **Workaround:** use the scalar form (no surrounding JSON brackets): ```bash hermes config set gateway.platforms.telegram.group_allowed_chats "-5488240624" hermes config set gateway.platforms.telegram.group_allow_from "*" ``` When `_coerce_allow_set` sees a non-JSON scalar string like `"-5488240624"`, `str.split(",")` correctly returns `{"-5488240624"}` and matching works. ## Root cause hypothesis `hermes config set` writes the value as a YAML scalar by stringifying whatever was passed. When the user passes a JSON literal (because the CLI has no native list syntax), the literal is quoted whole instead of being parsed into a YAML sequence. Two viable fix directions (for upstream to choose): 1. **Write side (preferred):** in `hermes config set`, detect when the value is a valid JSON literal (starts with `[` or `{`). If so, parse it and emit the YAML structure directly (`yaml.dump` with proper flow style), not as a quoted scalar. Plain scalars keep current behavior. 2. **Read side (tolerant fallback):** extend `_coerce_allow_set` to attempt `json.loads(raw)` when the string looks like a JSON array/object, falling back to the current `str.split(",")` only if that fails. Recommend direction (1) because: - Fix is at the source, all consumers benefit automatically - Read-side tolerance can mask other write-side issues in the future ## Suggested test cases ```python # test_hermes_config_set_list.py import subprocess, yaml from pathlib import Path CFG = Path.home() / ".hermes" / "config.yaml" def test_list_written_as_list(): subprocess.run(["hermes", "config", "set", "test.key", '["a","b"]'], check=True) parsed = yaml.safe_load(CFG.read_text()) assert isinstance(parsed["test"]["key"], list) assert parsed["test"]["key"] == ["a", "b"] # cleanup subprocess.run(["hermes", "config", "unset", "test.key"], check=True) def test_scalar_still_works(): subprocess.run(["hermes", "config", "set", "test.key", "hello"], check=True) parsed = yaml.safe_load(CFG.read_text()) assert parsed["test"]["key"] == "hello" subprocess.run(["hermes", "config", "unset", "test.key"], check=True) def test_comma_string_still_works(): subprocess.run(["hermes", "config", "set", "test.key", "a,b,c"], check=True) parsed = yaml.safe_load(CFG.read_text()) assert parsed["test"]["key"] in (["a", "b", "c"], "a,b,c") # back-compat subprocess.run(["hermes", "config", "unset", "test.key"], check=True) ``` ## Environment - hermes-agent version: latest (installed via `~/.hermes/hermes-agent/`, this session 2026-08-01) - Config path: `~/.hermes/config.yaml` (per `hermes config path`) - Tested with `python3 -c "import yaml; ..."` (PyYAML present) ## Reporter context Discovered while configuring a Telegram group allowlist for a team support bot. The user expects `group_allowed_chats: ["-5488240624"]` to mean "this chat and only this chat", which is a security-relevant config. The current behavior silently downgrades it to "match the literal string `\"-5488240624\"`" — which matches nothing.

signals.title: False positive: "TERMINAL_CWD deprecated" warning on every gateway start (env var, not .env)
signals.text: ## Summary Hermes shows a deprecation warning on every start even though the user **never set** `TERMINAL_CWD` in `~/.hermes/.env` (the only occurrence is a commented-out `# TERMINAL_CWD=.`): ``` ⚠ Deprecated .env settings detected: ⚠ TERMINAL_CWD=/path/to/project found in .env — this is deprecated. Move to config.yaml instead: terminal: cwd: /your/project/path Then remove the old entries from ~/.hermes/.env ``` ## Root cause (traced in source) 1. `cli.py:7706` (`_restore_session_cwd`) sets `os.environ["TERMINAL_CWD"]` when a session with a recorded cwd is resumed (`/resume`, `--resume`, continuing an old session). The env var then **outlives the session** and sticks to the shell/process env. 2. `gateway/run.py:2395` calls `warn_deprecated_cwd_env_vars()`, which reads `os.environ.get("TERMINAL_CWD")` (config.py:2151) — i.e. **process env**, not the .env **file**. 3. `doctor.py:436-437` explicitly documents the intended behavior: deprecated env vars should be *"checked in the .env file, not process env, so config→env bridges like terminal.cwd → TERMINAL_CWD do not false-positive."* So `warn_deprecated_cwd_env_vars()` contradicts doctor.py: it checks process env, which the config bridge / session-restore populates legitimately, and reports a user-facing deprecation warning that is a false positive. ## Repro - Any session whose process env already contains `TERMINAL_CWD` (e.g. after resuming a session created in a project dir). - `env -u TERMINAL_CWD hermes chat -q ok` suppresses the warning; with `TERMINAL_CWD` set it appears. Verified: with env set → 1 warning, without → 0. ## Expected `warn_deprecated_cwd_env_vars()` should read the **.env file** (like `doctor.py` does) instead of `os.environ`, so a launch-artifact / config-bridge value never triggers a user-facing "you have a deprecated setting" warning. At minimum, skip the warning when `terminal.cwd` in config.yaml is non-explicit (".") and the env value matches the session-restore path. ## Environment - Hermes Agent v0.20.1 (2026.8.13) - OS: Linux Mint - Source: cli
signals.author: orlandocalvin

signals.title: Windows: hermes update always fails (live hermes.exe cannot be renamed); reboot-scheduled quarantine never releases the lock and pollutes PendingFileRenameOperations
signals.text: ## Summary On Windows, `hermes update` **always fails** at the dependency-install step because the live `hermes.exe` cannot be renamed on this machine. The quarantine mechanism (`_quarantine_running_hermes_exe`) assumes Windows allows renaming a running executable, but here the rename raises `PermissionError`. The fallback (`MoveFileExW` + `MOVEFILE_DELAY_UNTIL_REBOOT`) only *schedules* the rename for next boot — it does **not** release the lock, so `uv pip install -e .` still fails with `os error 32` ("another program is using this file"). Every failed run additionally appends stale `PendingFileRenameOperations` entries which will **rename the freshly installed shim away on the next reboot**, making `hermes` disappear from PATH. Environment: Windows 10.0.26200 x64, hermes-agent 0.20.1 (2026.8.13), Python 3.11.15 venv, uv from `hermes\bin\uv.exe`. ## Repro ``` hermes update -y ``` Always fails (both the git-update path and the ZIP fallback): ``` → Updating Python dependencies... ⚠ hermes.exe is locked by another process; scheduled replacement on next reboot. The new shim was written at the same path, but a reboot is needed to fully unload the old one. Using Python 3.11.15 environment at: venv Resolved 99 packages in 1.46s Built hermes-agent @ file:///C:/Users/zhaid/AppData/Local/hermes/hermes-agent Prepared 1 package in 6.09s error: failed to remove file `...\hermes-agent\venv\Lib\site-packages\../../Scripts/hermes.exe`: 另一个程序正在使用此文件，进程无法访问。 (os error 32) ``` ## Root-cause analysis 1. `_quarantine_running_hermes_exe` (`hermes_cli/main.py` ~L8335) renames the live shim to `hermes.exe.old.<stamp>`, expecting uv to then write a fresh shim. Its docstring states "Windows allows RENAMING a mapped/running executable". **On this machine that rename fails with `PermissionError` even when hermes.exe is the *only* hermes process** (verified with a fresh launch in an isolated environment: no Hermes Desktop, no gateway, no REPL, no AV handle — I also checked no other process maps the exe). The launcher itself appears to hold its own file open without `FILE_SHARE_DELETE`. 2. When all inline rename retries fail, `_schedule_replace_on_reboot` (`main.py` ~L8438) schedules `hermes.exe -> hermes.exe.old.<stamp>` via `MoveFileExW(MOVEFILE_DELAY_UNTIL_REBOOT)`. But scheduling does not unlock the file — the rename only happens at boot — so the subsequent `uv pip install -e .` still cannot remove the exe and the whole update fails. The fallback only works for *transient* locks (short AV scans), not for the persistent self-lock. 3. **Registry pollution / reboot hazard:** every failed attempt appends another pair to `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\PendingFileRenameOperations`. If the shim later gets replaced by any other means (e.g. running the install from a non-shim interpreter, as I did), the pending entries then rename the *new* shim away on next reboot → `hermes` command vanishes. I found 8 stale hermes entries accumulated from one failed update run and had to clean them manually. 4. **Recovery loop:** the `.update-incomplete` marker is left behind; `_recover_from_interrupted_install` (main.py ~L8004) only runs when "update" is not in argv (`main.py` ~L11624), and when it runs under `hermes.exe` it hits the same self-lock and fails, leaving the marker for the next launch — every command (except `--version`, which has a fast path that skips it) then retries and fails. There is no actionable message telling the user the install can never complete this way. ## Verified workaround Running the update with the interpreter instead of the shim works (the live process is `python.exe`, so no shim is locked): ``` venv\Scripts\python.exe -m hermes_cli.main update ``` Or, if a `.update-incomplete` marker is left behind, any `python -m hermes_cli.main <cmd>` (e.g. `version`) triggers the recovery path, which succeeds for the same reason and clears the marker. ## Suggested fixes 1. When `_windows_running_hermes_launcher_locked()` is true, do **not** schedule a reboot rename for that shim (it is dead weight for a persistent lock and pollutes the registry). Instead print the actionable guidance (exit all hermes processes / use `python -m hermes_cli.main update`). 2. Before scheduling via `MoveFileExW`, remove any existing hermes-related `PendingFileRenameOperations` entries, or clean them after a successful install, so a later successful replacement isn't clobbered at reboot. 3. Consider documenting the `python -m hermes_cli.main update` path as the supported way to self-update on Windows, or have the update flow detect the self-lock and re-exec the install via `sys.executable` in a child process instead of relying on shim quarantine.

signals.title: [Bug]: False-positive "Deprecated .env settings" TERMINAL_CWD warning on every startup (self-reported by config bridge)
signals.text: ### Bug Description ## Bug Description The CLI startup prints a false-positive deprecation warning: ``` ⚠ Deprecated .env settings detected: ⚠ TERMINAL_CWD=/mnt/c/Users/andyf found in .env — this is deprecated. ``` ...even though `TERMINAL_CWD` is **not** set anywhere in `~/.hermes/.env` (verified: the file has no such entry, Windows registry env vars are clean, and a fresh WSL session has no such variable). ## Root Cause Two pieces of code contradict each other: 1. `cli.py` (~line 694-702) **force-exports** `terminal.cwd` from `config.yaml` into `os.environ["TERMINAL_CWD"]` (comment says: "CLI: always export (overrides stale .env or inherited values)"). With a default `cwd: .`, the exported value is the resolved absolute startup path. 2. `hermes_cli/config.py` `warn_deprecated_cwd_env_vars()` (line 2182) reads `os.environ.get("TERMINAL_CWD")` and, when `config.terminal.cwd` is not an "explicit path" (i.e. one of `.`, `auto`, `cwd`, `""`), assumes the variable must have come from `.env` and warns. So Hermes exports the variable itself and then warns about itself. Any stock config with `cwd: .` triggers the warning on every startup. ## Steps to Reproduce 1. `config.yaml` has `terminal.cwd: .` (the default) 2. `.env` contains no `TERMINAL_CWD` line 3. Start the CLI (`hermes`) 4. Observe the deprecation warning despite nothing being set in `.env` ## Expected Behavior No warning when the variable was not set by the user in `.env` — in particular, no warning when `os.environ["TERMINAL_CWD"]` exactly matches the value the config bridge itself exported. ## Suggested Fix - In `warn_deprecated_cwd_env_vars()`, skip the warning when `os.environ["TERMINAL_CWD"]` equals the resolved value of `terminal.cwd` (e.g. `str(Path(cwd).resolve())`), or pass an explicit flag from the bridge context; **or** - Have the bridge skip exporting `TERMINAL_CWD` when the config value is non-explicit (`.`, `auto`, `cwd`, `""`). ## Environment - Hermes Agent v0.20.2 (2026.8.16) - WSL2 (Ubuntu), local terminal backend - CLI (not gateway) ### Steps to Reproduce 1. config.yaml has terminal.cwd: . (the default) 2. .env contains no TERMINAL_CWD line 3. Start the CLI (hermes) 4. Observe the deprecation warning despite nothing being set in .env ### Expected Behavior No warning when TERMINAL_CWD was not set by the user in .env — especially when the env var value matches the one the config bridge exported itself. ### Actual Behavior CLI prints "⚠ Deprecated .env settings detected: TERMINAL_CWD=/mnt/c/Users/andyf found in .env" on every startup, even though .env has no such entry (verified). Root cause: cli.py force-exports terminal.cwd into os.environ["TERMINAL_CWD"], then warn_deprecated_cwd_env_vars() (hermes_cli/config.py:2182) sees it and misattributes it to .env. ### Affected Component CLI (interactive chat) ### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related) N/A (CLI only) ### Debug Report ```shell N/A — prefer not to upload personal data ``` ### Operating System Ubuntu 22.04 ### Python Version _No response_ ### Hermes Version _No response_ ### Additional Logs / Traceback (optional) ```shell ``` ### Root Cause Analysis (optional) _No response_ ### Proposed Fix (optional) _No response_ ### Are you willing to submit a PR for this? - [ ] I'd like to fix this myself and submit a PR

signals.title: False-positive 'Deprecated .env settings' warning when terminal.cwd is '.' (local backend)
signals.text: ## Summary False-positive **"Deprecated .env settings detected"** warning on every startup when `terminal.cwd` is set to `.` (follow-the-launch-dir) with the local terminal backend — even though `.env` no longer contains `TERMINAL_CWD`. ## Reproduction 1. `config.yaml`: ```yaml terminal: cwd: . ``` 2. `.env` has no uncommented `TERMINAL_CWD` (in my case it is commented out: `# TERMINAL_CWD=.`). 3. Launch `hermes` (CLI or TUI) from any directory. Observed warning (stderr): ``` ⚠ Deprecated .env settings detected: ⚠ TERMINAL_CWD=<absolute launch dir> found in .env — this is deprecated. Move to config.yaml instead: terminal: cwd: /your/project/path Then remove the old entries from <hermes home>/.env ``` ## Expected No warning. `TERMINAL_CWD` is bridged from `terminal.cwd` by the CLI itself, not a leftover `.env` entry. `.` is the documented way to keep the working directory as the launch directory. ## Actual Warning printed at every startup. Functionality is unaffected (cwd resolution works), but the warning is misleading — there is nothing to migrate. ## Root cause `warn_deprecated_cwd_env_vars` in `hermes_cli/config.py:2190` detects the deprecation by reading the **environment variable** `os.environ.get("TERMINAL_CWD")` (config.py:2196-2197), not by inspecting the `.env` file. Meanwhile the CLI bridge in `cli.py:649-651` **always overwrites** `terminal.cwd` with `os.getcwd()` for the local backend: ```python if effective_backend == "local": terminal_config["cwd"] = os.getcwd() ``` and force-exports it (`cli.py:700-704`): `os.environ["TERMINAL_CWD"] = str(terminal_config[config_key])`. Additionally, `config_has_explicit_cwd` excludes placeholder values `{".", "auto", "cwd", ""}` (config.py:2208), so `cwd: .` is treated as "no explicit path" and the warning fires even though the env var was produced by the config bridge, not `.env`. The check cannot distinguish a config-bridged value from a genuine `.env` leftover. ## Suggested fix - Read the `.env` file directly (parse for an uncommented `TERMINAL_CWD=` line) instead of sampling the environment, and/or - Skip the warning when the current `TERMINAL_CWD` equals the config-bridged value (e.g. the launch dir substituted for `.` by the local backend), and/or - Treat `.` (and the shared placeholder set `{".", "auto", "cwd"}` already defined at `cli.py:646`) as an explicit user intent in `config_has_explicit_cwd`. ## Environment - OS: Windows 11, git-bash shell - Hermes Agent v0.20.3 (2026.8.16.2), install dir `C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\hermes\hermes-agent` - Python 3.11.15 - Local terminal backend (`terminal.env_type` unset / local)

signals.title: [Bug]: False-positive "Deprecated .env settings" TERMINAL_CWD warning on plain `hermes chat -q` (incidental gateway.run import from relay_runtime)
signals.text: ### Bug Description Hermes v0.20.4 (Linux, local terminal backend, `terminal.cwd: .` in config.yaml) prints a false-positive deprecation warning on every chat startup: ``` ⚠ Deprecated .env settings detected: ⚠ TERMINAL_CWD=/root found in .env — this is deprecated. Move to config.yaml instead: terminal: cwd: /your/project/path Then remove the old entries from ~/.hermes/.env ``` even though `TERMINAL_CWD` is **not set anywhere in `~/.hermes/.env`** (line 214 is commented out: `# TERMINAL_CWD=.`). ### Steps to Reproduce 1. config.yaml: `terminal: { backend: local, cwd: . }` 2. `~/.hermes/.env` has no uncommented `TERMINAL_CWD` 3. Run from any directory: `hermes chat -q "x"` 4. Warning appears on stderr before the reply Reproducible even with a pristine environment (`env -i` with only PATH/HOME/SHELL/LANG/TERM), i.e. not caused by any stale shell export. ### Root Cause (traced) The emitting call site is **`gateway/run.py:2441-2444`** — module-level code that runs whenever `gateway.run` is imported. On the plain CLI path (no gateway involved), this import happens incidentally: ``` hermes chat -q x → run_agent.run_conversation → agent.relay_runtime.begin_turn → relay_runtime._segments_config() (relay_runtime.py:174) → from gateway.run import _load_gateway_config # late import → gateway/run.py module-level warn_deprecated_cwd_env_vars() (line 2444) ``` Underlying problem: `warn_deprecated_cwd_env_vars()` inspects `os.environ` (not the .env file), and `cli.py`'s own config bridge force-exports `terminal.cwd` into `TERMINAL_CWD` at startup (cli.py ~line 700). So the warning reports a value that Hermes itself put there — it cannot distinguish a bridged value from a genuine .env entry. The check also runs before `load_hermes_dotenv()` re-applies the config bridge. The "remove from ~/.hermes/.env" hint is misleading because the value never came from .env. ### Expected Behavior No deprecation warning when `TERMINAL_CWD` is not set in `.env`, regardless of what os.environ contains (bridged, restored-session, or worktree values are all legitimate runtime state). ### Workaround (confirmed on 0.20.4) `hermes config set terminal.cwd /root` — an explicit path short-circuits the warning. Verified clean across: bridged value equal to cwd, exported foreign value, and no-value cases. ### Related - #88829 (config-bridge self-report, CLI startup) — this issue adds the second trigger path (relay_runtime → gateway.run) that fires per-turn on plain chat, not just startup - #89016 (terminal.cwd='.' local backend) — PR #89124 has a fix for the startup path - #85695 (gateway start) - Fix PRs under review: #87034, #88533, #88552, #89124 ### Suggested Fix 1. Read deprecated-cwd vars from the .env file itself (as #87034/#88533/#89124 propose) instead of os.environ, and 2. Guard the module-level call in `gateway/run.py` so the warning only runs when the gateway is the actual entry point (not on incidental late imports from relay_runtime / oneshot / CLI tool paths).

signals.title: Bug: Windows CLI 'hermes update' cannot succeed — updater self-locks its own launcher exe (EACCES/WinError 32), preflight excludes self
signals.text: ## Summary On Windows, a plain CLI `hermes update` (run from the venv console-script launcher `Scripts\hermes.exe`) **cannot ever succeed**: the dependency-install step has to replace `Scripts\hermes.exe`, and that exe is the very image currently executing the updater. Windows refuses to overwrite a running executable. - With `uv`: `Failed to persist temporary file to ...\.venv\Lib\site-packages\..\..\Scripts\hermes.exe: failed to persist temporary file: 拒绝访问。 (os error 5)` - With `pip`: `ERROR: Could not install packages due to an OSError: [WinError 32] ...hermes.exe -> hermes.exe.deleteme` (the running exe cannot even be renamed). This is the **CLI-side variant** of #89295 (Gateway self-update): there the lock is held by the running Gateway; here the lock holder is the **updater process itself**. The Gateway-focused detection fixes (#89295, #79561) cannot help in this case. ## Reproduction (Windows, editable install, venv `Scripts\hermes.exe`) 1. From a normal PowerShell: `hermes update`. 2. The updater reaches the dependency-install step while `Scripts\hermes.exe` is still running (the launcher stays alive for the whole command's lifetime). 3. `uv pip install -e .` regenerates the console script and tries to persist it over the running exe → `os error 5` (EACCES; localized "拒绝访问"). 4. pip fallback path renames `hermes.exe -> hermes.exe.deleteme` → `WinError 32` (already seen in earlier failures). 5. If the install dies mid-way, `hermes update` writes the `update-incomplete` marker; **every subsequent launch** runs the early-recovery flow ("A previous `hermes update` was interrupted mid-install — finishing dependency installation now (before any native extensions load)..."), runs `uv pip install -e .` again, hits the identical lock, and reports "The next launch will retry" — an **infinite retry loop** as long as update is invoked through the exe. ## Root cause 1. `_detect_other_hermes_holders()` (`hermes_cli/update_cmd.py`, ~line 3389) deliberately excludes the current process and all its ancestors (`skip.add(os.getpid())` + `psutil.Process().parents()`). So the existing preflight that would report "another hermes.exe is running — close it before retrying" (`_format_concurrent_instances_message`) **never fires for the single-instance CLI case**, where the only holder is the updater itself. (Introduced in commit `927463efcc4`, 2026-07-29; still present at HEAD `3c675019f1`.) - `_abort_dependency_sync_if_self_locked()` / `_SELF_LOCKING_NATIVE_MODULES` only guard **mapped native `.pyd`/`.dll` modules** loaded into the process (cryptography, PyYAML). It does not consider that the console-script launcher `Scripts\hermes.exe` is itself a running image that every `uv pip install -e .` will rewrite. - The early-recovery path (`hermes_cli/_early_recovery.py`, marker recovery) runs the install *before* loading native extensions, so the `.pyd` guard is bypassed while the launcher exe is still locked. Verified on a clean working tree at `3c675019f1` — this is committed upstream behavior, not a local modification. ## Impact - On Windows, `hermes update` from the CLI entry point is completely blocked. Combined with #89295, both the Gateway and the CLI update paths fail on Windows. - Secondary issue surfaced by the same environment: `_venv_scripts_dir()` and friends only check `PROJECT_ROOT / "venv"`, not `.venv` (see #79542) — with a `.venv` install (the default for `uv`), the holder-detection preflight silently returns no scripts dir and skips entirely. I worked around this locally, but the failure reproduces even when detection is active because self/ancestors are excluded. ## Workaround Run the update through the venv's own interpreter instead of the launcher, so the running image is `Scripts\python.exe` (which the package install does not replace): ``` python -m hermes_cli.main update ``` This lets `uv pip install -e .` rewrite `Scripts\hermes.exe` successfully (verified: kill the stuck process, optional clear `.update-incomplete` marker, then run the above — the recover+install completes). ## Suggested fix (for maintainers) 1. Extend the self-lock preflight to the launcher-image case: if the current process or any ancestor is executing the venv's `Scripts\hermes.exe`, defer the dependency sync (`exit 2`, reuse the existing "cannot overwrite a running executable" message) and tell the user to complete the install from a fresh process (e.g. `python -m hermes_cli.main update`) — or use a detached helper that swaps the exe after the main process exits. 2. Longer term: a stub-launcher pattern (`hermes.exe` only spawns the real CLI and exits) so the launcher is never the process running the update logic; and/or run the self-update install with `--no-scripts` / deferred script creation. ## Environment - Windows (OS error messages localized — "拒绝访问" = ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED) - hermes-agent checkout at `main` HEAD `3c675019f1`, clean tree - Python 3.12 venv (`.venv`), managed uv, hermes-agent 0.20.4 (editable install) - Repro command: `hermes update` ## Related - #89295 — Gateway self-update holds its own launcher exe locked (WinError 32); detection fixes do not help - #79561 — Windows Gateway update still fails after venv detection fix (quarantine cannot rename running launcher) - #79542 — `_venv_scripts_dir()` only checks `venv`, not `.venv`
signals.author: whengu

signals.title: Desktop: BOTS roster preview sticks to a stale finished session despite correct backend (app-side index + touch-on-open)
signals.text: ## Summary In the BOTS section of the Hermes desktop sidebar, the preview row for some profiles shows an old, finished session, and clicking the row opens that old session — even though the active/newest sessions exist in the profile's `state.db` and the backend (`profiles.list`, `last_session` / `list_sessions_rich(order_by_last_active=True)`) returns them in the correct order. After a full app restart and clearing the Electron Local Storage the pane briefly shows the correct previews, but the stale state reproduces on the next roster fetch / after opening a row. ## Environment - macOS 26.x (Apple Silicon) - Hermes Desktop (Electron) — agent core v0.20.4 (2026.8.18), containing `8484786` (BOTS roster preview align) and `7dd945b9` (dedupe + canonical chats) - Multiple profiles (default + 7 named), mixture of desktop sessions and CLI sessions (`hermes -p <name> chat -q`) - Bot Mode / Bots pane active (default plugin) ## Steps to reproduce (observed) 1. Use several profiles. Keep a long-running session in profile A (e.g. default). Create sessions in profiles B/C only via CLI (`hermes -p B chat -q ...`), so the newest data in those `state.dbs` comes from outside the app. 2. Open the BOTS pane. Some rows correctly show the newest session; others (here: default, seth, mac-admin) show a **finished, older session** (in our case: a 2-day-old hidden session, a previous-day session, and a 3-week-old session) although newer sessions exist in those `state.dbs`. 3. Clicking such a row opens the displayed stale session instead of the active one (the symptom of #88200, which is supposed to be fixed by PR #88690). 4. Fully quit the app, clear `~/Library/Application Support/Hermes/Local Storage/leveldb/`, restart: the pane briefly shows the correct previews, then the stale state returns after further interaction / roster refresh. ## Diagnostic data - **Backend is correct:** direct `SessionDB.list_sessions_rich(source=None, limit=20, order_by_last_active=True, compact_rows=True)` returns the active/newest session first for all affected profiles. - **Touch-on-open:** opening/viewing a session updates `sessions.last_activity_at` with provenance `unknown` and an empty description (no chat-activity code). A mac-admin session from 2026-07-31 received such an update on 2026-08-19 16:17 after a stray command — a 3-week-old session became "most recently active" again. This is a self-fulfilling loop: the pane shows the stale row → opening/touching it renews its activity → it stays "last session". - **App-side index:** `hermes.desktop.sessionSeenCounts`, `hermes.desktop.lastSessionId(.profile.<name>)`, `hermes.desktop.sessionOrder`, `hermes.desktop.sessionTiles.v2` in the Electron Local Storage are rebuilt from UI interactions after a storage reset — the Local Storage is the only app-side persistence (Session Storage / Partitions / SharedStorage contain no `hermes.desktop` markers). - **hidden sessions are not filtered** when the roster preview is chosen: a hidden (`hidden=1`) session from 2026-08-17 was shown as the default profile's preview while the pinned active session was newer. ## Expected behavior - The BOTS row preview and the session opened on click describe the same, most relevant (non-archived, non-hidden) session — ideally sourced from the backend's `last_session`/`preferred_session` resolution. - Viewing/opening a session (touch) should not count as conversation activity for roster ordering (or should use a separate "viewed" field that does not displace `last_activity_at`). ## Suggested fix direction 1. Skip `archived`/`hidden` sessions when selecting the roster preview (`_latest_profile_session_row`). 2. Do not let preview/open interactions write `last_activity_at` without provenance (separate touch/view field, or provenance check). 3. Prefer the backend-computed `last_session` over the app-local index when they diverge (single source of truth for roster ordering). ## Workaround (used locally) - Mark ghost sessions `archived=1` in their profile `state.db` (data preserved), fully quit the app, clear Local Storage leveldb, restart. The pane then stays on the active sessions. Requires a manual DB edit — not user-friendly. ## Related - #88200 (BOTS sidebar preview shows wrong session content on click — closed via #88690; covers the pin/preferred path only) - #88340 (duplicate roster identities), #88341 (dedupe + canonical chats), #88690 (pinned canonical Bot Chat salvage) - #88918 (canonical Bot Chat stuck on 429), #89556 (re-opening focused session from Bots panel hangs), #89834 (clicking bot after group chat does not show the bot's chat)
signals.author: HORUS-71

signals.title: [Architecture] Desktop ownership must be sticky and generation-bound across multi-source operations
signals.text: ## Summary Hermes Desktop has crossed an important architectural threshold. With the recent multi-source work, it no longer behaves primarily as “one gateway with aliases”; it now has the foundations of a real multi-backend client: - registered-gateway switching from Sessions; - explicit `(connectionId, profile)` request routing; - background sockets retained across foreground changes; - per-source last-profile state; - Current-versus-Primary terminology; - atomic activation with lease/epoch-based publication; - packaged-build preservation of Nanostores batching; - adapter-owned messaging session namespaces; - source-aware Bot thread hydration; - truthful updater partial-completion/native-binding recovery. The next architectural problem is no longer route discovery. It is **ownership continuity**. Desktop increasingly establishes a qualified owner correctly, then some downstream layer treats part of that owner as optional metadata: it drops source/profile/generation, crosses an API boundary, and later reconstructs ownership from endpoint shape, foreground state, a bare resource/session ID, or whichever registration currently looks plausible. The proposed invariant is: > **Every Desktop operation and backend-owned object must retain the qualified owner and generation established when authority was obtained. No downstream layer may replace either dimension with foreground state, endpoint inference, bare-ID lookup, or a newly resolved registration.** This issue is a Desktop-specific architecture interlock. It does not supersede #88680, #90142, #90144, #90145, or the concrete implementation issues below. It connects them into the ownership model Desktop now needs as multi-source behavior becomes normal rather than exceptional. --- ## Why this deserves a Desktop architecture issue The repository already has the general rules: - #88680 — preserve Desktop connection × profile route identity end-to-end; - #90142 — qualified identity must become monotonically more specific, never less; - #90144 — proof scope must equal mutation scope; - #90145 — recovery/teardown must be fenced by durable generation identity. Desktop is where those rules now meet in one product architecture. A source-qualified route is not sufficient if a later filesystem call uses the foreground gateway. A qualified route is not sufficient if a stored session ID becomes bare UI identity. A connection/profile pair is not sufficient if an asynchronous completion from an older activation can still publish into a newer activation. A correct runtime route is not sufficient if persistence, authorization, outbound delivery, or repair tooling each reconstruct ownership independently. The Desktop contract therefore needs to make **qualified ownership + generation** one continuous property from creation/resolution through routing, resource access, persistence, UI identity, background work, replay, and teardown. --- ## Architectural model Desktop should distinguish these concepts explicitly: ```text Route identity = (connectionId, desktopProfile) Backend namespace = (backendId/transportOwner, targetProfile) Runtime identity = (transportOwner, runtimeProfile, activationGeneration) Durable resource identity = (backendOwner, persistenceProfile/store, resourceId, resourceGeneration?) Authorization identity = (owner, authorizationEvidence, authorizationGeneration) Foreground selection = pointer to one current route ``` The exact types can evolve. The important point is that these are **not interchangeable**. `connectionId` identifies a registered Desktop source. `desktopProfile` identifies the Desktop-facing route/profile the user selected. `targetProfile` identifies the backend namespace actually addressed, including alias cases. `backendId`/transport owner identifies the logical backend independently of foreground selection and, eventually, independently of mutable endpoint text. `activationGeneration` identifies the specific publication/activation incarnation that authorized follow-on work. A session/resource/job may then add its own durable generation or lineage where IDs can be reused or ownership can transfer. --- ## The defect class The common unsafe flow is: ```text 1. Desktop positively resolves qualified owner Q at generation G. 2. A downstream API keeps only a projection of Q. 3. Time/foreground/registry state changes. 4. The downstream layer reconstructs the missing dimensions. 5. The operation executes against Q2/G2 while behaving as though it still represents Q/G. ``` That reconstruction can be internally convincing. Every downstream subsystem may agree on the same reconstructed owner while the operation is nevertheless acting on the wrong source, profile, resource, credential domain, or generation. This is more dangerous than an obvious routing failure because the system can return success while mutating a valid but unintended backend. --- ## Concrete interlocks ### #89719 / #90048 — shipped route-identity reconstruction residual #89719 shipped the registered-gateway Sessions switcher and explicit `(connection, profile)` routing foundation. The important residual is tracked by #90048: after Desktop already has an exact registry `connectionId`, compatibility matching can reduce the descriptor to URL/SSH-host-shaped transport attributes and infer the source again. That is the canonical anti-pattern: ```text exact source identity -> weaker transport coordinates -> inferred source identity ``` Required rule: - existing explicit `connectionId` is authoritative; - do not overwrite it through post-dial inference; - legacy matching is permitted only for genuinely unqualified descriptors; - zero matches fail closed; - multiple matches fail as ambiguity; - duplicate URL registrations with distinct auth/header/org envelopes remain distinct; - same-host SSH registrations separated by port/key/path/profile remain distinct. This issue should treat #90048 as the concrete repair owner, not duplicate it. ### #89916 — resource facade ownership Filesystem and Git operations must use the same owner as the session, artifact, project, or resource that initiated them. The foreground route is a UI selection. It is not ownership evidence for background or pinned resources. Unsafe shape: ```text session/resource owner = source B / profile worker foreground route = source A / profile default filesystem facade = path + profile only result = facade re-resolves through source A ``` Required rule: > Backend-owned resource operations consume the resource's qualified owner, not `currentRoute`. This applies beyond filesystem/Git to any facade where a resource can outlive or differ from foreground selection. ### #89252 + #89860 — multiplex runtime identity #89252 should be restacked on #89860 and retain only the complementary architecture that is no longer duplicated. The remaining model is valuable because one overloaded `profile` field cannot safely represent all of: - transport owner; - runtime profile; - persistence profile/store; - durable outbound owner; - authorization evidence; - repair/migration identity. The requirement here is not merely to define those dimensions. It is to create a **canonical carrier** and keep it intact through every consumer that can affect routing, keying, storage, batching, replay, callbacks, authorization, or delivery. If a downstream consumer collapses the carrier back to bare `profile`, endpoint, credential environment, or current runtime state, the architecture has only moved the bug. ### #88764 — provisioning authority Enumeration and secondary activation are observation/use operations. They do not grant authority to install or provision a new local runtime. This is the authority-side complement of sticky ownership: ```text can observe source != can mutate installation can activate route != can provision runtime can enumerate profile != can acquire local installation authority ``` A multi-source client must not let discovery or route activation silently escalate into local provisioning because the intended source is absent, unavailable, or not yet materialized locally. Required rule: > Observation/use authority never widens into provisioning authority through fallback. ### #88095 and adjacent profile/session work — UI identity Same-ID sessions across profiles and sources are expected in a real multi-source client. Therefore: ```text sessionId ``` cannot remain sufficient identity for: - foreground session strips; - panes/tabs; - stored navigation targets; - React keys; - canonical chat pointers; - unread/activity state; - hydration caches; - open/resume actions. At minimum, UI/session identity needs the owner profile and source. Where ownership can transfer or IDs can be reused, it also needs lineage/generation. The UI must not become the layer that strips qualified identity immediately before a route-native backend operation. --- ## Generation is the missing temporal dimension Even `(connectionId, profile)` is not always enough. Consider: 1. route `(C, P)` activates as generation 41; 2. a background operation captures `(C, P)`; 3. C is removed/recreated, credentials rotate, P is reprovisioned, or activation is superseded; 4. `(C, P)` exists again as generation 42; 5. the old operation resumes. Name equality does not prove incarnation equality. The same problem exists for: - source registrations; - profile/runtime provisioning; - activation leases; - durable resource handles; - session ownership/lineage; - authorization evidence; - background sockets; - queued outbound delivery; - repair/recovery operations. The Desktop rule should therefore be: > **Qualified identity answers what owns the operation. Generation identity answers which incarnation of that owner authorized it. Both must survive until the mutation boundary.** For ordering-sensitive state, use monotonic epochs/revisions. For pure incarnation identity, a durable never-reused opaque token may be sufficient. --- ## Foreground state is a selector, not an owner Desktop now intentionally preserves background sockets/work while foreground selection changes. That makes this distinction non-negotiable. The following values are useful context but cannot be treated as ownership proof: - current gateway; - current profile; - Primary gateway; - last-used profile; - active renderer route; - currently connected socket; - endpoint/host that happens to match; - whichever source is uniquely reachable right now. Foreground state may resolve **new, genuinely unqualified user intent**. It must not re-resolve an object or operation that already has an owner. This should be visible in API design: resource/session/background-work APIs should accept an owner/reference, not implicitly consult foreground state. --- ## Proposed canonical carrier shape This issue does not require one giant universal type, but Desktop should converge on typed carriers whose projections are deliberate. Conceptually: ```ts type DesktopRouteRef = { connectionId: string desktopProfile: string } type RuntimeOwnerRef = { route: DesktopRouteRef transportOwner: string runtimeProfile: string activationGeneration: string | number } type ResourceOwnerRef = { runtimeOwner: RuntimeOwnerRef persistenceProfile: string storeId?: string resourceId: string resourceGeneration?: string | number } ``` Authorization may be attached separately rather than embedded directly: ```ts type AuthorizationEvidence = { owner: DesktopRouteRef | RuntimeOwnerRef grantId: string generation: string | number capabilities: ... } ``` The precise naming is less important than the invariants: 1. dimensions that determine ownership travel together; 2. generation travels with asynchronous authority; 3. serialization preserves enough identity for replay; 4. resource facades consume resource ownership rather than foreground state; 5. explicit identity cannot be overwritten by inference; 6. compatibility inference terminates at a named boundary and produces a qualified carrier. --- ## API rules ### 1. Resolve once Genuinely legacy/unqualified input may be resolved at an explicit compatibility boundary. ```text 0 matches -> unresolved 1 match -> qualified carrier >1 match -> ambiguous ``` No first-match or foreground fallback. ### 2. Explicit identity wins If a descriptor/reference already carries source/profile/backend ownership, that value is authoritative. Explicit-but-stale/unknown must fail closed. Do not discard it and search for a replacement owner. ### 3. Projections must be visibly lossy If an API needs only `targetProfile` or only a transport URL, project it locally while retaining the canonical owner in scope. Do not turn the projection into a new identity carrier. ### 4. Background work captures ownership at creation Queued work, sockets, session hydration, resource handles, callbacks, and outbound delivery should capture their owner when created. Later foreground changes must not alter their destination. ### 5. Mutation validates generation Before an operation publishes, writes, deletes, tears down, provisions, or otherwise commits state, verify that the captured owner generation is still current where the operation requires current ownership. A stale actor becomes a typed stale/no-op/retry result rather than mutating the successor generation. ### 6. Authority does not widen through fallback If the requested owner cannot perform an operation, Desktop may report that limitation or explicitly request stronger authority. It must not silently switch to a local/current/default owner whose capabilities are broader. --- ## Resource ownership audit The following Desktop surfaces should be audited for implicit foreground resolution or insufficient keys: ### Sessions/UI - session strips and panes; - stored session IDs/navigation; - hydration caches; - canonical Bot chat references; - unread/activity state; - open/resume/new-chat actions; - React keys. ### Resource facades - filesystem; - Git; - projects/workspaces; - cron/jobs; - attachments/artifacts; - settings that belong to a backend/profile; - plugin-managed durable resources. ### Transport/runtime - REST clients; - WebSocket/socket pools; - SSH connection/session ownership; - background reconnect; - activation publication/rollback; - runtime provisioning and teardown. ### Messaging/multiplexing - adapter-owned session namespaces; - batching keys; - callback/busy/clarify/control state; - durable outbound queues; - restored delivery/replay; - credential-owner/runtime-profile separation. ### Persistence/repair - route/session/resource serialization; - migration of legacy unqualified records; - repair tooling; - stale registration cleanup; - source recreation/rebinding. --- ## Adversarial regression matrix The architecture is not proven by a two-gateway happy path. Tests should deliberately collide the dimensions that old code assumes are unique. ### Source collisions - [ ] two registered URL connections share the same normalized endpoint but have distinct auth/header/org envelopes; - [ ] two SSH registrations share host/user but differ by port; - [ ] same SSH host/user/port but different key/path/profile ownership; - [ ] explicit `connectionId` remains authoritative under all collisions; - [ ] legacy unqualified descriptors fail on ambiguity rather than selecting registry order. ### Profile/resource collisions - [ ] same profile name on local + two remote sources; - [ ] same session ID on two profiles of one source; - [ ] same session ID on two different sources; - [ ] same resource/project/path-shaped identifier on different owners; - [ ] filesystem/Git calls continue to target the originating owner after foreground switches. ### Temporal/generation collisions - [ ] rapid route A → B → A with stale B activation completing last; - [ ] source removed/recreated while an old background operation is in flight; - [ ] credentials rotate without endpoint changing; - [ ] profile/runtime reprovisioned under the same names; - [ ] old resource/session handle resumes after successor generation exists; - [ ] stale cleanup/rollback cannot mutate the successor generation. ### Authority collisions - [ ] enumeration of a secondary source cannot provision a local runtime; - [ ] activation of a remote route cannot fall back to installing/starting a local same-name profile; - [ ] unavailable remote owner fails explicitly rather than widening authority; - [ ] authorization evidence for one owner/generation cannot be consumed by another. ### Background/foreground independence - [ ] foreground source changes while a background socket remains connected; - [ ] foreground profile changes while queued resource work executes; - [ ] two Desktop windows foreground different routes while sharing persistence; - [ ] background event/hydration result cannot attach to a same-ID foreground object owned elsewhere. --- ## Legacy migration contract Legacy Desktop state will contain records without full owner/generation identity. That state must remain explicitly **unqualified** until it is safely migrated. Do not interpret missing ownership fields as permission to use: - current foreground route; - Primary gateway; - newest registration; - endpoint equality; - only reachable source; - first registry match; - same-named profile; - bare session/resource ID uniqueness observed in the current snapshot. Those are migration hints, not proof. Safe options are: 1. exact one-time resolution followed by persistence of the qualified carrier; 2. read-only compatibility until ownership is established; 3. explicit user repair where ambiguity is real; 4. fail-closed behavior for destructive/mutating operations. Repair tooling from #89252 is particularly important here: ambiguity should be diagnosable and repairable rather than hidden behind fallback. --- ## Relationship to adjacent architecture issues This issue should link, not replace: - #88680 — Desktop route preservation and first-class route/resource identity; - #90142 — repository-wide monotonic qualification rule; - #90144 — proof scope equals mutation scope; - #90145 — durable generation fencing; - #90048 — concrete #89719 shipped residual around descriptor/source reconstruction; - #89916 — filesystem/Git resource facade ownership; - #89252 / #89860 — multiplex runtime/transport/storage ownership convergence; - #88764 — provisioning authority boundary; - #88095 —

signals.title: architecture(desktop): make route identity immutable, generation-bound, and resource-owned across multi-gateway Desktop
signals.text: ## Summary Desktop now has real multi-gateway routing, but the architecture still treats route identity as reconstructible metadata rather than an immutable authority proof. #89719 successfully shipped registered-gateway switching and broad `(connectionId, profile)` propagation across REST, WebSocket, sessions, messaging, cron, projects, settings, and status state. Background gateways retain sockets and continue work. That is the correct product direction. However, one review finding crossed into `main`: `resolvedConnectionId()` can take a descriptor that already corresponds to an exact registry route and reconstruct a weaker identity from URL or `user@host`, selecting the first match. Legal duplicate registrations can therefore alias: - identical URLs with different auth mode, headers, credentials, Cloud organization, or account; - identical SSH user/host pairs with different port, key path, remote Hermes path, or remote profile. Because the rest of the new source-aware machinery then follows that reconstructed ID consistently, the result is a particularly convincing split-brain: the system can be internally coherent under the wrong source identity. That concrete defect should be fixed, but it exposes a deeper class that needs an architectural contract rather than another matcher patch. ## Core design principle > Once identity becomes more specific, no downstream layer may make it less specific and later infer the missing dimensions from foreground, endpoint, transport, or mutable registry state. Exact route identity must be **sticky, monotonic, generation-bound, and resource-owned**. ## Current evidence ### 1. Exact route provenance already exists before transport details are lost The existing `desktop-remote-route` planner resolves registry provenance before URL normalization, OAuth, SSH tunnelling, or other transport steps discard distinguishing information. Its identity matcher includes the dimensions that actually distinguish legal registrations: - auth mode; - headers; - token envelope; - Cloud organization; - SSH host/user/port; - key path; - remote Hermes path; - remote profile. For non-primary matches it accepts only a unique result. This is the right place in the pipeline to freeze route ownership. ### 2. `resolvedConnectionId()` weakens that proof after the fact The compatibility helper added by #89719 reconstructs identity from: - normalized `baseUrl` for remote/Cloud; - normalized `user@host` for SSH. It uses the first registry match and its descriptor type does not make an already-resolved `connectionId` authoritative. This can overwrite the exact identity already established by the route planner. ### 3. Source scoping is broad, but ownership is still ambient in many consumers `hermesApi()` injects the renderer's currently active source into requests. That works for foreground-global actions, but existing resources such as sessions, cron jobs, projects, approvals, OAuth flows, artifacts, and files should execute against their **owning route**, not whatever route happens to be foreground when an asynchronous callback finally runs. This becomes load-bearing now that background gateways remain live across foreground switches. ### 4. Some namespaces are source-aware at transport boundaries but still bare internally Gateway event dispatch now compares composite source/profile scope, which is correct. But many downstream stores and transient maps still key by bare runtime/session IDs, with source provenance kept separately or inferred from the active route. Copied/restored Hermes homes can reproduce IDs exactly. Multiple registered gateways make those duplicate namespaces concurrent. ### 5. Source switching still relies on manual global-state invalidation `wipeSessionListsForGatewaySwitch()` explicitly clears sessions, cron, messaging, unread paint, transcript tails, artifacts, and other gateway-bound state. This works only as long as every new source-owned store is remembered in the wipe list. That is an omission-prone correctness mechanism. Multi-gateway state should be partitioned by route identity so switching changes the visible partition instead of destructively reusing one global namespace. ## The deeper class issues ### A. Identity proof is not monotonic A registered route and an unqualified legacy descriptor should not share one loose shape. Suggested direction: ```ts type ResolvedRoute = | { identity: { kind: 'registered' connectionId: ConnectionId connectionGeneration: number } profile: ProfileKey transport: TransportDescriptor } | { identity: { kind: 'legacy-unregistered' provenance: 'environment' | 'profile-v1' | 'settings-v1' } profile: ProfileKey transport: TransportDescriptor } ``` Only the legacy-unregistered branch may enter compatibility inference. A registered descriptor must never have its identity overwritten by a weaker downstream guess. ### B. Registration identity, physical backend identity, principal, and locator are conflated Desktop needs explicit equivalence relations for concepts that are currently easy to treat as interchangeable: - **registration identity** — saved `connectionId`; - **registration generation** — which endpoint/credential envelope that ID currently denotes; - **physical runtime identity** — backend installation / `installId`; - **authorization principal** — account, Cloud org, credential set, permission envelope; - **locator** — URL, SSH host, tunnel endpoint. These answer different questions. Two registrations may share a locator but represent different principals. Two locators may reach one physical installation. A registry ID can be edited in place to point at a different runtime. Physical sameness does not prove authorization equivalence. Callers should explicitly choose the relation they require instead of using a generic "same connection" test. ### C. The route algebra overloads omission, `local`, `primary`, and legacy fallback These are semantically distinct: - omitted / null connection selector; - explicit `local`; - registry `primary`; - `lastUsed`; - unknown or removed ID; - legacy profile-routed fallback. V2 routing should represent this structurally rather than through magic-string normalization. Suggested direction: ```ts type ConnectionSelector = | { kind: 'registered'; id: ConnectionId } // including `local` | { kind: 'legacy-primary' } ``` `primary` and `lastUsed` should resolve user intent into a concrete registered route **before** an operation begins. They should not be consulted later as fallback authority for an already-started operation. ### D. Gateway activation is coordinated but not one transaction A foreground switch currently spans independently changing facts: - registry entry and credential envelope; - resolved descriptor; - WebSocket URL; - opened socket; - active gateway pointer; - active profile pointer; - renderer connection descriptor; - ambient REST connection/profile; - cache invalidations; - `lastUsed`; - new-chat ownership. Descriptor resolution and socket activation should not be independent proofs. The activation path that actually prepares the socket should return the exact descriptor and identity used to establish it. The outcome should be typed and explicit: ```ts type ActivationReceipt = | { status: 'activated' route: RouteKey activationEpoch: number connection: HermesConnection socketInstanceId: string } | { status: 'already-active' route: RouteKey activationEpoch: number } | { status: 'superseded' | 'removed' | 'offline' | 'ambiguous' | 'cancelled' requested: RouteIntent current: RouteKey } ``` Only an exact successful receipt may authorize success side effects. This directly interlocks with #89586 / #89609: a declined activation must not resolve indistinguishably from a successful one, especially for same-source profile switches where comparing only `connectionId` proves nothing. ### E. A connection ID identifies a mutable slot, not an immutable route A registry entry can be materially edited while retaining the same ID. For example, `homelab` can change from endpoint/credential A to endpoint/credential B while stale callbacks, sockets, caches, and resources still carry only `homelab`. Material edits already trigger backend/socket recycling, which is necessary but not sufficient as the architecture grows. Introduce a monotonically increasing registration generation: ```ts type RouteKey = { connectionId: ConnectionId connectionGeneration: number profile: ProfileKey } ``` Every descriptor, socket, request, response, event, cache entry, persisted resource handle, and activation receipt should carry the generation. Results from an obsolete generation may finish but must not commit into the new generation's state. This closes ABA-style edit/remove/re-add races and makes descriptor/socket agreement provable. ### F. Ambient active-route state must not authorize mutations on existing resources Foreground-global actions can use the current route. Existing resources should carry their owner. Instead of: ```ts archiveSession(sessionId) ``` prefer: ```ts archiveSession({ owner: session.route, sessionId: session.id }) ``` The same principle applies to: - session mutations and hydration; - cron jobs and runs; - projects and repo/worktree operations; - approvals and input requests; - OAuth flows; - artifacts; - filesystem and Git operations; - background/tile/window actions. This directly interlocks with #89916: filesystem and Git facades need the same route identity as the resource/session that owns them, not merely the current foreground gateway. ### G. Resource namespaces must be source-qualified, not just transport-qualified The canonical resource identity should include route ownership: ```ts type ResourceKey = { route: RouteKey resourceId: string } ``` At minimum, audit and qualify: - runtime session IDs; - stored session IDs and lineage aliases; - unscoped stream pins; - approvals and input requests; - provider-wait / compaction / drafting state; - transcript tails; - unread/read watermarks; - pin mirrors; - cron job and run IDs; - project IDs and project scope; - artifacts; - OAuth flow/session IDs; - query and capability cache keys; - window/HUD/quick-entry session references. Unscoped events should be pinned per socket or `RouteKey`, never through one renderer-global ref shared by multiple retained gateways. ### H. Manual cache wiping should stop being a correctness boundary Gateway-owned state should be partitioned by route identity. Foreground switching should select another partition rather than globally clearing one namespace and hoping every source-owned store was included. Generation revocation can explicitly retire obsolete partitions after connection edits/removals, but ordinary switching should not require destructive global wipes. This also aligns state lifetime with the already-shipped behavior where background gateway sockets remain alive and continue work. ### I. Compatibility needs a versioned protocol and retirement path Absence of `connectionId` can currently mean too many things: - older Electron main; - environment-provided unregistered route; - genuinely local legacy route; - ambiguous registry match; - accidentally dropped exact identity; - failed lookup. Optional fields are not a sufficient compatibility protocol. Prefer an explicit versioned IPC contract: ```ts type ConnectionProtocol = | { version: 1; route: LegacyRouteDescriptor } | { version: 2; route: RegisteredRouteDescriptor } ``` A v2 registry-scoped call must produce a v2 registered route. Legacy compatibility should remain explicitly unregistered unless a unique, full-fidelity pre-dial match proves ownership. Compatibility paths should also expose diagnostics/telemetry so they can be retired rather than becoming permanent alternate authority models. ### J. Multi-window and registry-write concurrency need explicit semantics Desktop supports multiple full renderer windows while `lastUsed` and registry entries are global persisted state. Define and test: - whether `lastUsed` is installation-global, window-specific, or primary-window-owned; - what happens when one window removes/edits a connection another window is activating; - how concurrent registry mutations are serialized; - whether writes use a registry revision / compare-and-swap contract. A monotonically increasing registry revision should make stale write rejection explicit. ## Required invariants The architecture should eventually be able to state and mechanically test all of these: 1. Once exact registered identity exists, no downstream layer can replace it with inferred identity. 2. Registry ordering cannot affect route resolution. 3. Zero or multiple compatibility matches fail explicitly. 4. Socket route, descriptor route, REST route, UI route, and activation receipt agree on one `RouteKey`. 5. A same-source profile activation decline produces no success side effects. 6. Edit/remove/re-add during dial cannot publish an obsolete generation. 7. Old-generation responses/events cannot commit after generation replacement. 8. Identical resource IDs on two gateways remain independent. 9. Unscoped events on simultaneous retained sockets cannot cross-pin. 10. Explicit `local` never aliases omitted legacy-primary routing. 11. One stalled activation cannot permanently wedge later user intent. 12. Multi-window activation and registry edits produce a serializable result. ## Diagnostics / observability Every routed operation should be traceable without logging secrets. Include a correlation tuple such as: ```text connectionId connectionGeneration profile activationEpoch socketInstanceId requestId resourceId ``` A split-brain should be diagnosable from one trace rather than inferred from contradictory UI symptoms. ## Implementation sequence ### Phase 1 — immediate shipped defect - Treat an existing descriptor `connectionId` as authoritative. - Never overwrite it through post-dial inference. - Restrict compatibility inference to genuinely unqualified legacy descriptors. - Reuse the full-fidelity pre-dial identity contract from #88922 / #88697. - Fail closed on zero or multiple matches. - Add duplicate URL/auth/org/header and SSH port/key/path/profile witnesses. ### Phase 2 — canonical route identity - Introduce structured `RouteKey` with connection generation. - Distinguish registered routes from legacy-unregistered routes at the type boundary. - Make explicit `local` a real registered identity, never omission. ### Phase 3 — activation transaction - Return a typed activation receipt from the prepare/dial/publish path. - Return the exact descriptor used by the activated socket. - Consume activation verdicts at all callers before any success side effects. - Bound activation leases / unresolved IPC so one operation cannot wedge the switch coordinator indefinitely. ### Phase 4 — resource ownership - Add `RouteKey` ownership to sessions, cron, projects, OAuth flows, artifacts, FS/Git resources, and other durable/background objects. - Remove ambient foreground routing from mutations against existing resources. ### Phase 5 — route-partitioned state - Source-qualify cache/store keys. - Replace broad switch-time wipe correctness with route-owned partitions and generation revocation. ### Phase 6 — compatibility and concurrency hardening - Version the Desktop IPC routing contract. - Add compatibility diagnostics and retirement criteria. - Add registry revisioning / serialized write semantics. - Define multi-window ownership of `lastUsed` and route mutations. ## Acceptance / adversarial matrix The closing test matrix should include at least: - two URL registrations with the same normalized URL but different auth mode; - same URL with different token/header envelopes; - same Cloud URL under different org/account identity; - two SSH registrations with same user/host but different port; - different key path; - different remote Hermes path; - different remote profile; - exact descriptor `connectionId` survives all of the above; - ambiguous legacy descriptor returns no registered identity; - `(homelab, default)` -> `(homelab, research)` decline leaves route/caches/preferences unchanged; - edit connection generation while activation is in flight; - remove and recreate a connection ID while old work is still completing; - two gateways with identical stored/runtime session IDs; - copied Hermes home with identical project/job/session IDs on two active sources; - simultaneous unscoped stream events from two retained sockets; - explicit local operations while registry primary is remote; - two Desktop windows switching different sources and mutating registry state concurrently. ## Interlocks / provenance - #89719 — shipped registered-gateway switcher and broad `(connectionId, profile)` propagation; this issue is the architectural follow-through from the merged residual. - #88325 / @dokterdok — substantive source of #89719's fifteen-commit salvage; provenance remains preserved. - #88307 — product request implemented by #89719. - #88922 / #88697 — exact pre-dial route identity architecture that must remain authoritative rather than being weakened post-dial. - #89586 / #89609 — activation-verdict work: completion must prove publication, not merely promise resolution. - #89483 — adjacent atomic-publication work that exposed the need to distinguish prepared, activated, superseded, and declined states. - #89622 — lifecycle race witness around activation leases / target disposal. - #88095 — complementary foreground session/profile ownership work. - #89916 — resource facade ownership: FS/Git must follow the owning route, not ambient foreground state. ## Non-goals This is not a request to replace all compatibility code immediately or to break single-source Desktop behavior. The goal is to establish one canonical identity/ownership model so compatibility code is explicitly fenced and cannot weaken exact v2 identity. It is also not sufficient to solve this by expanding `resolvedConnectionId()` with more matcher fields. That repairs the current witness but leaves the defect class open anywhere identity can later be erased and reconstructed. ## Definition of done This issue is complete when Desktop can prove, by type contract and adversarial tests, that: - exact route identity never becomes less specific downstream; - mutable registrations are generation-bound; - successful activation returns an authoritative receipt; - every durable/background resource carries its owning route; - source-qualified resources cannot alias across gateways; - foreground switching does not determine ownership of already-existing resources; - compatibility inference is explicit, ambiguity-safe, observable, and retireable; - multi-window and registry mutation semantics are serializable and documented. The target architecture should make the current #89719 split-brain impossible to represent, not merely unlikely to reproduce.
