signals.title: [Bug]: Running kanban/tool workers are invisible in Desktop UI (session list filters them; Bots ACTIVE NOW ignores worker activity)
signals.text: ### Bug Description Long-running kanban worker runs (`hermes -p <profile> ... chat -q work kanban task <id>` spawned by the dispatcher) are completely invisible in the Desktop UI while they run: 1. **Session list:** worker sessions never appear in the SESSIONS sidebar. `tui_gateway/methods_session.py` hard-codes `deny = frozenset({"kanban", "tool"})` when building the session list, with no config override. For workers that run 10–30 minutes (coding tasks with test suites), the user sees no evidence that anything is running. 2. **Bots tab / ACTIVE NOW:** the per-bot "last active" timestamp and the ACTIVE NOW row only reflect bot **chat** activity (DMs / group acks). A profile whose kanban worker is actively running for 12+ minutes still shows "3 hr ago", and ACTIVE NOW lists only the chief. Verified concurrently: `ps` shows the worker process alive and mid-run while the Bots tab shows the profile as idle. Together this makes Bot Mode feel unresponsive/dead during exactly the moments it is doing its heaviest work — the user's only recourse is `hermes kanban list` in a terminal. Setup: Bot Mode v2 with 6 specialist profiles + default chief; Desktop (macOS) connected via **Remote gateway** to a central `hermes serve` on a Linux VPS (loopback + SSH tunnel); kanban dispatcher embedded in gateway. Possibly related (neighboring areas, none tracks this gap itself): #89756, #88897, #77829. _Report compiled with agent assistance; both symptoms verified live on our deployment._ ### Steps to Reproduce 1. Bot Mode v2 with at least one specialist profile; kanban dispatcher running. 2. Create a kanban task assigned to that profile with a long-running body (e.g. a code change with tests), let the dispatcher spawn the worker. 3. While the worker runs: SESSIONS sidebar shows no session for it; Bots tab shows the profile's last chat time (stale) and no ACTIVE NOW entry. ### Expected Behavior - Sessions sidebar: worker sessions with a live agent should be listable (ideally behind a config flag, e.g. `sessions.show_active_workers`, shown as their own group analogous to TELEGRAM/CRON JOBS, and hidden again once finished so the list is not flooded). - Bots tab: a profile should count as active (ACTIVE NOW + fresh "last active", possibly tagged "kanban") while a kanban/tool worker is running under that profile, falling back to the last chat timestamp when the worker ends. - Note: the second `deny` use in `methods_session.py` (TUI auto-resume) should probably keep excluding workers — auto-resume onto a worker session would be wrong; only the list surface needs the override. ### Actual Behavior While a kanban worker is running (verified via `ps`: `hermes -p coding ... chat -q work kanban task <id>` alive 12+ minutes): - SESSIONS sidebar shows no session entry for the worker. - Bots tab shows the worker's profile with a stale timestamp ("3 hr ago", from its last chat), and ACTIVE NOW lists only the chief profile. - No error output — the work completes fine; it is purely a visibility gap. The only way to see the running work is `hermes kanban list` in a terminal. ### Affected Component Other ### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related) _No response_ ### Debug Report ```shell Not attaching the automated debug-share upload (contains org config/log details we prefer not to publish). Key evidence inline instead: - `tui_gateway/methods_session.py` (v0.20.4): `deny = frozenset({"kanban", "tool"})` in the session-list builder (and a second, correct use in TUI auto-resume). - Observed 2026-08-19 ~22:35 CEST: `ps` shows `hermes -p coding ... chat -q work kanban task <id>` alive for 12+ min while Bots tab shows "Coding · 3 hr ago" and ACTIVE NOW lists only the chief; SESSIONS sidebar shows no entry for the worker session. Happy to provide targeted log excerpts on request. ``` ### Operating System Backend: Debian-based Linux VPS (kernel 6.x); Desktop client: macOS 15 (Darwin 25.5) ### Python Version 3.11.15 ### Hermes Version v0.20.4 (2026.8.18) ### Additional Logs / Traceback (optional) ```shell ``` ### Root Cause Analysis (optional) _No response_ ### Proposed Fix (optional) _No response_ ### Are you willing to submit a PR for this? - [ ] I'd like to fix this myself and submit a PR

signals.title: False-positive "TERMINAL_CWD found in .env" deprecation warning on every startup
signals.text: Every TUI startup prints this even though `.env` never sets `TERMINAL_CWD`: ``` ⚠ Deprecated .env settings detected: ⚠ TERMINAL_CWD=/Users/you found in .env — this is deprecated. ``` **Root cause** `warn_deprecated_cwd_env_vars()` in `hermes_cli/config.py` decides ".env sets TERMINAL_CWD" from the process environment alone. But Hermes exports that variable into `os.environ` itself at runtime: `gateway/run.py:2504`, `cli.py:8473` (session restore), `cron/scheduler.py:5087` (per job), `tui_gateway/server.py:12559`, plus the worktree paths in `cli.py:20298` and `hermes_cli/cli_commands_mixin.py:1287`. So any install where `config.yaml` keeps the default `terminal.cwd: .` (which doesn't count as "explicit" in the checker) warns on every startup, with nothing to migrate. The config-to-env bridge is not the setter either; it explicitly skips `cwd: .`. **Repro** 1. Clean `~/.hermes/.env` with no `TERMINAL_CWD` line 2. `config.yaml` with default `terminal.cwd: .` (or no terminal section) 3. Start the TUI after any code path above has run (gateway, session restore, cron) 4. Warning prints, and the suggested migration is a no-op **Fix** Gate the warning on what `.env` actually contains: read `HERMES_HOME/.env` and warn only when an uncommented `TERMINAL_CWD=` (or `export TERMINAL_CWD=`) line exists. Same for `MESSAGING_CWD`. Patch with a regression test is ready; PR to follow.
signals.author: tw-migz

signals.title: [Bug]: API server GET /health ignores API_SERVER_KEY while other routes require it
signals.text: ### Bug Description When the API server is enabled **and** `API_SERVER_KEY` is set, `GET /health` still returns HTTP 200 **without** an `Authorization` header. Other OpenAI-compatible routes on the same listener (`GET /v1/models`, `POST /v1/chat/completions`) correctly reject missing/invalid bearers with HTTP 401 (`gateway_auth_error`). Docs say `API_SERVER_KEY` is required for every deployment, including loopback. The unauthenticated `/health` route contradicts that and makes it easy for clients (and status checks) to think “the API is open” when chat is actually gated. `GET /health/detailed` **does** call `_check_auth`. The simple `/health` handler does not. Observed on Hermes Agent v0.20.2. Confirmed by reading `gateway/platforms/api_server.py` (`_handle_health` vs `_handle_health_detailed`). Intentionally **not** attaching `hermes debug share` output — it would include host identity, config, and logs. ### Steps to Reproduce 1. Enable the API server with a non-placeholder `API_SERVER_KEY` (loopback bind is enough). 2. Start the gateway so the API server is listening on the default loopback port. 3. `curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:8642/health` (no Authorization) 4. `curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:8642/v1/models` (no Authorization) 5. Repeat step 4 with `Authorization: Bearer $API_SERVER_KEY`. ### Expected Behavior Either: - `GET /health` requires the same bearer as `/v1/models` and `/v1/chat/completions`, **or** - docs explicitly mark `/health` as a public liveness probe (and clients such as the Raycast “API Server Status” command should not treat an unauthenticated 200 as “fully configured”). ### Actual Behavior - `GET /health` with no Authorization → HTTP 200 `{"status":"ok",...}` - `GET /v1/models` / `POST /v1/chat/completions` with no Authorization → HTTP 401 - `GET /health/detailed` requires the bearer ### Affected Component - Gateway (Telegram/Discord/Slack/WhatsApp) - Other (API server / OpenAI-compatible HTTP) ### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related) - N/A (CLI only) ### Debug Report Omitted on purpose (privacy). Reproduction is the curl sequence above against a stock loopback API server. ### Operating System macOS ### Python Version 3.11.x ### Hermes Version 0.20.2
signals.author: RaviTharuma

signals.title: [Setup]: install domain hermes-agent.nousresearch.com serving invalid TLS certificate (Let's Encrypt cert expired 2026-08-18) — Quick Install one-liner fails
signals.text: ### What happened The Quick Install one-liner from the README fails for all new users because `hermes-agent.nousresearch.com` is serving an invalid TLS certificate: ``` $ curl -fsSL https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.sh | bash curl: (60) SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate ``` ### Diagnosis The server is presenting a certificate from an unknown private issuer instead of a publicly trusted one: ``` $ echo | openssl s_client -connect hermes-agent.nousresearch.com:443 -servername hermes-agent.nousresearch.com 0 s:/O=NetAlerts/CN=hermes-agent.nousresearch.com i:/O=NetAlerts/CN=NetAlerts Services Verify return code: 21 (unable to verify the first certificate) ``` Certificate Transparency history (crt.sh) shows the domain's Let's Encrypt R13 certificate **expired 2026-08-18** (yesterday as of filing). A newer Let's Encrypt YR2 certificate was issued 2026-07-21 (valid to 2026-10-19) but does not appear to be deployed. The host (45.54.28.16, NetActuate anycast) now serves what looks like a hosting-appliance fallback cert ("NetAlerts"). Verified from two independent networks, and DNS answers are consistent across Cloudflare/Google resolvers, so this is server-side, not client-side. ### Impact - `curl -fsSL https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.sh | bash` fails (macOS, and presumably all platforms) - `iex (irm https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.ps1)` presumably fails the same way - Docs links (`hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/...`) fail with TLS errors - Risk that frustrated new users bypass verification with `curl -k`, which this incident shows is exactly the wrong habit to teach ### Workaround that worked Fetching the same script from the repo and running it locally: ``` curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/main/scripts/install.sh -o hermes-install.sh bash hermes-install.sh ``` ### Suggested fix Deploy the already-issued YR2 certificate (or re-issue) on the web host serving `hermes-agent.nousresearch.com`.
signals.author: AlexKlayy

signals.title: RFC: per-Bot credential grants — make credential access declared instead of emergent
signals.text: ## Summary Hermes has no first-class notion of a **credential grant** — a declared statement that Bot X may use credential Y. Whether a profile can reach a given secret is instead an emergent side effect of four unrelated mechanisms: 1. which `.env` file happens to hold the value (`<profile>/.env`, seeded empty at create), 2. whether the *shell environment* happens to hold it (fall-through), 3. whether someone symlinked `auth.json` between profiles (the pattern #19436 asks to bless), 4. whether `agent/secret_scope.py` is enforcing, which today depends on `gateway.multiplex_profiles` being on. Because access is emergent rather than declared, the system fails in **both directions at once**: credentials leak between profiles that should be isolated, *and* there is no supported way to deliberately share one — or to give a Bot its own login for a third-party service. This issue proposes making the grant explicit. It is an RFC: the mechanism below is a starting point, not a settled design. ## Evidence: both failure directions are live **Accidental sharing** — an open cluster, not isolated bugs: - #84079 — platform credentials from the default profile are applied to every profile, causing N-way turn fan-out - #66930 — bare profiles (no `.env`) inherit Matrix credentials from root `~/.hermes/.env` - #87722 — secondary-profile cron delivery escapes secret scope and uses default-profile credentials - #77969 — profile-scoped `.env` load overwrites process-global `os.environ`, clobbering other profiles' adapters - #71143 — cloned profile inherits platform bot tokens; second gateway serves the same bot - #83182, #83391 — cron delivery and the Channels page resolve the wrong bot token under multiplex **No supported deliberate sharing** — #19436 asks for `hermes profile create --link-auth <base>`, and today has to hand-roll `ln -sf` against `auth.json` and rely on `utils.atomic_replace`'s symlink-preserving behavior being load-bearing. That both classes are open simultaneously is the tell: the problem is not a bug in sharing or a bug in isolation, it is the absence of a place to *say which one you meant*. ## Current state (verified) - **Per-profile `.env`, seeded empty.** `create_profile` writes a `.env` at 0600 with the header *"API keys and tokens set here override the shell environment"* ([hermes_cli/profiles.py](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/main/hermes_cli/profiles.py) — the seeding block). The comment there records exactly this confusion: without the file, *"the profile silently inherited API keys from the shell environment — users reasonably read that as 'the new profile reads the root .env'."* Seeding an empty file makes the file exist; it does not make the fall-through stop. - **`agent/secret_scope.py` already implements the hard part.** It is a fail-closed, context-local, profile-scoped resolver: `set_secret_scope(mapping)` installs the active profile's secrets on a contextvar that propagates into worker threads, and `get_secret(name)` raises rather than falling back to `os.environ` when a scope is missing. **But** the fail-closed behavior is gated on `set_multiplex_active(True)`, which is only called at gateway startup when `gateway.multiplex_profiles` is set. Everywhere else — CLI, TUI, desktop, cron, Bot Mode — it transparently reads `os.environ`. - **`agent/credential_pool.py`** manages same-provider failover across multiple credentials and already reads through `secret_scope`. - **Bot Mode defaults to sharing.** Per the [Bot Mode guide](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/main/website/docs/user-guide/bot-mode.md): *"by default the new Bot shares one OAuth/token pool with the main profile, so credential refreshes cannot invalidate each other."* Sensible for provider keys; wrong as a universal default for third-party service logins. So the enforcement primitive exists and is good. What is missing is (a) a declared grant model to enforce *against*, and (b) enforcement outside the multiplex gateway. ## Why this matters beyond the bug cluster The industry model this is converging on is per-agent, incrementally granted access. xAI's [Grok Bot](https://docs.x.ai/grok-bot/overview) (launched 2026-08-11) frames setup as *"Create a Bot, message it, and grant access as needed"* — each Bot holds **its own logins** and its own browser sessions, and capability accrues through use rather than being configured up front. Hermes' Bot Mode is already close on the social model (persistent Bots, Bot Chat, group chats, routines, bot-to-bot messaging). Credentials are the axis where it is furthest away: a Hermes Bot cannot hold its own account for a service, and the default is to share the operator's pool. Closing this is worth more toward "a roster of specialists you actually trust with work" than any further creation-UX polish. ## Proposal (RFC) **1. Declare grants per profile.** A `credentials:` block in the profile's own config, naming what this Bot may resolve and where it comes from: ```yaml credentials: # Share the operator's pool — today's Bot Mode default, now explicit. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: { from: default } XAI_API_KEY: { from: default } # This Bot's own login. Lives in <profile>/.env, never resolved by others. GITHUB_TOKEN: { from: self } # Explicitly borrowed from a named profile (the supported form of #19436). SLACK_BOT_TOKEN: { from: profile, name: comms-bot } ``` with **deny-by-default**: a name not listed does not resolve, and never falls through to `os.environ` or the root `.env`. **2. Make `secret_scope` the universal enforcement point.** Decouple fail-closed behavior from `gateway.multiplex_profiles` and drive it from whether the active profile declares a `credentials:` block. Profiles without one keep exactly today's behavior, so this is opt-in and back-compatible; profiles with one get deny-by-default everywhere — CLI, TUI, desktop, cron, and gateway alike. This is a smaller change than it sounds because the call sites already route through `get_secret`. **3. Grant incrementally, in conversation.** The Grok-like half. When a Bot hits an ungranted name, the fail-closed raise should surface as a *request* — "this Bot needs `GITHUB_TOKEN`; grant from the shared pool, or add its own?" — resolved by the operator and written back to the grant block. This is the piece that makes per-Bot credentials usable rather than a config chore. **4. Retire the symlink pattern** by making `{ from: profile, name: ... }` the blessed form, closing #19436 without every downstream tool reinventing `ln -sf`. ## Open questions - **Where do grants live?** A `credentials:` block in `config.yaml` is discoverable but puts an access-control policy in a file the agent can edit — note #79030 (shell bypasses `patch`/`write_file` guardrails on sensitive config) and #70942 (`auth.json` missing from write-denied paths). A separate `grants.yaml` on the write-denied list may be safer. - **Migration.** Every existing profile behaves as `from: default` for everything. Is opt-in-per-profile enough, or does this need a `hermes profile grants audit` to show what each profile *currently* resolves before anyone flips it? - **Interaction with `credential_pool`.** Pool failover across several keys for one provider needs the grant to name a pool, not a single variable. - **Does `from: default` deserve to stay the Bot Mode default?** It is right for provider keys and wrong for service logins. Possibly the default should be per-key-class rather than global. - **Scope of enforcement.** Subprocesses spawned with `env=dict(os.environ)` are the classic leak path (#77969). Deny-by-default is only real if the spawn path is scrubbed too — that may be the largest slice of the work. ## Related - #19436 — native auth-sharing across forked profiles (the deliberate-sharing half) - #84079, #66930, #87722, #77969, #71143, #83182, #83391 — the accidental-sharing cluster - #21574 — per-user agent isolation and identity-based permissions - #78802 — principal-to-profile authorization for multiplexed gateways - #79030, #70942 — sensitive-config write guardrails, relevant to where grants are stored - #90319 / #90331 — agent-callable profile creation; a Bot created by an agent should be grantable the same way

signals.title: Bot Mode group threads share one stream and keep answering the previous topic
signals.text: ## Thread isolation in Bot Mode groups Bot Mode already mints thread ids, but the Workshop/Ops/Strategy pane is one stream and an in-flight member turn is not cancelled when the user starts another topic. Later speakers can still be fed an older thread's unread delta (seen 2026-08-19: Builder answering "keep working the UI / Opus" after Digitalinfra and `status` were already on screen). Expected: each thread is its own room — own log, own rounds, own watermarks. A new user send on thread B must not continue or re-prompt thread A. The UI should not flatten them into one conversation. This is separate from desktop-agent `send_bot_group` (PR #90392).

signals.title: reasoning_effort: ultra reliably triggers Response remained truncated after 4 continuation attempts
signals.text: ### Describe the bug With `agent.reasoning_effort: ultra` the agent reliably hits provider `max_output_tokens` and reports: ``` Response truncated (finish_reason='length') - model hit max output tokens ... Error: Response remained truncated after 4 continuation attempts ``` Reproduced on every non-trivial prompt — the model spends its single-turn token budget on the long chain-of-thought before the actual answer is emitted, so Hermes auto-continues 4 times and still never finishes the turn. ### To Reproduce 1. `~/.hermes/config.yaml`: ```yaml model: provider: opencode-go model: muse-spark-1.2-contributor base_url: https://opencode.ai/zen/go/v1 agent: reasoning_effort: ultra max_turns: 150 ``` 2. Restart the gateway. 3. Send any normal prompt (e.g. asking the agent to answer a question / do a small task) in desktop chat. 4. Observe 4x `Response truncated (finish_reason='length')` then final error `Response remained truncated after 4 continuation attempts`. ### Expected behavior Either: - `ultra` automatically raises `_ephemeral_max_output_tokens` / `max_tokens` for the turn so the thinking + answer fit in one continuation chain, or - the continuation budget is higher / progressive (so 4 retries is enough), or - docs warn that `ultra` requires a long-output model / higher cap. Currently the `ultra` preset is unusable with the default provider caps — the user is forced to drop to `medium`/`low`. ### Environment - Hermes Agent v0.20.4 (2026.8.18), install method `git`, Python 3.11.15, macOS 15.7.7 - Provider `opencode-go` / `muse-spark-1.2-contributor` (also affects other `custom`/OpenAI-compatible providers when `reasoning_effort: ultra`) - `agent.reasoning_effort: ultra` (confirmed via config get → `ultra`) - `gateway_timeout: 1800`, `agent.max_turns: 150` ### Related - #46833 — thinking models on `custom`/Ollama always truncate, truncation-retry fix PR #12152 (`_ephemeral_max_output_tokens` + progressive boost) — same symptom but `ultra` still reproduces - #9372 — `NVIDIA Build API z-ai/glm4.7 returns model hit max output tokens` — same `finish_reason='length'` loop - Community workaround repo `TENBIGTOES/hermes-ollama-truncation-fix` documents the identical `Response remained truncated after 3 continuation attempts` loop - Temporary workaround: set `agent.reasoning_effort` to `medium` and restart gateway (or add "简洁回答" to prompt) ### Additional context Happy to provide gateway logs / transcript if needed. The issue is deterministic with `ultra` — switching to `medium` immediately stops the truncation, switching back to `ultra` immediately reproduces it. Suggest wiring `reasoning_effort` into the ephemeral `max_tokens` boost so `ultra` automatically gets a proportionally larger window.
signals.author: scllqk

signals.title: [Bug]: Desktop multi-connection — remote file tree shows UNREADABLE (ENOENT) though the remote workspace exists and the agent reads it fine
signals.text: ## Bug Description In the new desktop multi-connection feature I registered two remote Hermes gateways (a Linux Proxmox LXC and a Linux notebook) and switch to them from the Sessions status-bar switcher. Chat and the agent work on the remote (it creates and reads files in the correct remote path). But the right-sidebar file tree shows **"Could not read this folder (ENOENT)"** for both remotes, and the automatic retry never recovers. ## Steps to Reproduce 1. Add two `remote-gateway` connections in Settings → Gateways (auth: OAuth/session cookie). 2. Switch to a remote gateway from the bottom status-bar gateway switcher (Sessions view). 3. Wait for the session to load; the agent/chat works on the remote. 4. Look at the right-sidebar workspace file tree → shows "UNREADABLE — Could not read this folder (ENOENT)". 5. The bottom status bar shows the correct remote cwd (e.g. `/home/rafpigna/Sviluppo/mailflow`), and that directory exists on the remote. ## Expected Behavior The file tree should list the remote workspace directory that the session reports and that the agent can access. ## Actual Behavior "Could not read this folder (ENOENT)" persistently, on both remotes; the local connection works. The agent, using the WebSocket session path, reads and writes the same directory successfully — so only the sidebar file listing is broken. ## Affected Component Other (desktop app — remote workspace file tree / file-ops routing) ## Messaging Platform N/A (CLI only) ## Debug Report Omitted deliberately: `hermes debug share` uploads conversation content and personal data that are not needed for this diagnosis, and the report here is very large. System, environment and version details are provided below. ## Operating System - Desktop app host: Windows 11 - Remote LXC: Debian 13 (Proxmox, unprivileged) - Remote notebook: CachyOS (Arch-based) ## Python Version 3.11.15 (desktop venv) ## Hermes Version - Desktop: v0.20.4 (dev/source build; renderer build stamp 2026-08-19 23:28 UTC) - Remote LXC: v0.20.0 - Remote notebook: v0.20.3 ## Root Cause Analysis Server side is clean: `hermes_cli/web_server.py` `_fs_path()` (web_server.py:2105) does not rebase the path — it requires an absolute path and only does `Path().expanduser().resolve()` — and `fs_list` (web_server.py:2847) returns `{"error": "ENOENT"}` only when `os.scandir(target)` raises `FileNotFoundError`. An existing remote path (the agent wrote and listed a file under `/home/rafpigna/Sviluppo/mailflow`) must therefore list successfully server-side. The failure is in the REST FS bridge routing: the file tree reads over `GET /api/fs/list` via the Electron `hermes:api` bridge, routed by `desktopFsProfile()` — `apps/desktop/src/lib/desktop-fs.ts:40-44` documents that "without the active profile, the Electron api bridge hits the primary (local) backend even when the user switched to a remote profile". The request appears to land on the local backend, where the Linux remote path does not exist → ENOENT. The agent path (WebSocket) routes to the remote correctly; only the REST file listing does not. ## Proposed Fix Make the `hermes:api` FS routing honor the active remote connection scoped by `$connection` (profile + baseUrl), instead of falling back to the primary/local backend, so `/api/fs/*` (list / read-text / write-text / read-data-url / git-root / default-cwd) resolve against the selected remote gateway.
signals.author: rafpigna

signals.title: [Bug]: Desktop spillover cache stores raw MCP JSON-RPC envelope instead of text content
signals.text:
## Summary When an MCP tool result exceeds the inline context budget, the desktop app's spillover cache (`~/.hermes/cache/spillover/`) writes the **raw JSON-RPC response envelope** to disk as a single-line JSON string — e.g. `{"result": "# Markdown content with \n escapes...", "structuredContent": {...}}` — instead of extracting and writing the actual text content. The agent then receives a 200KB+ one-line JSON blob that is hostile to pagination, `read_file` line-offset navigation, and any downstream markdown tooling. ## Reproduction 1. Configure a remote MCP server whose tools return large text payloads (e.g. a research archive server with a `read_guide` tool returning ~106KB of markdown, or `get_conversation_text` returning ~80KB). 2. Call the tool from a desktop chat session. 3. Observe the spillover file written to `~/.hermes/cache/spillover/call-<uuid>.txt`. ## Actual behavior The spill file contains the raw envelope: ```json {"result": "# Jac's Memex — Research Guide for Claude

You have access to...", "structuredContent": {"result": "..."}} ``` — 216,583 characters, **0 newlines**, 1 line total. The inner `result` string contains the real markdown with literal `
` escapes. `read_file` on this file returns one giant numbered line; offset/limit pagination is useless. ## Expected behavior The spill file should contain the extracted text content — i.e. the value of the `result` field (or the concatenated `text` of the MCP `content[]` array) — written as plain text/markdown with real newlines. That's what the agent actually needs to page through, and it's what smaller (non-spilled) results already deliver inline. ## Impact Any MCP workflow with large text results (research archives, document stores, conversation readers) hits this on nearly every call. The agent has to detect the JSON envelope, `json.loads()` it, extract the inner string, write a reconstructed file to `/tmp`, and then read *that* — pure overhead on every large call. ## Environment - Hermes Desktop (macOS 15.6.1), profile `default` - MCP server: remote HTTP (`https://…/mcp`), streamable transport - Model: moonshotai/kimi-k3 via nous ## Suggested fix In the spillover writer (wherever the oversized-result fallback saves to `~/.hermes/cache/spillover/`), extract the MCP text content before writing: if the result has a `content` array with `type: "text"` items, join their `text` fields; else if the JSON has a string `result` field, write that string directly. Write with real newlines, not JSON-escaped.
signals.author: jacmullen

signals.title: Desktop: messages sent to a WS-detached session after reconnect are silently dropped (no resume, no error)
signals.text: ## Summary After a transient WebSocket disconnect (laptop sleep / network blip — not a crash), messages sent **into an already-open session** are silently dropped: the client shows them as sent, but they never reach the backend (no `tui prompt accepted` in `gui.log`, no new row in the `messages` table), and **no error is surfaced to the user**. The session looks alive in the UI but is effectively dead. Distinct from #87920 (session view goes stale, but *sending a message recovers* via rebind) and #77127 (TOCTOU race between teardown and `session.resume`): here the resume/rebind path is **never triggered at all**, so sending a message does not recover the session — it disappears. ## Environment - Hermes Agent v0.20.3 (2026.8.16.2), git install - macOS (Desktop app, local backend via `hermes serve`) - Python 3.11.15 ## Timeline (from logs) | Time (local) | Event | |---|---| | 02:40:25 | WS closed: `client_disconnect(code=1006)`, `detached_sessions=3` | | 02:40:26 | WS reconnects (**1 s later — well inside the 20 s orphan-reap grace window**) | | — | No `session.resume` is re-issued for the previously open sessions after reconnect | | +20 s | Orphan reaper tears down the detached in-memory sessions (DB rows survive) | | hours later | User sends messages into the old session → **never reach backend**, no `prompt accepted` log, no DB row, no UI error | ## Log evidence (sanitized — localhost only) ``` 2026-08-19 02:40:25,692 INFO tui_gateway.ws: ws closed peer=127.0.0.1:57686 reason=client_disconnect(code=1006,reason=) messages=872 parse_errors=0 dispatch_crashes=0 send_failures=0 reaped_sessions=0 detached_sessions=3 2026-08-19 02:40:26,550 INFO tui_gateway.ws: ws accepted peer=127.0.0.1:61244 ``` After the reconnect there are **zero** `session.resume` / `tui prompt accepted` records for the detached sessions (checked `gui.log`), and the session's last DB message stays at the pre-disconnect timestamp — confirming the later sends never arrived. ## Root cause (source reading) - `tui_gateway/ws.py:429-476` — WS teardown detaches non-`close_on_disconnect` sessions and hands them to the grace-windowed orphan reaper. - `tui_gateway/server.py:1125-1163` (`_schedule_ws_orphan_reap`) — 20 s grace; a reconnect + `session.resume` that re-binds a live transport cancels the reap (comment: *"a quick reconnect / session.resume that re-binds a live transport cancels the reap"*). - The desktop client reconnects the WS transport but does **not** re-issue `session.resume` for sessions that were open before the disconnect — resume is only triggered on route change / explicit session selection (`use-route-resume.ts`, `use-prompt-actions/submit.ts`). The UI store still believes the session is live, so `submit.ts` takes the fast path (existing runtime id) instead of the resume path → the prompt is sent to a session the backend already reaped → silently dropped. ## Suggested fix directions 1. On WS reconnect, desktop should re-resume the sessions that were attached before the disconnect (or at minimum detect a dead runtime on submit and fall back to `session.resume`). 2. Surface a user-visible error/notice when a send fails to reach a live session instead of dropping it silently. 3. Backend could return a distinguishable error when a prompt targets a reaped/unknown runtime session. ## Related issues - #87920 — GUI session view goes stale on WS reconnect (different symptom: sending a message recovers the view) - #77127 — WS disconnect teardown race can close/orphan a session reconnected via `session.resume` - #53374 — Desktop creates new session after sleep (WS disconnect, session context lost)
signals.author: A2chitect

signals.title: `/reasoning off` hides thinking instead of disabling it, concealing that you are still paying for it
signals.text: ## Summary `/reasoning off` reads as "turn thinking off" but is the **display** toggle — it hides thinking from the transcript and leaves the model thinking (and billing) exactly as before. The actual disable is `/reasoning none`. The two spellings sit next to each other in the same command with no hint that they do unrelated things. ## Where Both the CLI and the gateway route `off` to the display branch: - `hermes_cli/cli_commands_mixin.py` — `if arg in {"hide", "off"}` → `display.show_reasoning = False` - `gateway/slash_commands.py` — documented as `/reasoning hide|off Hide model reasoning from responses` The effort disable is a separate branch reached only by `none` (or `false` / `disabled`), which produces `{"enabled": False}`. ## Why it matters This is a silent, self-concealing failure. A user who wants to stop paying for thinking types the most natural word for it, the thinking text disappears from their screen, and they reasonably conclude it worked — while every turn still spends reasoning tokens. The one symptom that would reveal the mistake is the thing the command just hid. It also masks unrelated bugs in the same area. #90412 fixed a Nous profile bug where a real `{"enabled": false}` was dropped before it reached the Portal; that bug was reported from the desktop app, where the toggle sets a genuine disable. It went unreported from the terminal for ~3 months, and `/reasoning off` hiding the evidence is a plausible reason why. ## Related inconsistency `off` means *disabled* when it arrives as config rather than as a slash argument: YAML parses a bare `reasoning_effort: off` to boolean `False`, and `parse_reasoning_effort(False)` returns `{"enabled": False}`. So the same word means "hide it" as a command argument and "disable it" as a config value. (A *quoted* `reasoning_effort: "off"` is a third behavior — `parse_reasoning_effort` returns `None`, i.e. fall back to the default and keep thinking.) Worth noting `/reasoning off` is not documented anywhere in `website/docs`; the docs only show `/reasoning none` and `/reasoning hide`. ## Suggested fix Pick whichever fits the project's taste: 1. Drop `off` as an alias for `hide`, so it either disables or errors with a pointer to both spellings. 2. Keep it but warn: when a user types `/reasoning off`, hide the display **and** print a one-line note that thinking is still running and `/reasoning none` is what stops it. 3. Make `off` disable the effort (matching the config-value meaning) and leave `hide` as the display toggle. Option 2 is the least disruptive and kills the footgun outright.
signals.author: OutThisLife

signals.title: [Feature] Upgrade pre_api_request to a Transform hook — allow plugins to override model/provider/base_url per request
signals.text: # [Feature] Upgrade `pre_api_request` to a Transform hook — allow plugins to override model/provider/base_url per request ## Summary `pre_api_request` currently fires per provider attempt but is **observer-only** — its return value is ignored. I'd like it upgraded to a **Transform** hook (like `pre_transcription` and the `transform_*` family) so plugins can override request-time routing parameters (`model`, `provider`, `base_url`, `api_mode`, and optionally `extra_body`) before the LLM call is dispatched. ## Motivation ### 1. Peak/off-peak provider routing (cost savings) DeepSeek introduced peak/off-peak pricing (2026-08-17): off-peak is half of peak. For a cache-heavy agent workload (≈99% prompt-cache hit rate, tens of billions of cached input tokens/month), the cheapest channel differs by time of day: - **Off-peak** → DeepSeek direct API (cache-hit $0.007/M, the lowest cache price anywhere) - **Peak** → OpenRouter / third-party hosts (flat $0.07–$0.14/M output, no peak multiplier; cheaper than DeepSeek's peak $1.32/M output) An agent that runs 24/7 can save ~30–40% monthly by routing per-request: DeepSeek direct during off-peak hours, OpenRouter during peak hours. Today this is impossible without either (a) a fragile monkey-patch of `AIAgent._run_agent_loop()`, (b) an external LiteLLM proxy, or (c) a restart-requiring config flip. ### 2. Provider switch aligned with context compaction (zero-cost cache loss) Switching providers invalidates the prompt cache (a cache lives where it was written). Context compaction also invalidates it. Aligning a provider switch with a compaction event means the cache-miss cost is paid exactly once — the switch becomes effectively free. With a mutating `pre_api_request` hook, a plugin can detect that the previous turn compacted (e.g. via context-length delta or the compaction state exposed to plugins) and switch providers at that exact moment. ### 3. Task-type routing (existing community demand) The community plugin Hermes ARC / `topic_detect` (routes conversations by topic/domain) currently has to monkey-patch internals because no hook can cleanly change the model before a request (see #23739). ## Proposed change Make `pre_api_request` accept a return dict that overrides the outgoing request's routing parameters: ```python def on_pre_api_request(**kwargs): # kwargs: task_id, turn_id, api_request_id, session_id, model, provider, # base_url, api_mode, request_messages, approx_input_tokens, ... if _is_peak_hour() and _just_compacted(): return { "model": "deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash", "provider": "openrouter", "base_url": "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1", } return None # no change ctx.register_hook("pre_api_request", on_pre_api_request) ``` Semantics proposal (aligned with the existing hook taxonomy in `docs/plugins/hook-taxonomy.md`): - **Observer behavior preserved**: `None` / empty return → no change (backward compatible). - **Transform behavior added**: return a dict → fields are applied to the outgoing request, last-writer-wins per field in registration order (same model as `pre_transcription`). - Fields: `model`, `provider`, `base_url`, `api_mode`, and `extra_body` (for e.g. OpenRouter `session_id` sticky routing). - Errors in one callback must not break others (same isolation as existing hooks). ## Why this over a dedicated "compaction hook" A compaction hook answers *when* to switch; a mutating request hook answers *how*. The latter is the prerequisite — compaction is just one possible trigger among many (peak/off-peak, task type, queue pressure, quota depletion). A single transform-capable `pre_api_request` covers all of them, including cases nobody has imagined yet. ## Related issues - #23739 — allow `pre_llm_call` plugins to override model/provider at runtime (same root need, different hook) - #43237 — `transform_api_request` hook: plugin-accessible request middleware (this issue is essentially a narrower, concrete version of that proposal) - #72662 — DeepSeek peak-hour rate multiplier for cost tracking (adjacent: accurate cost accounting per peak/off-peak) ## Prior art in-tree `pre_transcription` (STT) is already a Transform hook that applies `prompt`, `language`, and `model` from a returned dict. The LLM request path is the notable gap. ## Acceptance criteria 1. A plugin can change `model`/`provider`/`base_url` per request via `pre_api_request` return value without touching core. 2. Returning `None` keeps current behavior byte-identical. 3. Documented in `website/docs/user-guide/features/hooks.md` with the new return contract. 4. Works for gateway sessions, CLI sessions, and subagents (delegated tasks).
signals.author: 0gl20shk0sbt36

signals.title: sessions import discards tool_use arguments and tool_result content
signals.text: `hermes_cli/foreign_sessions.py` discards tool call arguments and tool output when importing foreign sessions, so imported conversations lose the file contents, command output, and web fetches that make them intelligible. There are two affected sites. **Site 1 — `_flatten_blocks`, Claude Code (line ~117):** ```python elif btype == "tool_use": # Claude Code assistant block name = block.get("name") or "tool" parts.append(f"[ran tool: {name}]") elif btype == "tool_result": # Tool output echoed into a user message — not typed input. continue ``` Arguments are dropped and results are skipped entirely, so a session renders as a run of bare `[ran tool: Bash]` markers with no indication of what ran or what came back. **Site 2 — `parse_codex_session` (line ~266):** the same `[ran tool: {name}]` flattening, and `custom_tool_call_output` / `function_call_output` / `local_shell_call_output` payloads are never handled at all. ### Impact Measured on a local corpus of 26 Claude Code sessions: 3,045 `tool_use` arguments and 3,045 `tool_result` payloads discarded (~13.7M chars). Imported content was 429KB against 3.9MB of recoverable material — roughly a 9x loss. Sessions whose substance is tool work import as near-empty shells. Two related problems: 1. Sessions whose only content is tool activity fail with `No user/assistant conversation turns found` (line ~342) and are not imported at all. 2 of the 26 were lost this way. 2. Claude Code writes oversized tool results to `<session-dir>/tool-results/<id>.{json,txt}` and leaves a pointer in the JSONL. The importer stores the pointer rather than following it (13 such sidecars locally, 764KB). ### Suggested fix Render `tool_use` as `[tool: <name>] <arg-summary>` and `tool_result` as `[tool result]\n<content>`, preserving the plain user/assistant alternation the importer already enforces — no fabricated `tool_calls` structures. Guard the volume: replace binary payloads with a placeholder (a printable-character ratio test works well; Claude `view` on a PDF otherwise dumps megabytes of noise) and truncate long results with an explicit marker. I have a working patch against `fab8479` doing exactly this, including argument extraction that prefers `file_path` / `command` / `pattern` / `url` and falls back to compact JSON. Happy to open a PR if the approach looks right. Note `tests/hermes_cli/test_foreign_sessions.py` asserts the current behavior in two places (`[ran tool: Bash]` at :129, `[ran tool: shell]` at :148) plus four turn-count assertions, so those move with the fix. All 9 tests pass with both updated. ### Environment Hermes at `fab8479`, macOS 26.4, Python 3.11.
signals.author: harshitsnghl

signals.title: [Bug]: Clean TUI shutdown logs an unhandled BrokenPipeError from _log_exit (unguarded stderr write on the peer-closed path)
signals.text: ## Summary On a normal TUI shutdown, the gateway child dies with an unhandled `BrokenPipeError` **inside the handler that reports the clean exit**. The process was already exiting, so nothing is lost — but every ordinary TUI close writes a traceback into `~/.hermes/logs/tui_gateway_crash.log`, which makes routine teardown look like a crash. ``` === gateway exit · 2026-08-19 12:23:47 · reason=stdin EOF (peer closed) === === unhandled exception · 2026-08-19 12:23:47 === Traceback (most recent call last): File "<frozen runpy>", line 198, in _run_module_as_main File "<frozen runpy>", line 88, in _run_code File "tui_gateway/entry.py", line 490, in <module> main() File "tui_gateway/entry.py", line 465, in main if not handle_spurious_eof(_recovery_times, _log_exit): File "tui_gateway/_stdin_recovery.py", line 111, in handle_spurious_eof log_fn("stdin EOF (peer closed)") # type: ignore[operator] File "tui_gateway/entry.py", line 252, in _log_exit print(f"[gateway-exit] {reason}", file=sys.stderr, flush=True) BrokenPipeError: [Errno 32] Broken pipe ``` ## Root cause `_log_exit()` (`tui_gateway/entry.py`) guards its **disk** write but not its **stderr** write: ```python try: os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(_CRASH_LOG), exist_ok=True) with open(_CRASH_LOG, "a", encoding="utf-8") as f: f.write(...) except Exception: pass print(f"[gateway-exit] {reason}", file=sys.stderr, flush=True) # <-- line 252, unguarded ``` The asymmetry is the bug. `_log_exit` is reached from `handle_spurious_eof()` (`_stdin_recovery.py:111` and `:100`) on the `return False` paths — i.e. *precisely when the peer has closed the pipe*. When the TUI parent tears down the child, stdin **and** stderr go away together, so the one function whose entire job is "record that the peer closed" writes to a descriptor the peer just closed. The exception escapes `_log_exit` → `handle_spurious_eof` → `main()` and terminates the interpreter as an unhandled exception. ## Reproduction 1. Run the TUI gateway (`hermes --tui`, or the desktop app). 2. Close it normally. 3. `tail ~/.hermes/logs/tui_gateway_crash.log` Every clean shutdown produces the `SIGHUP → SIGTERM → gateway exit (stdin EOF) → unhandled exception` sequence. Not a regression or a one-off — same failure on this host at `2026-06-01 15:07:38` under an older build, at the then-current line `entry.py:192` in the same `print(...)` statement. The surrounding `_stdin_recovery` refactor since then moved the line numbers but preserved the unguarded write. ## Expected A clean shutdown should not emit a traceback. `_log_exit` is a best-effort logger and should be total. ## Suggested fix Guard the stderr write the same way the file write already is: ```python try: print(f"[gateway-exit] {reason}", file=sys.stderr, flush=True) except (BrokenPipeError, ValueError, OSError): pass ``` (`ValueError` covers a closed-file `sys.stderr`; `OSError` is the `EPIPE`/`EBADF` superclass.) Worth auditing sibling best-effort log helpers on the shutdown path for the same unguarded-stderr shape. ## Environment - Hermes Agent v0.20.4 (2026.8.18), install method `git` - macOS (Darwin 27.0.0), arm64 - Python 3.11.15 (bundled `.hermes-runtime`) - Backend: local; source: TUI gateway child spawned by the TUI parent *(Paths in the traceback above are relative to the install root; absolute user paths redacted.)*
signals.author: bhino50

signals.title: [Proposal]: Unify Desktop Preview and Browser into a human-agent Workspace Viewer
signals.text: ## Summary Hermes Desktop now has several strong but separate content and browser-adjacent experiences: - a preview rail for files and generated artefacts - rendered Markdown, source, diff and editing - image and PDF viewers - inline audio and video players in chat - a persistent in-app Browser webview with address bar, history, console and DevTools - `open_preview` / `read_preview` for the agent - separate `browser_*` / `browser_exec` automation backends The individual pieces are useful, but the product model is fragmented. A non-technical user should not need to understand whether something is a preview, artefact, attachment, webview or separate agent-browser session. A developer should not lose console, source, diff, DevTools or browser-routing control in order to get a simpler default experience. This issue proposes a product direction for feedback before implementation: evolve the existing preview rail into one cohesive, progressively disclosed **Workspace Viewer**, with explicit human/agent control handoff for visible browser work. ## Current behaviour and gap The URL mode in the preview rail is already a real persistent Electron `<webview>`: - address bar, back/forward/reload - console and DevTools - persistent cookies through `persist:hermes-preview` - agent-side open and read access However: 1. The visible Browser is still architecturally separate from semantic agent browser automation. 2. URL browsing is a singleton surface, while files and artefacts use separate preview tabs. 3. Audio and video play inline in chat but are not dedicated preview-tab file types. 4. There is no explicit **Take control / Return to Hermes** ownership contract for login, CAPTCHA, 2FA or other human-only steps. 5. The visible UI exposes the implementation history rather than one mental model for “what I am viewing or working on”. 6. On macOS, a live test found that 1Password Universal Autofill did not work inside the Hermes Browser webview, so login cannot currently rely on ordinary app-level autofill. ## Proposed product direction Present the surface to users as one **Viewer** while retaining advanced capabilities through progressive disclosure. ### Ordinary-user default - A visible **Open Viewer** entry offers **Browse the web**, **Open a file** and **View recent output**. - Websites, Markdown, documents, images, PDFs, media and generated artefacts open in one consistent tabbed surface. - Controls are content-aware rather than universal clutter. - A web tab clearly shows either **Hermes is working** or **Your turn**. - The user can choose **Take control**, complete a login or verification step, then choose **Return to Hermes**. - Infrastructure terms such as CDP, webContents IDs, providers and capability manifests stay out of the default flow. ### Developer and power-user disclosure - rendered/source/diff/edit modes - console and DevTools - viewport presets - inspect element or selected source lines → add to chat - multiple tabs and restored workspaces, once exact tab identity is safe - optional browser-source selection: visible Viewer, isolated local browser, cloud browser or explicitly granted existing profile - exact session/target diagnostics under Advanced The intent is not to remove technical control. It is to hide it until requested. ## Human/agent ownership contract A visible authenticated browser needs one unambiguous owner at a time. Suggested states: - human - agent active - waiting for human - verifying handoff - blocked/disconnected Suggested flow: 1. Hermes works visibly in the bound tab. 2. A human-only step is detected or requested. 3. The tab changes to **Your turn** and agent mutation authority is revoked. 4. The user completes the step without exposing credentials to the model. 5. The user selects **Return to Hermes**. 6. Hermes performs a read-only verification and resumes only if the exact tab generation is still valid. Once a turn is bound to the visible Viewer, failure must not silently route actions to a different local, cloud or headless browser. ## Security constraints - Exact profile, conversation, window, tab, webContents and generation binding. - UI ownership state must be backed by runtime enforcement. - Stale, closed, navigated or replaced tab capabilities fail closed. - Passwords, OTPs and passkeys must never cross model context, tool arguments/results, transcripts, logs or clipboard. - Existing-profile and site access remain explicit opt-ins. - Multiple tabs should come only after exact identity and ownership are proven. - Authentication may require a native user-initiated credential broker if OS/browser autofill cannot work, but that should be scoped separately after the ownership direction is accepted. ## Suggested staged delivery This is intentionally not proposed as one large PR. 1. **UX proposal/prototype:** validate mixed-content tabs and human handoff language. 2. **Cohesive Viewer shell:** discoverable open action, consistent tab chrome and audio/video file tabs, without changing automation authority. 3. **Ownership state machine:** Take control / Return to Hermes with fail-safe lifecycle. 4. **Read-only exact-tab bridge:** URL, title, snapshot, text and screenshot. 5. **Bounded visible mutations:** click, non-secret type, press, scroll and navigation. 6. **Authentication assistance:** separately scoped, user-initiated and secret-safe. 7. **Multiple web tabs and expert routing:** only after identity/ownership are mature. Each stage should be independently reviewable and useful. ## Relationship to existing work - #69951 asked for an in-app browser pane driven by browser tooling. The visible pane now exists; the agent-control half remains unresolved. - #89146 covers the narrow Open Browser discoverability gap and should retain ownership of that slice. - #84000 and PRs #85351 / #88203 explore a Chrome-extension shared-control lane. That is complementary but does not automatically bind the Desktop preview webview. - #89602 documents the macOS platform-passkey limitation in the embedded Browser. - #71375 covers browser-tool tab management rather than the Desktop Viewer product model. This proposal should build on those owners rather than replace or duplicate their work. ## Direction questions for maintainers 1. Is the current preview rail intended to evolve into a first-class mixed-content Viewer, or should the visible Browser remain a lightweight preview surface? 2. Should semantic agent browser automation eventually bind to the visible Desktop webview, or should visible human-assisted browsing remain a Chrome-extension/external-browser concern? 3. Does an explicit human/agent ownership contract fit the desired Desktop architecture? 4. Would the team prefer an interactive UX prototype/RFC before any production PRs? 5. If the direction is welcome, which narrow slice should be pursued first while preserving the existing issue/PR owners? ## Acceptance criteria for this issue This issue is successful if it produces architectural and product-direction feedback. It is not requesting approval for a platform-sized implementation in one PR.
signals.author: ctaylor86

signals.title: codex_app_server runtime reintroduces #15561: a failed turn returns without `failed: true`, so /v1/runs emits run.completed with empty output and zero usage
signals.text: **Version:** hermes-agent 0.20.3 ## Summary #15561 fixed `run.completed`-on-failure for results produced by `run_agent` / `conversation_loop`, by having `_handle_runs` branch on `result["failed"]`. The `codex_app_server` runtime reintroduces the same false-green through a different producer: it reports a failed turn via `completed: False` + `error`, and never sets `failed: True`. The result is a run that terminates as: ```json {"event": "run.completed", "run_id": "run_…", "output": "", "usage": {"input_tokens": 0, "output_tokens": 0, "total_tokens": 0}} ``` with `GET /v1/runs/{id}` reporting `status: "completed"`, `last_event: "run.completed"`, and no `error` — for a turn that failed and produced nothing. ## Impact Any orchestrator that drives Hermes through the API server records a successful run that did no work. For scheduled or unattended agents this is the worst available failure mode: the cadence keeps reporting green, the provider error never surfaces, and no downstream check fires. It is also silent in exactly the situation you most want a signal — the moment a healthy deployment first hits a dead or exhausted provider credential. `run.failed` works correctly for the same underlying fault when the turn is handled by `conversation_loop`, so the symptom is intermittent and looks like flakiness rather than a contract gap. ## Root cause **Producer** — `agent/codex_runtime.py`, terminal return (0.20.3: L917-940, `final_response` at L925): ```python return { "final_response": turn.final_text, # "" when the turn errored "messages": messages, "api_calls": api_calls, "completed": not turn.interrupted and turn.error is None, # False "partial": turn.interrupted or turn.error is not None, # True "interrupted": _user_interrupted, "error": turn.error, # the error IS carried ... # but no "failed": True } ``` Reached after the `should_retire` handler (L806-820) has already logged the turn error: ``` WARNING agent.codex_runtime: codex app-server session retired (turn error: <provider error>) ``` **Consumer** — `gateway/platforms/api_server.py`, `_handle_runs` (0.20.3: L6953, L6968): ```python elif isinstance(result, dict) and result.get("failed"): -> run.failed else: final_response = result.get("final_response", "") if isinstance(result, dict) else "" -> run.completed, output=final_response, usage=usage ``` `completed: False` and a non-null `error` are both ignored, so the result falls to the `run.completed` branch and `final_response` defaults to `""`. `agent/conversation_loop.py` does set `failed: True` on its failure paths, which is why #15561's fix holds there and not here. ## Reproduction ### Unit-level (no credentials required) Feed a `codex_app_server`-shaped result through the terminal branch of `_handle_runs`: ```python result = { "final_response": "", "messages": [], "api_calls": 1, "completed": False, "partial": True, "interrupted": False, "error": "turn ended status=failed: <provider error>", } usage = {"input_tokens": 0, "output_tokens": 0, "total_tokens": 0} # expected: run.failed, error preserved # actual: run.completed, output="", usage.total_tokens=0 ``` ### Observed end to end On an API-server lane configured with `model.openai_runtime: codex_app_server`, against a provider whose credential had been revoked server-side: - run terminated `completed` / `output: ""` / `total_tokens: 0`, at the same second the journal logged `agent.codex_runtime: codex app-server session retired (turn error: Codex authentication failed …)`; - a subsequent run against the identical fault was handled by `conversation_loop` (`ERROR agent.conversation_loop: Non-retryable client error: 401`) and correctly emitted `run.failed`. Observed twice. It is not currently forceable on demand from our side: once the credential is fully revoked, the auth gate short-circuits ahead of the codex transport and every run takes the correctly-failing `conversation_loop` path. Reaching the faulty path needs a codex turn that *starts* and then errors — e.g. a mid-turn child failure or a tripped post-tool watchdog, both of which set `should_retire`. We are filing on the code analysis rather than holding for a live recipe; the producer/consumer behaviour above was verified against the pinned 0.20.3 sources. ## Suggested fix — both sides **1. Producer.** Have the `codex_app_server` terminal return set `"failed": True` whenever `turn.error` is not None, matching the contract `conversation_loop` already follows. **2. Consumer defence.** In `_handle_runs`, do not emit `run.completed` when `error` is non-null or `completed` is `False`, even if a runtime omitted `failed`: ```python elif isinstance(result, dict) and ( result.get("failed") or result.get("error") or result.get("completed") is False ): -> run.failed ``` Either change alone closes the observed case. We'd argue for both: #15561 chose the narrow producer-flag check, and this issue is that decision regressing the moment a second runtime reached the same consumer. A terminal status that downstream automation trusts should not depend on every current and future runtime remembering to set one optional key. Related: #15561 (closed, same class, `conversation_loop` producer), #71633 (`codex_app_server` bypasses `fallback_providers` on billing/quota failures — adjacent, same runtime, distinct defect).
signals.author: dialthewolff

signals.title: /v1/runs has no channel to deliver a run-scoped secret to the run environment — credentials can only travel as model context
signals.text: **Version:** hermes-agent 0.20.3 ## Summary `POST /v1/runs` has no channel for delivering a per-run secret to the run's execution environment. Every field it accepts — `input`, `instructions`, `conversation_history`, `previous_response_id`, `session_id` — is model context: prompted, persisted to the session transcript, and logged. The only credential on the wire today is the caller's own `API_SERVER_KEY`, which authenticates the caller to Hermes and is not usable as the run's identity to a third system. Orchestrators that wake Hermes through the API server need the run to hold a short-lived, run-scoped credential for calling *back* into the orchestrator. Without a secret channel the options are all bad: bake one static credential into the Hermes host environment and lose per-run scoping, or push the token through `input`/`instructions` and put a bearer token into prompts, transcripts and logs. ## Why this is not solvable client-side The natural workaround — putting the token in the run payload — is the thing that must not happen. Concretely, in the Paperclip gateway adapter (paperclipai/paperclip#9956), the run body already carries runtime identity as prompt text: ``` Paperclip runtime identity: - Agent ID: … - Company ID: … - Run ID: … - Paperclip API URL: … ``` along with an instruction to use an API key "when a Paperclip API key is available" — a key that has nowhere to arrive from. If that gap is closed by threading the token through the same payload surface, the 401s stop and a run-scoped bearer token starts landing in model context instead. That is a worse outcome than the bug. ## Ask A dedicated write-only field on run creation, e.g.: ```json POST /v1/runs { "input": "…", "instructions": "…", "secrets": { "PAPERCLIP_API_KEY": "<run-scoped token>" } } ``` with these properties: 1. **Injected into the run's process environment**, not into the prompt, system prompt, or conversation history. 2. **Never persisted** to the session transcript or state store. 3. **Never echoed** — absent from `GET /v1/runs/{id}`, from every SSE frame on `/v1/runs/{id}/events` including error and status events, and from server logs at any level. The server should redact on the way in rather than relying on callers to avoid reading it back. 4. **Run-scoped lifetime** — dropped when the run terminates, not inherited by a later run that resumes the same `session_id`. 5. **Bounded by operator policy** — an allowlist of injectable variable names in gateway config, so an API-key holder cannot set arbitrary environment variables (e.g. `PATH`, `LD_PRELOAD`) in the Hermes host process. Names outside the allowlist should be rejected explicitly rather than silently dropped. Point 5 matters as much as the others: an unrestricted env-injection field would be a privilege-escalation surface, turning "can create runs" into "can influence how the host executes them". ## Related - paperclipai/paperclip#9956 — the downstream symptom: every orchestrator callback from a gateway-executed agent returns 401, because no channel delivers the run-scoped credential. - #2971 — structured run events and resumable interactions on the API server (adjacent surface, distinct ask). Filed separately from the per-run execution-context proposal because this one is a credential-handling boundary rather than an ergonomics gap, and the two should not share a design review.
signals.author: dialthewolff

signals.title: [Enhancement] Structured per-run execution context for /v1/runs: task metadata, cwd, and policy-bounded execution options
signals.text: **Version:** hermes-agent 0.20.3 ## Summary `POST /v1/runs` accepts `input`, `instructions`, `session_id`, `conversation_history`, `previous_response_id` and a model route. Anything else a caller needs to vary *per run* has no field to travel in, so it must either be flattened into the prompt or pinned lane-wide in `config.yaml`. That forces a one-lane-per-posture deployment model: every group of runs that differs in working directory, toolset, or turn budget needs its own gateway process, its own `HERMES_HOME`, and its own port. For an orchestrator driving a handful of differently-configured agents, most of the operational benefit of a shared worker disappears. Three related gaps, filed together because they all stem from the same missing abstraction. ## The governing invariant Stated first because it should shape the design rather than be bolted on: > **A client may restrict the capabilities already granted to a gateway lane, but may never widen them.** And: **prefer explicit rejection over silent narrowing.** If a lane permits `[terminal, file]` and a run requests `[terminal, file, browser]`, the request should be rejected — not silently reduced to `[terminal, file]`. Silent narrowing means a caller cannot distinguish "applied" from "ignored", which is how a run quietly does less than the operator's automation believes it did. This applies uniformly to every field below: cwd roots, toolsets, numeric limits, model routes, approval posture. The property to preserve is that holding an `API_SERVER_KEY` grants no authority the operator did not already grant the lane. ## 3a — Run/task/wake metadata There is no structured channel for caller-side correlation identifiers. A client can push them into the prompt (and today's clients do), but nothing the *tools* run by the agent can read, and nothing that lets agent-side logs be correlated to an orchestrator run without parsing free text. `Idempotency-Key` carries a correlation id on the wire but reaches nothing inside the run. **Ask:** a `context` object on run creation, exposed to the run as environment variables under a reserved prefix: ```json {"context": {"run_id": "…", "task_id": "…", "wake_reason": "…", "payload": {...}}} ``` Non-secret by definition — anything sensitive belongs in the separate secrets channel (#90438), not here. ## 3b — Working directory and workspace Every run on a lane inherits that lane's single `terminal.cwd`. Concurrent runs therefore share a working directory and can collide on files, and a run that needs a specific checkout cannot be expressed without standing up a dedicated lane. **Ask:** `cwd`, and optionally `worktree`, on run creation. **Bounded by:** an operator-configured allowlist of permitted roots. A `cwd` outside the allowlist is rejected with a clear error, never clamped to the lane default — silently running in the wrong directory is worse than failing. ## 3c — Constrained execution options Toolsets, max turns, checkpoints and reasoning effort are all lane-wide today. Toolsets come from `platform_toolsets.api_server`; turn limits and checkpoints from `config.yaml`. **Ask:** an `options` object on run creation covering at least toolsets, max turns, checkpoints and reasoning effort. **Bounded by:** - `options.toolsets` must be a **subset** of the lane's configured toolsets. A name the lane does not permit is a rejection, not a silent drop. - Numeric limits capped at the lane's configured maximum; a request above the cap is rejected. - If approval mode ever becomes per-run, it may only tighten relative to the lane setting, never loosen it. ## Related: a route-conflict rough edge Adjacent and cheap to fix alongside this. `_handle_runs` calls `_request_route_conflict_error(...)`, which rejects a request that supplies `model`/`provider` together with a `session_id`. Since a client using session continuity always sends `session_id`, the one per-run override that *is* supported is unusable in that mode — the request comes back as a route conflict rather than as a clear statement of the rule. Either allow `model` alongside `session_id` when the session is new, or return an error that names the constraint explicitly. ## Related issues - #90438 — run-scoped secret delivery. Deliberately **not** part of this proposal: credential handling is a different security boundary and should not share a design review with per-run ergonomics. - #2971 — structured run events and resumable clarify/approval interactions. - paperclipai/paperclip#7899 — the same per-run env expectation, unmet in a different adapter, which suggests the gap is not specific to one client. ## Context Found while evaluating the Hermes API server as an execution backend for an orchestrator that currently shells out to `hermes chat` locally. The local CLI expresses all of the above per invocation (`--in`, `-t`, `--max-turns`, `--checkpoints`, plus process environment); the API server expresses none of it per run. Closing that gap is what would make the API server a drop-in replacement for the CLI path rather than a differently-shaped one.
signals.author: dialthewolff

signals.title: fix: tighten AgentMail API key regex to avoid false positives
signals.text: ## Summary The secret redaction pattern for AgentMail API keys was too broad, causing ordinary identifiers like "am_example_identifier" to be falsely masked as secrets. ## Root Cause The regex pattern matched any 10+ alphanumeric characters after "am_", which is a common pattern for generic identifiers. ## Fix Changed the pattern to which: - Requires lowercase hex characters only (real AgentMail keys use hex format) - Requires 32+ characters after the prefix (reducing false positives) ## Test Plan - [x] Verified safe identifiers like "am_example" are not redacted - [x] Verified real AgentMail-like keys (32+ hex chars) are still redacted - [x] All 56 existing redaction tests pass Closes NousResearch/hermes-agent#10983
signals.author: nightq

signals.title: [security] fix(vision): enforce URL safety in media downloads
signals.text: ## Summary This PR hardens the vision media download boundary so the concrete download helpers enforce the same private/internal URL policy as their public validators. It addresses a residual helper-level variant of the vision/media SSRF hardening family: the public wrappers validate with `tools.url_safety.is_safe_url()`, but the lower-level helpers that open outbound HTTP connections did not enforce that central policy before the initial request. - Adds a shared pre-connect URL-safety guard for image and video downloads. - Keeps redirect-target revalidation for both media types using the same guard. - Adds regression tests proving loopback URLs are rejected before an HTTP client is opened. ## Security issues covered | Issue | Impact | Severity | |-------|--------|----------| | Vision media download helpers did not enforce `is_safe_url()` before the initial fetch | A direct or future caller of `_download_image()` / `_download_video()` could bypass the central private/internal URL policy and fetch loopback or metadata-style targets | Medium / defense-in-depth | ## Before this PR - `_validate_image_url()` rejected private/internal URLs with `tools.url_safety.is_safe_url()`. - `_download_image()` and `_download_video()` only applied `check_website_access()` before the initial request. - The helper comments described SSRF protection, but the initial helper fetch itself did not enforce the central private/internal URL policy. - Redirect targets were checked, but the first request URL was not checked at the helper boundary. ## After this PR - `_download_image()` rejects unsafe image URLs before constructing an `httpx.AsyncClient`. - `_download_video()` rejects unsafe video URLs before constructing an `httpx.AsyncClient`. - Redirect checks for both helpers use the same shared `_ensure_safe_download_url()` helper. - Regression tests lock in that loopback URLs do not open a client connection. ## Why this matters Hermes Agent already has a central SSRF policy for private, loopback, link-local, and metadata-style addresses. The public image/video tool wrappers currently call the validator before downloading, but the lower-level helpers are separately tested and documented as SSRF-protected. Keeping enforcement at the sink prevents future refactors or direct helper reuse from accidentally bypassing the central policy. ## How this differs from related public PRs This patch is related to earlier public vision/media hardening, but it fixes a different layer: - `#2679` added the original `is_safe_url()` validation and redirect revalidation for vision images. - `#3845` added website-policy checks and image content validation. - `#19301` added the video analysis path with similar redirect checks. Those changes either validated at the wrapper layer or checked redirect targets. This PR adds the missing sink-level pre-connect guard for the initial image/video URL inside the helpers that actually open outbound HTTP connections. It does not replace the existing wrapper or redirect checks; it makes the sink enforce the same policy. ## Attack flow ```text caller-controlled media URL -> tools.vision_tools._download_image() / _download_video() -> pre-patch helper checked only website policy before the initial request -> private/internal URL could be fetched if the helper was called directly ``` ## Affected code | Issue | Files | |-------|-------| | Missing helper-level initial URL-safety enforcement | `tools/vision_tools.py` | | Regression coverage | `tests/tools/test_vision_tools.py`, `tests/tools/test_video_analyze.py` | ## Root cause Vision media download helper boundary: - The central `is_safe_url()` check lived in `_validate_image_url()`, outside the concrete download sink. - `_download_image()` and the later-added `_download_video()` reused `is_safe_url()` for redirect targets, but not for the initial request URL. - `check_website_access()` is a website policy check and should not be treated as equivalent to private/internal URL safety. ## CVSS assessment | Issue | CVSS v3.1 | Vector | |-------|-----------|--------| | Helper-level private/internal URL fetch bypass | 5.3 Medium | `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N` | Rationale: - This is bounded as medium/defense-in-depth because current public tool wrappers already perform preflight validation. - The impact is server-side access to internal HTTP resources if these helpers are invoked directly or reused by a future path without duplicating wrapper validation. ## Safe reproduction steps On current `origin/main`, a local harness can demonstrate that the helpers fetch loopback even while the central policy rejects it: ```text image-helper is_safe_url False image-helper downloaded True 69 video-helper is_safe_url False video-helper downloaded True 13 seen ['/secret.png', '/secret.mp4'] ``` After this PR, the same harness is blocked before any request reaches the local server: ```text image-helper is_safe_url False image-helper blocked_or_error ValueError Blocked image download from private/internal address: http://127.0.0.1:<port>/secret.png video-helper is_safe_url False video-helper blocked_or_error ValueError Blocked video download from private/internal address: http://127.0.0.1:<port>/secret.mp4 seen [] ``` ## Expected vulnerable behavior - The central URL-safety policy rejects loopback/private media URLs. - The concrete media download helpers should not be able to fetch a URL that the central policy rejects. - Pre-patch, the helpers could fetch those URLs when invoked directly. ## Changes in this PR - Imports `is_safe_url()` once at module scope. - Adds `_ensure_safe_download_url()` as the shared media download guard. - Calls the guard before the initial image download request. - Calls the guard before the initial video download request. - Reuses the guard for image and video redirect targets. - Adds focused tests ensuring private URL downloads are rejected before `httpx.AsyncClient` is constructed. ## Files changed | Category | Files | What changed | |----------|-------|--------------| | Runtime guard | `tools/vision_tools.py` | Shared helper-level URL-safety guard for image/video initial URLs and redirects | | Tests | `tests/tools/test_vision_tools.py` | Image helper loopback rejection regression | | Tests | `tests/tools/test_video_analyze.py` | Video helper loopback rejection regression | ## Maintainer impact - Narrow change limited to `tools/vision_tools.py` and focused tests. - Public image/video wrapper behavior remains compatible for safe URLs. - The central SSRF policy is now enforced at the download sink as well as at wrapper validation. - No unrelated files are changed. ## Fix rationale The safest durable boundary is the function that actually opens outbound HTTP connections. Wrapper-level validation is useful, but it is easier to regress when helpers are reused by new tool paths. signals.title: fix(tools): send_message schema required fields match runtime enforcement
signals.text: ## Summary `SEND_MESSAGE_SCHEMA` declared `required: []` but `_handle_send()` immediately errors if either `target` or `message` is absent: ```python if not target or not message: return tool_error("Both 'target' and 'message' are required when action='send'") ``` This mismatch means LLMs and schema validators see no required fields, so missing-field calls fail silently at runtime instead of being caught at call-construction time. **Fix:** Set `"required": ["target", "message"]` so the schema matches the actual enforcement. Note: `action='list'` calls don't need `target`/`message`, but the `list` action is clearly described in the field descriptions and the tool docstring already instructs calling `list` first when a target is unknown. ## Test plan - [ ] `send_message(target="telegram", message="hi")` → delivers message - [ ] `send_message(action="list")` → returns channel list (no schema rejection) - [ ] `send_message(message="hi")` (missing target) → schema validator rejects before reaching handler Closes #32376 🤖 Contributed via [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/claude-code)

signals.title: fix(memory,run_agent): two real bug fixes from the #32848 audit
signals.text: ## Summary Two real bug fixes from the #32848 audit list. Both 1-line changes. ## Fix 1: holographic store — exact match instead of LIKE wildcard `plugins/memory/holographic/store.py:440`: ```python # Old: "SELECT entity_id FROM entities WHERE name LIKE ?" # New: "SELECT entity_id FROM entities WHERE name = ?" ``` The comment on the previous line said 'Exact name match' but the query used LIKE which treats `_` and `%` as SQL wildcards. So `name='test_entity'` would also match `testXentity`, `testAentity`, etc. Real bug. ## Fix 2: cross-thread interrupt clearing in gateway mode `run_agent.py:3133`: ```python # Old: _set_interrupt(False) # New: _set_interrupt(False, self._execution_thread_id) ``` The pattern elsewhere in this file (lines 2294-2295 and 2338-2339) is `_set_interrupt(<bool>, self._execution_thread_id)`. The 3133 call was missing the second arg, defaulting to the current thread. In gateway mode where `_hydrate_todo_store` may be called from a different thread than the execution thread, this cleared the interrupt for the wrong thread. ## Risk Low. Both are 1-line, behavior-preserving fixes with the test suite covering the affected paths. Fixes #32848 (parts 5 and 7)
