signal.title: fix(desktop): stop decoding the HERMES_HOME registry read as utf-8
signal.text: ## What does this PR do? `readWindowsUserEnvVar()` reads `HERMES_HOME` out of `HKCU\Environment` and decodes `reg.exe`'s stdout as UTF-8: ```ts stdout = exec('reg', ['query', 'HKCU\\Environment', '/v', name], { encoding: 'utf8', windowsHide: true, timeout: 5000 }) ``` `reg.exe` is a native console program; its stdout carries the machine code page. The value being read is a filesystem path. **Measured on ja-JP Windows 11 (ACP=932), Node v24.17.0.** `setx HERMES_PROBE "C:\十能予\hermes"`, then the same `reg query` captured as bytes: ``` raw bytes 83 value hex 43 3a 5c 8f 5c 94 5c 97 5c 5c 6865726d6573 C : \ 十 能 予 \ hermes parsed, utf8 "C:\\\ufffd\\\ufffd\\\ufffd\\\\hermes" parsed, sjis "C:\\\u5341\u80fd\u4e88\\hermes" backslashes utf8 5 sjis 2 values equal false parent exists, utf8 false parent exists, sjis true ``` The three characters each have `0x5C` as their CP932 trail byte, and `0x5C` is the path separator. So the UTF-8 decode does not shorten the path, it **lengthens** it by three segments. There are 52 such characters in CPython's CP932 double-byte table, and they are ordinary ones: 表 十 能 予 構 貼. **What it costs.** `parseRegQueryValue` matches on `\S+` for the name and takes the rest of the line as the value, so a mangled value parses cleanly. The caller in `main.ts` is: ```ts const fromRegistry = readWindowsUserEnvVar('HERMES_HOME') if (fromRegistry) { return normalizeHermesHomeRoot(fromRegistry) } // LOCALAPPDATA fallback below is never reached ``` A corrupted string is still truthy, so the desktop resolves `HERMES_HOME` to a directory that does not exist rather than falling through to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes`. That is worse than the stale-snapshot gap this function was added to close (#45471): the fallback that would have produced a working home is skipped by a value that only looks valid. `parent exists utf8 = false` above is that outcome on a real host. **The fix.** Node exposes no API for the host ANSI or OEM code page, so rather than guess at one: - Take `reg`'s stdout as bytes (drop `encoding: 'utf8'`). - If every byte is `< 0x80`, the code page and UTF-8 agree by definition — decode and return, unchanged behaviour and no extra spawn. This is the path essentially every host takes. - If any byte is `>= 0x80`, the value is in a code page we cannot name. Re-read it through PowerShell base64-encoded from UTF-8 inside the child, so the bytes on the wire are ASCII and no code page is involved: ``` [Convert]::ToBase64String([Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetBytes( [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('HERMES_HOME','User'))) ``` That is the same trick `ui-tui/src/lib/clipboard.ts` and `hermes_cli/clipboard.py` already use for clipboard text, for the same reason. The trigger is a fact about the bytes, not a judgement about damage. I deliberately did not detect this by looking for `U+FFFD`: I measured on #89468 that the replacement output is not stable across runtimes (29 replacements on .NET Framework 4.8, 30 on .NET 8 and CPython 3.11 for identical input), so replacement characters are not a sound signal. The name is checked against `/^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$/` before it is interpolated into the PowerShell string. Today the only caller passes a literal, but the function is exported. **Note on the linter.** `scripts/check-windows-footguns.py` cannot see this file: `should_scan_file()` returns `True` only for `.py`, `.pyw`, `.pyi`. Every `.ts` under `apps/desktop/electron/` is outside the gate that exists to catch exactly this class of bug. ## Related Issue No separate issue — reporting it here with the measurement. Same class as #89878 / #89907 / #90017 / #90046, on the Electron side of the same seam. The Python half of `bounded_probe_run` is #90046; this is the TypeScript half, and it is independent of that PR. ## Type of Change - [x] 🐛 Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue) - [ ] ✨ New feature (non-breaking change that adds functionality) - [ ] 🔒 Security fix - [ ] 📝 Documentation update - [ ] ✅ Tests (adding or improving test coverage) - [ ] ♻️ Refactor (no behavior change) - [ ] 🎯 New skill (bundled or hub) ## Changes Made - `apps/desktop/electron/windows-user-env.ts` — added `isAsciiBytes()`; `readWindowsUserEnvVar()` now captures `reg` stdout as bytes and only decodes it as UTF-8 when it is pure ASCII. - `apps/desktop/electron/windows-user-env.ts` — added `readUserEnvVarAsBase64()`, a PowerShell re-read that base64-encodes the UTF-8 bytes inside the child, used only on the non-ASCII path. Env-var names are validated before interpolation. - `apps/desktop/electron/windows-user-env.test.ts` — four tests added: the ASCII fast path spawns only `reg`; a CP932 value is re-read as base64 and returns the correct path, with the old five-backslash result pinned as an assertion; a failed re-read returns `null`; a name that is not a plain identifier never reaches PowerShell. ## How to Test 1. On a CP932 host: ```powershell mkdir C:\十能予 -Force setx HERMES_PROBE "C:\十能予\hermes" ``` Then, in a new shell: ```js const { execFileSync } = require('node:child_process') const raw = execFileSync('reg', ['query','HKCU\\Environment','/v','HERMES_PROBE'], { windowsHide: true }) console.log(raw.toString('hex')) console.log(JSON.stringify(raw.toString('utf8'))) console.log(JSON.stringify(new TextDecoder('shift_jis').decode(raw))) ``` The backslash count goes from 2 to 5, and `fs.statSync` on the parent of the UTF-8 result throws. Output above is from that run. 2. The test file, run directly under `node --test` with the type annotations stripped — 14 pass (10 pre-existing, unchanged). I did not run it through the repo's vitest runner: the desktop workspace's dependencies are not installed on my host, so `npm test -w apps/desktop` is not something I can honestly claim to have run. 3. Against the pre-patch source, keeping the new tests: 2 failed / 12 passed. The other two pass either way on purpose — one pins that the ASCII path still spawns only `reg` so the common case cannot regress, the other pins the name-validation guard, which is new but not what the bug was. Note on the checklist below: I left the full-suite box unchecked for the reason in 2. ## Checklist ### Code - [x] I've read the [Contributing Guide](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) - [x] My commit messages follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) (`fix(scope):`, `feat(scope):`, etc.) - [x] I searched for [existing PRs](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pulls) to make sure this isn't a duplicate - [x] My PR contains **only** changes related to this fix/feature (no unrelated commits) - [ ] I've run `pytest tests/ -q` and all tests pass - [x] I've added tests for my changes (required for bug fixes, strongly encouraged for features) - [x] I've tested on my platform: Windows 11, ja-JP (ACP=932), Node v24.17.0 ### Documentation & Housekeeping - [x] I've updated relevant documentation (README, `docs/`, docstrings) — or N/A - [x] I've updated `cli-config.yaml.example` if I added/changed config keys — or N/A - [x] I've updated `CONTRIBUTING.md` or `AGENTS.md` if I changed architecture or workflows — or N/A - [x] I've considered cross-platform impact (Windows, macOS) per the [compatibility guide](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#cross-platform-compatibility) — or N/A - [x] I've updated tool descriptions/schemas if I changed tool behavior — or N/A ## Screenshots / Logs I have a ja-JP (ACP=932) Windows host and can measure anything else on that locale. *(Measured on my host. signal.title: [Bug]: Desktop spillover cache stores raw MCP JSON-RPC envelope instead of text content
signal.text:
## Summary When an MCP tool result exceeds the inline context budget, the desktop app's spillover cache (`~/.hermes/cache/spillover/`) writes the **raw JSON-RPC response envelope** to disk as a single-line JSON string — e.g. `{"result": "# Markdown content with \n escapes...", "structuredContent": {...}}` — instead of extracting and writing the actual text content. The agent then receives a 200KB+ one-line JSON blob that is hostile to pagination, `read_file` line-offset navigation, and any downstream markdown tooling. ## Reproduction 1. Configure a remote MCP server whose tools return large text payloads (e.g. a research archive server with a `read_guide` tool returning ~106KB of markdown, or `get_conversation_text` returning ~80KB). 2. Call the tool from a desktop chat session. 3. Observe the spillover file written to `~/.hermes/cache/spillover/call-<uuid>.txt`. ## Actual behavior The spill file contains the raw envelope: ```json {"result": "# Jac's Memex — Research Guide for Claude

You have access to...", "structuredContent": {"result": "..."}} ``` — 216,583 characters, **0 newlines**, 1 line total. The inner `result` string contains the real markdown with literal `
` escapes. `read_file` on this file returns one giant numbered line; offset/limit pagination is useless. ## Expected behavior The spill file should contain the extracted text content — i.e. the value of the `result` field (or the concatenated `text` of the MCP `content[]` array) — written as plain text/markdown with real newlines. That's what the agent actually needs to page through, and it's what smaller (non-spilled) results already deliver inline. ## Impact Any MCP workflow with large text results (research archives, document stores, conversation readers) hits this on nearly every call. The agent has to detect the JSON envelope, `json.loads()` it, extract the inner string, write a reconstructed file to `/tmp`, and then read *that* — pure overhead on every large call. ## Environment - Hermes Desktop (macOS 15.6.1), profile `default` - MCP server: remote HTTP (`https://…/mcp`), streamable transport - Model: moonshotai/kimi-k3 via nous ## Suggested fix In the spillover writer (wherever the oversized-result fallback saves to `~/.hermes/cache/spillover/`), extract the MCP text content before writing: if the result has a `content` array with `type: "text"` items, join their `text` fields; else if the JSON has a string `result` field, write that string directly. Write with real newlines, not JSON-escaped.

signal.title: fix(tools): send_message schema required fields match runtime enforcement
signal.text: ## Summary `SEND_MESSAGE_SCHEMA` declared `required: []` but `_handle_send()` immediately errors if either `target` or `message` is absent: ```python if not target or not message: return tool_error("Both 'target' and 'message' are required when action='send'") ``` This mismatch means LLMs and schema validators see no required fields, so missing-field calls fail silently at runtime instead of being caught at call-construction time. **Fix:** Set `"required": ["target", "message"]` so the schema matches the actual enforcement. Note: `action='list'` calls don't need `target`/`message`, but the `list` action is clearly described in the field descriptions and the tool docstring already instructs calling `list` first when a target is unknown. ## Test plan - [ ] `send_message(target="telegram", message="hi")` → delivers message - [ ] `send_message(action="list")` → returns channel list (no schema rejection) - [ ] `send_message(message="hi")` (missing target) → schema validator rejects before reaching handler Closes #32376 🤖 Contributed via [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/claude-code)

signal.title: fix(types): use typing.Callable instead of lowercase 'callable'
signal.text: ## Summary Fix from issue #32848 audit (item 13). The lowercase `callable` is the builtin `any()`-style predicate function, not a type. The intended type was `typing.Callable`. ## Changes - `run_agent.py:48` — added `Callable` to typing import - `run_agent.py:5098, 5105` — `callable` → `Callable` - `tools/delegate_tool.py:31` — added `Callable` to typing import - `tools/delegate_tool.py:728` — `callable` → `Callable` ## Behavior The Python interpreter doesn't catch this at runtime (callable is always truthy when used as an annotation under PEP 563 deferred evaluation). signal.title: fix(memory,run_agent): two real bug fixes from the #32848 audit
signal.text: ## Summary Two real bug fixes from the #32848 audit list. Both 1-line changes. ## Fix 1: holographic store — exact match instead of LIKE wildcard `plugins/memory/holographic/store.py:440`: ```python # Old: "SELECT entity_id FROM entities WHERE name LIKE ?" # New: "SELECT entity_id FROM entities WHERE name = ?" ``` The comment on the previous line said 'Exact name match' but the query used LIKE which treats `_` and `%` as SQL wildcards. So `name='test_entity'` would also match `testXentity`, `testAentity`, etc. Real bug. ## Fix 2: cross-thread interrupt clearing in gateway mode `run_agent.py:3133`: ```python # Old: _set_interrupt(False) # New: _set_interrupt(False, self._execution_thread_id) ``` The pattern elsewhere in this file (lines 2294-2295 and 2338-2339) is `_set_interrupt(<bool>, self._execution_thread_id)`. The 3133 call was missing the second arg, defaulting to the current thread. In gateway mode where `_hydrate_todo_store` may be called from a different thread than the execution thread, this cleared the interrupt for the wrong thread. ## Risk Low. Both are 1-line, behavior-preserving fixes with the test suite covering the affected paths. Fixes #32848 (parts 5 and 7)

signal.title: feat(computer_use): Hermes Desktop drives your machine while the agent runs elsewhere (carries #61507)
signal.text: When Desktop is pointed at a remote backend, `computer_use` runs where the agent runs. The person watching is here, the screen it drives is there, and nothing in the product said so. Dan Bennett built the way out in [#61507](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/61507): Desktop starts a loopback-only `hermes computer-use bridge` beside itself and opens an authenticated WebSocket *outward* to the backend, which then reaches the user's own keyboard without anyone tunnelling anything. That PR was written against a very different `main` and could not be rebased, so this carries it forward on top of the provider seam in [#90380](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/90380), with Dan's commits and authorship intact. Two things changed in the carry, both because the original was global where the product is not: **The bridge is a property of the session, not of the process.** One gateway serves a Desktop client, a phone on Telegram, and a cron tick in the same process, and only the first of those may drive the user's Mac. So the backend files each bridge under the identity its credential carried — provider, principal, profile — and `computer_use` resolves it per call from the connection's own verified scope, failing closed when there is no match. A second Desktop cannot capture the first one's calls, and nothing in `config.yaml` is required to make the common case work. **Every remote+profile pair owns its own socket.** The original kept one global connection, which a profile pool cannot use. The Electron side now lives in `electron/computer-use-bridge.ts` rather than ~320 inline lines of `main.ts`, with per-scope ownership, cancellation generations, and a shared sidecar; pool teardown releases a profile's claim through the pool stopper's new `onEvict` funnel. A Desktop install with no local agent runtime has no sidecar to host. That is a normal state, not a failure to retry, so it is resolved once and Settings says so in place of the toggle description instead of letting the switch look like it worked. Bridge behaviour (`provider`, `bridge_url`, `bridge_timeout_seconds`) is `config.yaml`; only the bearer token is a secret in `.env`. Stacked on [#90380](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/90380) — review that one first. Co-authored-by: Dan Bennett <dan@danbennett.me>

signal.title: [security] fix(vision): enforce URL safety in media downloads
signal.text: ## Summary This PR hardens the vision media download boundary so the concrete download helpers enforce the same private/internal URL policy as their public validators. It addresses a residual helper-level variant of the vision/media SSRF hardening family: the public wrappers validate with `tools.url_safety.is_safe_url()`, but the lower-level helpers that open outbound HTTP connections did not enforce that central policy before the initial request. - Adds a shared pre-connect URL-safety guard for image and video downloads. - Keeps redirect-target revalidation for both media types using the same guard. - Adds regression tests proving loopback URLs are rejected before an HTTP client is opened. ## Security issues covered | Issue | Impact | Severity | |-------|--------|----------| | Vision media download helpers did not enforce `is_safe_url()` before the initial fetch | A direct or future caller of `_download_image()` / `_download_video()` could bypass the central private/internal URL policy and fetch loopback or metadata-style targets | Medium / defense-in-depth | ## Before this PR - `_validate_image_url()` rejected private/internal URLs with `tools.url_safety.is_safe_url()`. - `_download_image()` and `_download_video()` only applied `check_website_access()` before the initial request. - The helper comments described SSRF protection, but the initial helper fetch itself did not enforce the central private/internal URL policy. - Redirect targets were checked, but the first request URL was not checked at the helper boundary. ## After this PR - `_download_image()` rejects unsafe image URLs before constructing an `httpx.AsyncClient`. - `_download_video()` rejects unsafe video URLs before constructing an `httpx.AsyncClient`. - Redirect checks for both helpers use the same shared `_ensure_safe_download_url()` helper. - Regression tests lock in that loopback URLs do not open a client connection. ## Why this matters Hermes Agent already has a central SSRF policy for private, loopback, link-local, and metadata-style addresses. The public image/video tool wrappers currently call the validator before downloading, but the lower-level helpers are separately tested and documented as SSRF-protected. Keeping enforcement at the sink prevents future refactors or direct helper reuse from accidentally bypassing the central policy. ## How this differs from related public PRs This patch is related to earlier public vision/media hardening, but it fixes a different layer: - `#2679` added the original `is_safe_url()` validation and redirect revalidation for vision images. - `#3845` added website-policy checks and image content validation. - `#19301` added the video analysis path with similar redirect checks. Those changes either validated at the wrapper layer or checked redirect targets. This PR adds the missing sink-level pre-connect guard for the initial image/video URL inside the helpers that actually open outbound HTTP connections. It does not replace the existing wrapper or redirect checks; it makes the sink enforce the same policy. ## Attack flow ```text caller-controlled media URL -> tools.vision_tools._download_image() / _download_video() -> pre-patch helper checked only website policy before the initial request -> private/internal URL could be fetched if the helper was called directly ``` ## Affected code | Issue | Files | |-------|-------| | Missing helper-level initial URL-safety enforcement | `tools/vision_tools.py` | | Regression coverage | `tests/tools/test_vision_tools.py`, `tests/tools/test_video_analyze.py` | ## Root cause Vision media download helper boundary: - The central `is_safe_url()` check lived in `_validate_image_url()`, outside the concrete download sink. - `_download_image()` and the later-added `_download_video()` reused `is_safe_url()` for redirect targets, but not for the initial request URL. - `check_website_access()` is a website policy check and should not be treated as equivalent to private/internal URL safety. ## CVSS assessment | Issue | CVSS v3.1 | Vector | |-------|-----------|--------| | Helper-level private/internal URL fetch bypass | 5.3 Medium | `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N` | Rationale: - This is bounded as medium/defense-in-depth because current public tool wrappers already perform preflight validation. - The impact is server-side access to internal HTTP resources if these helpers are invoked directly or reused by a future path without duplicating wrapper validation. ## Safe reproduction steps On current `origin/main`, a local harness can demonstrate that the helpers fetch loopback even while the central policy rejects it: ```text image-helper is_safe_url False image-helper downloaded True 69 video-helper is_safe_url False video-helper downloaded True 13 seen ['/secret.png', '/secret.mp4'] ``` After this PR, the same harness is blocked before any request reaches the local server: ```text image-helper is_safe_url False image-helper blocked_or_error ValueError Blocked image download from private/internal address: http://127.0.0.1:<port>/secret.png video-helper is_safe_url False video-helper blocked_or_error ValueError Blocked video download from private/internal address: http://127.0.0.1:<port>/secret.mp4 seen [] ``` ## Expected vulnerable behavior - The central URL-safety policy rejects loopback/private media URLs. - The concrete media download helpers should not be able to fetch a URL that the central policy rejects. - Pre-patch, the helpers could fetch those URLs when invoked directly. ## Changes in this PR - Imports `is_safe_url()` once at module scope. - Adds `_ensure_safe_download_url()` as the shared media download guard. - Calls the guard before the initial image download request. - Calls the guard before the initial video download request. - Reuses the guard for image and video redirect targets. - Adds focused tests ensuring private URL downloads are rejected before `httpx.AsyncClient` is constructed. ## Files changed | Category | Files | What changed | |----------|-------|--------------| | Runtime guard | `tools/vision_tools.py` | Shared helper-level URL-safety guard for image/video initial URLs and redirects | | Tests | `tests/tools/test_vision_tools.py` | Image helper loopback rejection regression | | Tests | `tests/tools/test_video_analyze.py` | Video helper loopback rejection regression | ## Maintainer impact - Narrow change limited to `tools/vision_tools.py` and focused tests. - Public image/video wrapper behavior remains compatible for safe URLs. - The central SSRF policy is now enforced at the download sink as well as at wrapper validation. - No unrelated files are changed. ## Fix rationale The safest durable boundary is the function that actually opens outbound HTTP connections. Wrapper-level validation is useful, but it is easier to regress when helpers are reused by new tool paths. Enforcing `is_safe_url()` in the download helpers makes the policy local to the sink and keeps redirect checks consistent. ## Type of change - [x] Security fix - [x] Tests - [ ] Documentation update - [ ] Refactor with no behavior change ## Test plan - [x] Focused image/video SSRF regression tests. - [x] Full vision and video tool test files. - [x] Syntax check. - [x] Ruff check on touched files. - [x] Whitespace diff check. Executed with: ```bash python3.11 -m pytest -q -o addopts='' tests/tools/test_vision_tools.py::TestVisionSafetyGuards tests/tools/test_video_analyze.py::TestVideoAnalyzeTool::test_download_rejects_private_url_before_http_client python3.11 -m pytest -q -o addopts='' tests/tools/test_vision_tools.py tests/tools/test_video_analyze.py python3.11 -m py_compile tools/vision_tools.py tests/tools/test_vision_tools.py tests/tools/test_video_analyze.py python3.11 -m ruff check tools/vision_tools.py tests/tools/test_vision_tools.py tests/tools/test_video_analyze.py git diff --check ``` Results: ```text 5 passed 101 passed All checks passed! ``` ## Disclosure notes - This PR is intentionally bounded to helper-level initial URL validation in `tools/vision_tools.py`. - It does not claim that the public wrapper currently skips validation; it prevents the lower-level download sink from being unsafe if called directly or reused later. - No unrelated files were changed.

signal.title: docs(skills): local TTS optimization playbook — MLX parallel engine, stability, CJK chunking
signal.text: ## Summary Adds a **local-tts-optimization** skill documenting a production-validated tuning playbook for local TTS voice-clone engines on Apple Silicon — distilled from a real deployment that took Qwen3-TTS synthesis from 377s → 100.2s (RTF 0.53) for 822-char Chinese text without changing the model. ## Background Hermes users can wire any local TTS CLI via command providers (`tts.providers.<name>.type: command`), but the official skills catalog had no guidance for the common failure cluster: **timeouts on long text, slow CPU-only inference, and broken Chinese chunking**. This skill captures the fixes that worked in production so a user with the same symptom set doesn't rediscover them one by one. ## What's in it 1. **Engine comparison with measured numbers** — PyTorch CPU single/parallel vs MLX single/parallel (M5 Max, 822-char): the headline result is that MLX **single process is not** faster than tuned PyTorch parallelism; the win is **MLX × 4-process pool** (RTF 0.53). 2. **Architecture diagram** — split → round-robin into 4 worker groups → subprocess workers in an isolated MLX venv → PCM concat with silence gaps. Venv isolation is mandatory (`transformers 5.x` vs `qwen_tts`'s pinned 4.57.3). 3. **Stability checklist** — timeout 600, backlog 64, bind-probe instead of TCP connect (false-negative → spawn storms), flock spawn guard, POST failover, `no_proxy` for localhost, concurrency cap. 4. **CJK chunking** — Chinese has no spaces; space-based sentence splitting hard-cuts mid-word. Break on CJK punctuation, keep Latin punctuation whitespace-required (`3.14`/`Dr.` safe). Points at the core fix in `tools/tts_tool.py` (#84622). 5. **MLX setup gotchas** — `snapshot_download` misses `config.json` (patch `quantization: {group_size:64, bits:8}`), tokenizer files copied from the PyTorch model dir, `ref_audio` must be path or `mx.array`. 6. **Troubleshooting table** — every row is a symptom we hit with the measured cause and fix. ## Who should enable this - Anyone running a local TTS engine on Apple Silicon via a Hermes command provider or a plugin `StreamingTTSProvider` - Users hitting `timeout` on long text, slow generation, or mid-word Chinese breaks ## Platform compatibility | Platform | Impact | |---|---| | macOS Apple Silicon | ✅ Primary target (MLX, Metal) | | macOS Intel / Linux | ⚠️ MLX sections N/A; stability + CJK chunking + timeout guidance still apply | | Windows | ⚠️ Guidance applies partially (no MLX); timeout/CJK sections valid | ## Quick-start guide 1. Load the skill: `skills/productivity/local-tts-optimization/SKILL.md` 2. If your provider times out on long text: set `timeout: 600` in `tts.providers.<name>` 3. If Chinese output breaks mid-word: update to a build with #84622 (or apply the CJK-break regex locally) 4. If you want GPU speed: follow the MLX setup section (isolated venv + 4-process pool) ## Troubleshooting | Symptom | Cause | Fix | |---|---|---| | Skill not visible in `hermes skills` | frontmatter invalid | name/category/description required | | MLX `Received 500 parameters` | missing `quantization` in config | patch `{group_size:64, bits:8}` | | PYTHONPATH shadowing | Hermes env leaks into venv | `env -u PYTHONPATH` for venv commands |

signal.title: fix(profiles): find alias collisions without shelling out to where
signal.text: ## What does this PR do? `check_alias_collision()` shells out to `where` (Windows) / `which` (POSIX) and compares the decoded first line against a path it builds itself: ```python result = subprocess.run( ["where" if is_windows else "which", canon], capture_output=True, text=True, encoding='utf-8', errors='replace', timeout=5, ) existing_path = result.stdout.strip().splitlines()[0] expected = wrapper_dir / (f"{canon}.bat" if is_windows else canon) if existing_path == str(expected): ... # our own wrapper, safe to overwrite return f"'{canon}' conflicts with an existing command ({existing_path})" ``` `expected` comes from the filesystem and is correct. `existing_path` comes from a native console program decoded as UTF-8. `where.exe` writes the machine code page, so on a CJK host the two can never be compared meaningfully. `_get_wrapper_dir()` is `Path.home() / ".local" / "bin"`, so the wrapper path contains the user profile name. An account named in kana or kanji puts non-ASCII on both sides of that comparison. **Measured on ja-JP Windows 11 (ACP=932), Python 3.12.10.** A directory named 十能予 on PATH, holding `hermesprobe.bat`, then the same `where` call captured as bytes: ``` raw bytes 27 raw hex 43 3a 5c 8f 5c 94 5c 97 5c 5c 6865726d657370726f62652e626174 0d 0a C : \ 十 能 予 \ hermesprobe.bat CRLF cp932 'C:\\\u5341\u80fd\u4e88\\hermesprobe.bat\r\n' utf-8 + replace 'C:\\\ufffd\\\ufffd\\\ufffd\\\\hermesprobe.bat\r\n' backslashes expected 2 cp932 2 utf-8 5 match cp932 True match utf8 False ``` This is not the usual replacement-character story. All three characters have `0x5C` as their CP932 trail byte, and `0x5C` is the path separator, so the decode does not lose the path — it **adds three separators to it**. There are 52 such characters in CPython's CP932 double-byte table and they are ordinary ones: 表 十 能 予 構 貼. **What it costs.** `check_alias_collision` is called from eight places (`main.py` ×3, `web_routers/profiles.py` ×2, `cli_commands_mixin.py`, `backup.py` ×2), including profile import and backup restore. With the comparison unable to hold, the "this is our own wrapper, safe to overwrite" branch is unreachable, so re-creating an alias you already own fails with: ``` 'hermesprobe' conflicts with an existing command (C:\<?>\<?>\<?>\\hermesprobe.bat) ``` `errors='replace'` means nothing raises, so this surfaces only as that message. **The fix.** `shutil.which()` instead of the subprocess. It reads `PATH` and `PATHEXT` in-process and returns the first match — the same value `.splitlines()[0]` was taking — so no byte boundary exists to get the codepage wrong. `shutil` was already imported. The net change removes a spawn, a 5-second timeout, and two exception arms. One behaviour difference this introduces and then closes: `shutil.which` joins onto the PATH entry verbatim, so a Windows `PATH` carrying `C:/tools` yields `C:/tools\mybot.bat`, where `where` normalised the separator. `os.path.normcase` on both sides folds separator and case on Windows and is a no-op on POSIX. **The alternative I did not take.** Keeping the subprocess and passing `encoding=locale.getencoding()` is a one-line diff and matches #89907 / #90017. I preferred deleting the boundary: this lookup never needed a child process, `check-windows-footguns.py` already lists `shutil.which(` among its guard hints, and the diff comes out smaller. Happy to switch to the minimal form if you would rather keep the change surface at one line. ## Related Issue No separate issue — reporting it here with the measurement. Same family as #89878 / #89907 / #90017 / #90046, but this site does not merely mangle text for display: the corrupted string is an operand in an equality test against a correct path. ## Type of Change - [x] 🐛 Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue) - [ ] ✨ New feature (non-breaking change that adds functionality) - [ ] 🔒 Security fix - [ ] 📝 Documentation update - [ ] ✅ Tests (adding or improving test coverage) - [ ] ♻️ Refactor (no behavior change) - [ ] 🎯 New skill (bundled or hub) ## Changes Made - `hermes_cli/profiles.py` — `check_alias_collision()` resolves PATH with `shutil.which()` instead of `subprocess.run(["where"|"which", ...])`, and compares through `os.path.normcase`. - `tests/hermes_cli/test_profiles.py` — `test_windows_checks_bat_extension` and `test_traversal_alias_rejected_before_path_lookup` now patch `shutil.which` rather than `subprocess.run`. - `tests/hermes_cli/test_profiles.py` — four tests added: no child process is spawned for the lookup; a wrapper under a non-ASCII directory is recognised through a real PATH lookup; a PATH entry written with forward slashes still matches; and a byte-level assertion pinning what CP932 does under a UTF-8 decode. ## How to Test 1. On a CP932 host, reproduce the decode against the same call: ```powershell mkdir C:\十能予 -Force "@echo off" | Out-File -Encoding ascii C:\十能予\hermesprobe.bat $env:PATH = "C:\十能予;$env:PATH" ``` ```python import subprocess raw = subprocess.run(["where", "hermesprobe"], capture_output=True).stdout print(raw.hex()) print(ascii(raw.decode("cp932"))) print(ascii(raw.decode("utf-8", errors="replace"))) ``` The backslash count goes from 2 to 5. Output above is from that run. 2. `python -m pytest tests/hermes_cli/test_profiles.py -q` on that same host, against `upstream/main` and against this branch: ``` upstream/main 8 failed, 48 passed this branch 8 failed, 52 passed ``` The same eight fail on both, and none of them are in `TestAliasCollision`. They are pre-existing Windows failures in this file, four distinct causes: - two `assert 438 == 384` — a byte count that assumes LF line endings - two asserting a POSIX wrapper name against the `.bat` one Windows actually writes (`assert 'mybot.bat' == 'mybot'`) - two needing the symlink privilege (`OSError: [WinError 1314]`) - two `Path.read_text()` without `encoding=` raising `UnicodeDecodeError: 'cp932' codec can't decode byte 0x94` inside the test file itself The four extra passes are the four tests this PR adds. 3. Against the pre-patch source with the new tests kept, `-k AliasCollision` gives 1 failed / 4 passed. Only `test_path_lookup_does_not_spawn_a_child_process` is a genuine regression test off Windows — the others cannot fail on a UTF-8 host because there is no decode to get wrong there, and I would rather say that than imply four-way coverage. `test_wrapper_recognised_when_its_path_is_not_ascii` does a real PATH lookup with nothing mocked, so it is a real regression test on native Windows and a no-op assertion elsewhere. That pre-patch comparison was run in a Linux checkout of the same commit, not on the Windows host. Note on the checklist below: I ran `tests/hermes_cli/test_profiles.py` and the before/after comparison above, not the full `pytest tests/ -q`, so I left that box unchecked rather than claiming it. ## Checklist ### Code - [x] I've read the [Contributing Guide](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) - [x] My commit messages follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) (`fix(scope):`, `feat(scope):`, etc.) - [x] I searched for [existing PRs](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pulls) to make sure this isn't a duplicate - [x] My PR contains **only** changes related to this fix/feature (no unrelated commits) - [ ] I've run `pytest tests/ -q` and all tests pass - [x] I've added tests for my changes (required for bug fixes, strongly encouraged for features) - [x] I've tested on my platform: Windows 11, ja-JP (ACP=932), Python 3.12.10 ### Documentation & Housekeeping - [x] I've updated relevant documentation (README, `docs/`, docstrings) — or N/A - [x] I've updated `cli-config.yaml.example` if I added/changed config keys — or N/A - [x] I've updated `CONTRIBUTING.md` or `AGENTS.md` if I changed architecture or workflows — or N/A - [x] I've considered cross-platform impact (Windows, macOS) per the [compatibility guide](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#cross-platform-compatibility) — or N/A - [x] I've updated tool descriptions/schemas if I changed tool behavior — or N/A ## Screenshots / Logs I have a ja-JP (ACP=932) Windows host and can measure anything else on that locale. *(Measured on my host. Drafted with Claude.)*

signal.title: reasoning_effort: ultra reliably triggers Response remained truncated after 4 continuation attempts
signal.text: ### Describe the bug With `agent.reasoning_effort: ultra` the agent reliably hits provider `max_output_tokens` and reports: ``` Response truncated (finish_reason='length') - model hit max output tokens ... Error: Response remained truncated after 4 continuation attempts ``` Reproduced on every non-trivial prompt — the model spends its single-turn token budget on the long chain-of-thought before the actual answer is emitted, so Hermes auto-continues 4 times and still never finishes the turn. ### To Reproduce 1. `~/.hermes/config.yaml`: ```yaml model: provider: opencode-go model: muse-spark-1.2-contributor base_url: https://opencode.ai/zen/go/v1 agent: reasoning_effort: ultra max_turns: 150 ``` 2. Restart the gateway. 3. Send any normal prompt (e.g. asking the agent to answer a question / do a small task) in desktop chat. 4. Observe 4x `Response truncated (finish_reason='length')` then final error `Response remained truncated after 4 continuation attempts`. ### Expected behavior Either: - `ultra` automatically raises `_ephemeral_max_output_tokens` / `max_tokens` for the turn so the thinking + answer fit in one continuation chain, or - the continuation budget is higher / progressive (so 4 retries is enough), or - docs warn that `ultra` requires a long-output model / higher cap. Currently the `ultra` preset is unusable with the default provider caps — the user is forced to drop to `medium`/`low`. ### Environment - Hermes Agent v0.20.4 (2026.8.18), install method `git`, Python 3.11.15, macOS 15.7.7 - Provider `opencode-go` / `muse-spark-1.2-contributor` (also affects other `custom`/OpenAI-compatible providers when `reasoning_effort: ultra`) - `agent.reasoning_effort: ultra` (confirmed via config get → `ultra`) - `gateway_timeout: 1800`, `agent.max_turns: 150` ### Related - #46833 — thinking models on `custom`/Ollama always truncate, truncation-retry fix PR #12152 (`_ephemeral_max_output_tokens` + progressive boost) — same symptom but `ultra` still reproduces - #9372 — `NVIDIA Build API z-ai/glm4.7 returns model hit max output tokens` — same `finish_reason='length'` loop - Community workaround repo `TENBIGTOES/hermes-ollama-truncation-fix` documents the identical `Response remained truncated after 3 continuation attempts` loop - Temporary workaround: set `agent.reasoning_effort` to `medium` and restart gateway (or add "简洁回答" to prompt) ### Additional context Happy to provide gateway logs / transcript if needed. The issue is deterministic with `ultra` — switching to `medium` immediately stops the truncation, switching back to `ultra` immediately reproduces it. Suggest wiring `reasoning_effort` into the ephemeral `max_tokens` boost so `ultra` automatically gets a proportionally larger window.

signal.title: [Bug]: Desktop multi-connection — remote file tree shows UNREADABLE (ENOENT) though the remote workspace exists and the agent reads it fine
signal.text: ## Bug Description In the new desktop multi-connection feature I registered two remote Hermes gateways (a Linux Proxmox LXC and a Linux notebook) and switch to them from the Sessions status-bar switcher. Chat and the agent work on the remote (it creates and reads files in the correct remote path). But the right-sidebar file tree shows **"Could not read this folder (ENOENT)"** for both remotes, and the automatic retry never recovers. ## Steps to Reproduce 1. Add two `remote-gateway` connections in Settings → Gateways (auth: OAuth/session cookie). 2. Switch to a remote gateway from the bottom status-bar gateway switcher (Sessions view). 3. Wait for the session to load; the agent/chat works on the remote. 4. Look at the right-sidebar workspace file tree → shows "UNREADABLE — Could not read this folder (ENOENT)". 5. The bottom status bar shows the correct remote cwd (e.g. `/home/rafpigna/Sviluppo/mailflow`), and that directory exists on the remote. ## Expected Behavior The file tree should list the remote workspace directory that the session reports and that the agent can access. ## Actual Behavior "Could not read this folder (ENOENT)" persistently, on both remotes; the local connection works. The agent, using the WebSocket session path, reads and writes the same directory successfully — so only the sidebar file listing is broken. ## Affected Component Other (desktop app — remote workspace file tree / file-ops routing) ## Messaging Platform N/A (CLI only) ## Debug Report Omitted deliberately: `hermes debug share` uploads conversation content and personal data that are not needed for this diagnosis, and the report here is very large. System, environment and version details are provided below. ## Operating System - Desktop app host: Windows 11 - Remote LXC: Debian 13 (Proxmox, unprivileged) - Remote notebook: CachyOS (Arch-based) ## Python Version 3.11.15 (desktop venv) ## Hermes Version - Desktop: v0.20.4 (dev/source build; renderer build stamp 2026-08-19 23:28 UTC) - Remote LXC: v0.20.0 - Remote notebook: v0.20.3 ## Root Cause Analysis Server side is clean: `hermes_cli/web_server.py` `_fs_path()` (web_server.py:2105) does not rebase the path — it requires an absolute path and only does `Path().expanduser().resolve()` — and `fs_list` (web_server.py:2847) returns `{"error": "ENOENT"}` only when `os.scandir(target)` raises `FileNotFoundError`. An existing remote path (the agent wrote and listed a file under `/home/rafpigna/Sviluppo/mailflow`) must therefore list successfully server-side. The failure is in the REST FS bridge routing: the file tree reads over `GET /api/fs/list` via the Electron `hermes:api` bridge, routed by `desktopFsProfile()` — `apps/desktop/src/lib/desktop-fs.ts:40-44` documents that "without the active profile, the Electron api bridge hits the primary (local) backend even when the user switched to a remote profile". The request appears to land on the local backend, where the Linux remote path does not exist → ENOENT. The agent path (WebSocket) routes to the remote correctly; only the REST file listing does not. ## Proposed Fix Make the `hermes:api` FS routing honor the active remote connection scoped by `$connection` (profile + baseUrl), instead of falling back to the primary/local backend, so `/api/fs/*` (list / read-text / write-text / read-data-url / git-root / default-cwd) resolve against the selected remote gateway.

signal.title: hermes config set: list-of-strings values written as stringified JSON literal instead of YAML list
signal.text: # Bug: `hermes config set` silently stringifies list-of-strings values ## Summary `hermes config set <key> '<JSON literal>'` writes the entire literal as a **quoted string** into `~/.hermes/config.yaml` instead of a real YAML list. Downstream consumers that call `_coerce_allow_set` (or any other "accept list-or-comma-string" parser) get a single-element set containing the stringified JSON, which silently breaks allowlist matching — including security-relevant allowlists like `gateway.platforms.telegram.group_allowed_chats`. ## Reproduction ```bash # Setup: pick any list-typed key hermes config set gateway.platforms.telegram.group_allowed_chats '["-5488240624"]' # Inspect raw YAML — appears to be a quoted string, not a list grep -n -A1 'group_allowed_chats' ~/.hermes/config.yaml # Actual: group_allowed_chats: '["-5488240624"]' # Expected: group_allowed_chats: # - "-5488240624" # Confirm parsed type with PyYAML python3 -c 'import yaml; print(type(yaml.safe_load(open("$HOME/.hermes/config.yaml"))["gateway"]["platforms"]["telegram"]["group_allowed_chats"]).__name__)' # Actual: str # Expected: list ``` ## Impact - **Severity:** High — silently breaks authorization allowlists. No warning, no validation error. - **Surface area:** all list-typed config keys consumed by `_coerce_allow_set` in `gateway/authz_mixin.py:46-58`. Includes (verified by `search_files`): - `gateway.platforms.telegram.group_allowed_chats` - `gateway.platforms.telegram.group_allow_from` - Plus all `*_allow_from` / `*_allowed_users` / `*_allowed_chats` keys that pass through `_coerce_allow_set` - **Real-world consequence encountered:** Telegram group `user_id=8763334778` in chat `-5488240624` repeatedly logged `Blocked unauthorized user` despite being in a group explicitly added to the allowlist. Setting `require_mention=false` and `group_allow_from: ["*"]` had no effect until the value was rewritten as a YAML scalar. - **Workaround:** use the scalar form (no surrounding JSON brackets): ```bash hermes config set gateway.platforms.telegram.group_allowed_chats "-5488240624" hermes config set gateway.platforms.telegram.group_allow_from "*" ``` When `_coerce_allow_set` sees a non-JSON scalar string like `"-5488240624"`, `str.split(",")` correctly returns `{"-5488240624"}` and matching works. ## Root cause hypothesis `hermes config set` writes the value as a YAML scalar by stringifying whatever was passed. When the user passes a JSON literal (because the CLI has no native list syntax), the literal is quoted whole instead of being parsed into a YAML sequence. Two viable fix directions (for upstream to choose): 1. **Write side (preferred):** in `hermes config set`, detect when the value is a valid JSON literal (starts with `[` or `{`). If so, parse it and emit the YAML structure directly (`yaml.dump` with proper flow style), not as a quoted scalar. Plain scalars keep current behavior. 2. **Read side (tolerant fallback):** extend `_coerce_allow_set` to attempt `json.loads(raw)` when the string looks like a JSON array/object, falling back to the current `str.split(",")` only if that fails. Recommend direction (1) because: - Fix is at the source, all consumers benefit automatically - Read-side tolerance can mask other write-side issues in the future ## Suggested test cases ```python # test_hermes_config_set_list.py import subprocess, yaml from pathlib import Path CFG = Path.home() / ".hermes" / "config.yaml" def test_list_written_as_list(): subprocess.run(["hermes", "config", "set", "test.key", '["a","b"]'], check=True) parsed = yaml.safe_load(CFG.read_text()) assert isinstance(parsed["test"]["key"], list) assert parsed["test"]["key"] == ["a", "b"] # cleanup subprocess.run(["hermes", "config", "unset", "test.key"], check=True) def test_scalar_still_works(): subprocess.run(["hermes", "config", "set", "test.key", "hello"], check=True) parsed = yaml.safe_load(CFG.read_text()) assert parsed["test"]["key"] == "hello" subprocess.run(["hermes", "config", "unset", "test.key"], check=True) def test_comma_string_still_works(): subprocess.run(["hermes", "config", "set", "test.key", "a,b,c"], check=True) parsed = yaml.safe_load(CFG.read_text()) assert parsed["test"]["key"] in (["a", "b", "c"], "a,b,c") # back-compat subprocess.run(["hermes", "config", "unset", "test.key"], check=True) ``` ## Environment - hermes-agent version: latest (installed via `~/.hermes/hermes-agent/`, this session 2026-08-01) - Config path: `~/.hermes/config.yaml` (per `hermes config path`) - Tested with `python3 -c "import yaml; ..."` (PyYAML present) ## Reporter context Discovered while configuring a Telegram group allowlist for a team support bot. The user expects `group_allowed_chats: ["-5488240624"]` to mean "this chat and only this chat", which is a security-relevant config. The current behavior silently downgrades it to "match the literal string `\"-5488240624\"`" — which matches nothing.

signal.title: feat(tts): local MLX Qwen3-TTS streaming provider (qwen3tts-mlx)
signal.text: ## Summary Adds a **local MLX streaming TTS provider** (`qwen3tts-mlx`) so Hermes conversational voice (session speech, voice bubbles) can run on a local Qwen3-TTS voice-clone engine over Apple's MLX GPU path — no cloud dependency, custom voice clone support, ~4-9s TTFB per sentence instead of waiting ~47s for a whole buffer. ## Background Hermes already has a `StreamingTTSProvider` ABC (`tools/tts_streaming.py`) with cloud streamers (elevenlabs/openai/gemini/xai). Local TTS engines are supported for **synchronous** synthesis via command providers (`tts.providers.<name>.type: command`) — and users on Apple Silicon have been running exactly that (see `skills/productivity/local-tts-optimization`, PR #85041). But conversational voice falls back to per-sentence sync synthesis, which for a local engine means each sentence pays full model-load + whole-buffer latency. mlx-audio's Qwen3-TTS generator **is** a generator: with newline-separated input it yields audio per segment as soon as each finishes. Measured on M5 Max: 4 segments stream at t=4.2s/7.6s/11.6s/16.9s vs 47s for one whole-buffer call. This PR wires that capability into the existing streaming pipeline. ## Design - `@register("qwen3tts-mlx")` in `tools/tts_streaming.py`; class implements `available()` (MLX venv + worker script exist) and `stream(text)` - `stream()` spawns a dedicated **MLX venv subprocess** (`~/.hermes/tts/mlx_stream_worker.py`) and reads back frames of `[u32 length][int16 PCM]`. The worker splits text on newlines, synthesizes each segment via `model.generate(..., ref_audio, ref_text, lang_code="Chinese")`, and writes each PCM frame immediately. - **Subprocess isolation is mandatory**: mlx-audio pins `transformers 5.0.0rc3`, which conflicts with `qwen_tts`'s pinned `4.57.3` in the Hermes runtime venv (`check_model_inputs() missing 'func'`). Keeping MLX in its own venv and bridging via subprocess follows the same pattern as command providers. - Config surface is additive: `tts.streaming.provider: qwen3tts-mlx` selects it; `tts.streaming.qwen3tts-mlx.model_dir` / `.ref_audio` override defaults. ## Verification - `python -m pytest tests/tools/test_tts_streaming_mlx.py -x -q` → 6 passed (registry membership, availability, frame ordering, worker-failure propagation, section-based args) - Full streaming + chunking suite: 39 passed, 12 skipped - Live E2E on this machine: `Qwen3TTSMLXStreamer.stream("…\n…")` yielded 3 PCM frames (TTFB 8.8s incl. model load), correct 24kHz int16 layout ## Who should enable this - Apple Silicon users who run a local Qwen3-TTS voice-clone engine and want **conversational voice** (not just on-demand synthesis) with a custom cloned voice, no cloud cost, private by design - Anyone who already has the `local-tts-optimization` setup (PR #85041) and wants streaming voice on top ## Platform compatibility | Platform | Impact | |---|---| | macOS Apple Silicon | ✅ Primary (MLX + mlx-audio) | | macOS Intel / Linux | ⚠️ `available()` returns False without the MLX venv; no regression for other streamers | | Windows | ⚠️ No MLX; feature absent, no regression | ## Quick-start guide 1. Set up MLX env + worker per `skills/productivity/local-tts-optimization` (or the companion repo `x7peeps/hermes-tts-kit`) 2. `hermes config set tts.streaming.provider qwen3tts-mlx` 3. Speak to Hermes; voice messages/session speech now stream from the local engine with the cloned voice ## Troubleshooting | Symptom | Cause | Fix | |---|---|---| | `available()` False | MLX venv / worker missing | install per the local-tts-optimization skill | | worker exits non-zero | model dir or ref audio path wrong | set `tts.streaming.qwen3tts-mlx.model_dir` / `.ref_audio` | | `check_model_inputs()` error | PYTHONPATH shadowing transformers | ensure `env -u PYTHONPATH` in the subprocess cmd (already in code) | ## Resource guard: local MLX prefetch serialization (2026-08-17) `stream_tts_to_speaker` prefetches the next sentence while the current one plays (Semaphore(3)). For cloud providers that is network-bound and cheap; for the local MLX streamer every concurrent prefetch spawns an extra MLX worker subprocess (2-3GB RAM + GPU each). A 3-way prefetch therefore ran three local inference workers at once — tripling memory pressure and contending for the same GPU. Local streamers are now detected by the `_VENV` attribute they carry and serialize prefetch to 1 slot; cloud streamers keep 3-way. No new config knob; covered by a dedicated regression test (`test_local_mlx_streamer_serializes_prefetch`).

signal.title: fix(desktop): focus clarify panel so keyboard shortcuts work hands-free
signal.text: ## Summary When a clarify card appears mid-conversation, keyboard focus stays in the composer. The card's global keydown handler has a focus guard that stands down when focus is on a contenteditable/input — so **Arrow keys and letter shortcuts (1-9 / A-Z) were swallowed by the composer** and a pure-keyboard user couldn't drive the choices without first clicking the card. ## Fix As soon as the card is interactive (`ready` && has choices && not submitting), it **claims focus on its panel container** (`tabIndex={-1}` on the `form[data-clarify-choices]`). The global handler now sees a neutral focus target and Arrow/letter/Enter all work immediately, no mouse needed. Focus is claimed once (ref guard) and only when the card owns choices — a free-text-only clarify leaves composer focus alone. ## Test Plan - New test: `moves focus onto the panel so keyboard shortcuts work without a mouse` — after render, `document.activeElement` is the `[data-clarify-choices]` panel - Existing suite green (20 tests in clarify-tool.test.tsx, incl. the clicked-choice-Enter regression)

signal.title: architecture(desktop): make route identity immutable, generation-bound, and resource-owned across multi-gateway Desktop
signal.text: ## Summary Desktop now has real multi-gateway routing, but the architecture still treats route identity as reconstructible metadata rather than an immutable authority proof. #89719 successfully shipped registered-gateway switching and broad `(connectionId, profile)` propagation across REST, WebSocket, sessions, messaging, cron, projects, settings, and status state. Background gateways retain sockets and continue work. That is the correct product direction. However, one review finding crossed into `main`: `resolvedConnectionId()` can take a descriptor that already corresponds to an exact registry route and reconstruct a weaker identity from URL or `user@host`, selecting the first match. Legal duplicate registrations can therefore alias: - identical URLs with different auth mode, headers, credentials, Cloud organization, or account; - identical SSH user/host pairs with different port, key path, remote Hermes path, or remote profile. Because the rest of the new source-aware machinery then follows that reconstructed ID consistently, the result is a particularly convincing split-brain: the system can be internally coherent under the wrong source identity. That concrete defect should be fixed, but it exposes a deeper class that needs an architectural contract rather than another matcher patch. ## Core design principle > Once identity becomes more specific, no downstream layer may make it less specific and later infer the missing dimensions from foreground, endpoint, transport, or mutable registry state. Exact route identity must be **sticky, monotonic, generation-bound, and resource-owned**. ## Current evidence ### 1. Exact route provenance already exists before transport details are lost The existing `desktop-remote-route` planner resolves registry provenance before URL normalization, OAuth, SSH tunnelling, or other transport steps discard distinguishing information. Its identity matcher includes the dimensions that actually distinguish legal registrations: - auth mode; - headers; - token envelope; - Cloud organization; - SSH host/user/port; - key path; - remote Hermes path; - remote profile. For non-primary matches it accepts only a unique result. This is the right place in the pipeline to freeze route ownership. ### 2. `resolvedConnectionId()` weakens that proof after the fact The compatibility helper added by #89719 reconstructs identity from: - normalized `baseUrl` for remote/Cloud; - normalized `user@host` for SSH. It uses the first registry match and its descriptor type does not make an already-resolved `connectionId` authoritative. This can overwrite the exact identity already established by the route planner. ### 3. Source scoping is broad, but ownership is still ambient in many consumers `hermesApi()` injects the renderer's currently active source into requests. That works for foreground-global actions, but existing resources such as sessions, cron jobs, projects, approvals, OAuth flows, artifacts, and files should execute against their **owning route**, not whatever route happens to be foreground when an asynchronous callback finally runs. This becomes load-bearing now that background gateways remain live across foreground switches. ### 4. Some namespaces are source-aware at transport boundaries but still bare internally Gateway event dispatch now compares composite source/profile scope, which is correct. But many downstream stores and transient maps still key by bare runtime/session IDs, with source provenance kept separately or inferred from the active route. Copied/restored Hermes homes can reproduce IDs exactly. Multiple registered gateways make those duplicate namespaces concurrent. ### 5. Source switching still relies on manual global-state invalidation `wipeSessionListsForGatewaySwitch()` explicitly clears sessions, cron, messaging, unread paint, transcript tails, artifacts, and other gateway-bound state. This works only as long as every new source-owned store is remembered in the wipe list. That is an omission-prone correctness mechanism. Multi-gateway state should be partitioned by route identity so switching changes the visible partition instead of destructively reusing one global namespace. ## The deeper class issues ### A. Identity proof is not monotonic A registered route and an unqualified legacy descriptor should not share one loose shape. Suggested direction: ```ts type ResolvedRoute = | { identity: { kind: 'registered' connectionId: ConnectionId connectionGeneration: number } profile: ProfileKey transport: TransportDescriptor } | { identity: { kind: 'legacy-unregistered' provenance: 'environment' | 'profile-v1' | 'settings-v1' } profile: ProfileKey transport: TransportDescriptor } ``` Only the legacy-unregistered branch may enter compatibility inference. A registered descriptor must never have its identity overwritten by a weaker downstream guess. ### B. Registration identity, physical backend identity, principal, and locator are conflated Desktop needs explicit equivalence relations for concepts that are currently easy to treat as interchangeable: - **registration identity** — saved `connectionId`; - **registration generation** — which endpoint/credential envelope that ID currently denotes; - **physical runtime identity** — backend installation / `installId`; - **authorization principal** — account, Cloud org, credential set, permission envelope; - **locator** — URL, SSH host, tunnel endpoint. These answer different questions. Two registrations may share a locator but represent different principals. Two locators may reach one physical installation. A registry ID can be edited in place to point at a different runtime. Physical sameness does not prove authorization equivalence. Callers should explicitly choose the relation they require instead of using a generic "same connection" test. ### C. The route algebra overloads omission, `local`, `primary`, and legacy fallback These are semantically distinct: - omitted / null connection selector; - explicit `local`; - registry `primary`; - `lastUsed`; - unknown or removed ID; - legacy profile-routed fallback. V2 routing should represent this structurally rather than through magic-string normalization. Suggested direction: ```ts type ConnectionSelector = | { kind: 'registered'; id: ConnectionId } // including `local` | { kind: 'legacy-primary' } ``` `primary` and `lastUsed` should resolve user intent into a concrete registered route **before** an operation begins. They should not be consulted later as fallback authority for an already-started operation. ### D. Gateway activation is coordinated but not one transaction A foreground switch currently spans independently changing facts: - registry entry and credential envelope; - resolved descriptor; - WebSocket URL; - opened socket; - active gateway pointer; - active profile pointer; - renderer connection descriptor; - ambient REST connection/profile; - cache invalidations; - `lastUsed`; - new-chat ownership. Descriptor resolution and socket activation should not be independent proofs. The activation path that actually prepares the socket should return the exact descriptor and identity used to establish it. The outcome should be typed and explicit: ```ts type ActivationReceipt = | { status: 'activated' route: RouteKey activationEpoch: number connection: HermesConnection socketInstanceId: string } | { status: 'already-active' route: RouteKey activationEpoch: number } | { status: 'superseded' | 'removed' | 'offline' | 'ambiguous' | 'cancelled' requested: RouteIntent current: RouteKey } ``` Only an exact successful receipt may authorize success side effects. This directly interlocks with #89586 / #89609: a declined activation must not resolve indistinguishably from a successful one, especially for same-source profile switches where comparing only `connectionId` proves nothing. ### E. A connection ID identifies a mutable slot, not an immutable route A registry entry can be materially edited while retaining the same ID. For example, `homelab` can change from endpoint/credential A to endpoint/credential B while stale callbacks, sockets, caches, and resources still carry only `homelab`. Material edits already trigger backend/socket recycling, which is necessary but not sufficient as the architecture grows. Introduce a monotonically increasing registration generation: ```ts type RouteKey = { connectionId: ConnectionId connectionGeneration: number profile: ProfileKey } ``` Every descriptor, socket, request, response, event, cache entry, persisted resource handle, and activation receipt should carry the generation. Results from an obsolete generation may finish but must not commit into the new generation's state. This closes ABA-style edit/remove/re-add races and makes descriptor/socket agreement provable. ### F. Ambient active-route state must not authorize mutations on existing resources Foreground-global actions can use the current route. Existing resources should carry their owner. Instead of: ```ts archiveSession(sessionId) ``` prefer: ```ts archiveSession({ owner: session.route, sessionId: session.id }) ``` The same principle applies to: - session mutations and hydration; - cron jobs and runs; - projects and repo/worktree operations; - approvals and input requests; - OAuth flows; - artifacts; - filesystem and Git operations; - background/tile/window actions. This directly interlocks with #89916: filesystem and Git facades need the same route identity as the resource/session that owns them, not merely the current foreground gateway. ### G. Resource namespaces must be source-qualified, not just transport-qualified The canonical resource identity should include route ownership: ```ts type ResourceKey = { route: RouteKey resourceId: string } ``` At minimum, audit and qualify: - runtime session IDs; - stored session IDs and lineage aliases; - unscoped stream pins; - approvals and input requests; - provider-wait / compaction / drafting state; - transcript tails; - unread/read watermarks; - pin mirrors; - cron job and run IDs; - project IDs and project scope; - artifacts; - OAuth flow/session IDs; - query and capability cache keys; - window/HUD/quick-entry session references. Unscoped events should be pinned per socket or `RouteKey`, never through one renderer-global ref shared by multiple retained gateways. ### H. Manual cache wiping should stop being a correctness boundary Gateway-owned state should be partitioned by route identity. Foreground switching should select another partition rather than globally clearing one namespace and hoping every source-owned store was included. Generation revocation can explicitly retire obsolete partitions after connection edits/removals, but ordinary switching should not require destructive global wipes. This also aligns state lifetime with the already-shipped behavior where background gateway sockets remain alive and continue work. ### I. Compatibility needs a versioned protocol and retirement path Absence of `connectionId` can currently mean too many things: - older Electron main; - environment-provided unregistered route; - genuinely local legacy route; - ambiguous registry match; - accidentally dropped exact identity; - failed lookup. Optional fields are not a sufficient compatibility protocol. Prefer an explicit versioned IPC contract: ```ts type ConnectionProtocol = | { version: 1; route: LegacyRouteDescriptor } | { version: 2; route: RegisteredRouteDescriptor } ``` A v2 registry-scoped call must produce a v2 registered route. Legacy compatibility should remain explicitly unregistered unless a unique, full-fidelity pre-dial match proves ownership. Compatibility paths should also expose diagnostics/telemetry so they can be retired rather than becoming permanent alternate authority models. ### J. Multi-window and registry-write concurrency need explicit semantics Desktop supports multiple full renderer windows while `lastUsed` and registry entries are global persisted state. Define and test: - whether `lastUsed` is installation-global, window-specific, or primary-window-owned; - what happens when one window removes/edits a connection another window is activating; - how concurrent registry mutations are serialized; - whether writes use a registry revision / compare-and-swap contract. A monotonically increasing registry revision should make stale write rejection explicit. ## Required invariants The architecture should eventually be able to state and mechanically test all of these: 1. Once exact registered identity exists, no downstream layer can replace it with inferred identity. 2. Registry ordering cannot affect route resolution. 3. Zero or multiple compatibility matches fail explicitly. 4. Socket route, descriptor route, REST route, UI route, and activation receipt agree on one `RouteKey`. 5. A same-source profile activation decline produces no success side effects. 6. Edit/remove/re-add during dial cannot publish an obsolete generation. 7. Old-generation responses/events cannot commit after generation replacement. 8. Identical resource IDs on two gateways remain independent. 9. Unscoped events on simultaneous retained sockets cannot cross-pin. 10. Explicit `local` never aliases omitted legacy-primary routing. 11. One stalled activation cannot permanently wedge later user intent. 12. Multi-window activation and registry edits produce a serializable result. ## Diagnostics / observability Every routed operation should be traceable without logging secrets. Include a correlation tuple such as: ```text connectionId connectionGeneration profile activationEpoch socketInstanceId requestId resourceId ``` A split-brain should be diagnosable from one trace rather than inferred from contradictory UI symptoms. ## Implementation sequence ### Phase 1 — immediate shipped defect - Treat an existing descriptor `connectionId` as authoritative. - Never overwrite it through post-dial inference. - Restrict compatibility inference to genuinely unqualified legacy descriptors. - Reuse the full-fidelity pre-dial identity contract from #88922 / #88697. - Fail closed on zero or multiple matches. - Add duplicate URL/auth/org/header and SSH port/key/path/profile witnesses. ### Phase 2 — canonical route identity - Introduce structured `RouteKey` with connection generation. - Distinguish registered routes from legacy-unregistered routes at the type boundary. - Make explicit `local` a real registered identity, never omission. ### Phase 3 — activation transaction - Return a typed activation receipt from the prepare/dial/publish path. - Return the exact descriptor used by the activated socket. - Consume activation verdicts at all callers before any success side effects. - Bound activation leases / unresolved IPC so one operation cannot wedge the switch coordinator indefinitely. ### Phase 4 — resource ownership - Add `RouteKey` ownership to sessions, cron, projects, OAuth flows, artifacts, FS/Git resources, and other durable/background objects. - Remove ambient foreground routing from mutations against existing resources. ### Phase 5 — route-partitioned state - Source-qualify cache/store keys. - Replace broad switch-time wipe correctness with route-owned partitions and generation revocation. ### Phase 6 — compatibility and concurrency hardening - Version the Desktop IPC routing contract. - Add compatibility diagnostics and retirement criteria. - Add registry revisioning / serialized write semantics. - Define multi-window ownership of `lastUsed` and route mutations. ## Acceptance / adversarial matrix The closing test matrix should include at least: - two URL registrations with the same normalized URL but different auth mode; - same URL with different token/header envelopes; - same Cloud URL under different org/account identity; - two SSH registrations with same user/host but different port; - different key path; - different remote Hermes path; - different remote profile; - exact descriptor `connectionId` survives all of the above; - ambiguous legacy descriptor returns no registered identity; - `(homelab, default)` -> `(homelab, research)` decline leaves route/caches/preferences unchanged; - edit connection generation while activation is in flight; - remove and recreate a connection ID while old work is still completing; - two gateways with identical stored/runtime session IDs; - copied Hermes home with identical project/job/session IDs on two active sources; - simultaneous unscoped stream events from two retained sockets; - explicit local operations while registry primary is remote; - two Desktop windows switching different sources and mutating registry state concurrently. ## Interlocks / provenance - #89719 — shipped registered-gateway switcher and broad `(connectionId, profile)` propagation; this issue is the architectural follow-through from the merged residual. - #88325 / @dokterdok — substantive source of #89719's fifteen-commit salvage; provenance remains preserved. - #88307 — product request implemented by #89719. - #88922 / #88697 — exact pre-dial route identity architecture that must remain authoritative rather than being weakened post-dial. - #89586 / #89609 — activation-verdict work: completion must prove publication, not merely promise resolution. - #89483 — adjacent atomic-publication work that exposed the need to distinguish prepared, activated, superseded, and declined states. - #89622 — lifecycle race witness around activation leases / target disposal. - #88095 — complementary foreground session/profile ownership work. - #89916 — resource facade ownership: FS/Git must follow the owning route, not ambient foreground state. ## Non-goals This is not a request to replace all compatibility code immediately or to break single-source Desktop behavior. The goal is to establish one canonical identity/ownership model so compatibility code is explicitly fenced and cannot weaken exact v2 identity. It is also not sufficient to solve this by expanding `resolvedConnectionId()` with more matcher fields. That repairs the current witness but leaves the defect class open anywhere identity can later be erased and reconstructed. ## Definition of done This issue is complete when Desktop can prove, by type contract and adversarial tests, that: - exact route identity never becomes less specific downstream; - mutable registrations are generation-bound; - successful activation returns an authoritative receipt; - every durable/background resource carries its owning route; - source-qualified resources cannot alias across gateways; - foreground switching does not determine ownership of already-existing resources; - compatibility inference is explicit, ambiguity-safe, observable, and retireable; - multi-window and registry mutation semantics are serializable and documented. The target architecture should make the current #89719 split-brain impossible to represent, not merely unlikely to reproduce.
