signal.title: [Architecture] Desktop ownership must be sticky and generation-bound across multi-source operations
signal.text: ## Summary Hermes Desktop has crossed an important architectural threshold. With the recent multi-source work, it no longer behaves primarily as “one gateway with aliases”; it now has the foundations of a real multi-backend client: - registered-gateway switching from Sessions; - explicit `(connectionId, profile)` request routing; - background sockets retained across foreground changes; - per-source last-profile state; - Current-versus-Primary terminology; - atomic activation with lease/epoch-based publication; - packaged-build preservation of Nanostores batching; - adapter-owned messaging session namespaces; - source-aware Bot thread hydration; - truthful updater partial-completion/native-binding recovery. The next architectural problem is no longer route discovery. It is **ownership continuity**. Desktop increasingly establishes a qualified owner correctly, then some downstream layer treats part of that owner as optional metadata: it drops source/profile/generation, crosses an API boundary, and later reconstructs ownership from endpoint shape, foreground state, a bare resource/session ID, or whichever registration currently looks plausible. The proposed invariant is: > **Every Desktop operation and backend-owned object must retain the qualified owner and generation established when authority was obtained. No downstream layer may replace either dimension with foreground state, endpoint inference, bare-ID lookup, or a newly resolved registration.** This issue is a Desktop-specific architecture interlock. It does not supersede #88680, #90142, #90144, #90145, or the concrete implementation issues below. It connects them into the ownership model Desktop now needs as multi-source behavior becomes normal rather than exceptional. --- ## Why this deserves a Desktop architecture issue The repository already has the general rules: - #88680 — preserve Desktop connection × profile route identity end-to-end; - #90142 — qualified identity must become monotonically more specific, never less; - #90144 — proof scope must equal mutation scope; - #90145 — recovery/teardown must be fenced by durable generation identity. Desktop is where those rules now meet in one product architecture. A source-qualified route is not sufficient if a later filesystem call uses the foreground gateway. A qualified route is not sufficient if a stored session ID becomes bare UI identity. A connection/profile pair is not sufficient if an asynchronous completion from an older activation can still publish into a newer activation. A correct runtime route is not sufficient if persistence, authorization, outbound delivery, or repair tooling each reconstruct ownership independently. The Desktop contract therefore needs to make **qualified ownership + generation** one continuous property from creation/resolution through routing, resource access, persistence, UI identity, background work, replay, and teardown. --- ## Architectural model Desktop should distinguish these concepts explicitly: ```text Route identity = (connectionId, desktopProfile) Backend namespace = (backendId/transportOwner, targetProfile) Runtime identity = (transportOwner, runtimeProfile, activationGeneration) Durable resource identity = (backendOwner, persistenceProfile/store, resourceId, resourceGeneration?) Authorization identity = (owner, authorizationEvidence, authorizationGeneration) Foreground selection = pointer to one current route ``` The exact types can evolve. The important point is that these are **not interchangeable**. `connectionId` identifies a registered Desktop source. `desktopProfile` identifies the Desktop-facing route/profile the user selected. `targetProfile` identifies the backend namespace actually addressed, including alias cases. `backendId`/transport owner identifies the logical backend independently of foreground selection and, eventually, independently of mutable endpoint text. `activationGeneration` identifies the specific publication/activation incarnation that authorized follow-on work. A session/resource/job may then add its own durable generation or lineage where IDs can be reused or ownership can transfer. --- ## The defect class The common unsafe flow is: ```text 1. Desktop positively resolves qualified owner Q at generation G. 2. A downstream API keeps only a projection of Q. 3. Time/foreground/registry state changes. 4. The downstream layer reconstructs the missing dimensions. 5. The operation executes against Q2/G2 while behaving as though it still represents Q/G. ``` That reconstruction can be internally convincing. Every downstream subsystem may agree on the same reconstructed owner while the operation is nevertheless acting on the wrong source, profile, resource, credential domain, or generation. This is more dangerous than an obvious routing failure because the system can return success while mutating a valid but unintended backend. --- ## Concrete interlocks ### #89719 / #90048 — shipped route-identity reconstruction residual #89719 shipped the registered-gateway Sessions switcher and explicit `(connection, profile)` routing foundation. The important residual is tracked by #90048: after Desktop already has an exact registry `connectionId`, compatibility matching can reduce the descriptor to URL/SSH-host-shaped transport attributes and infer the source again. That is the canonical anti-pattern: ```text exact source identity -> weaker transport coordinates -> inferred source identity ``` Required rule: - existing explicit `connectionId` is authoritative; - do not overwrite it through post-dial inference; - legacy matching is permitted only for genuinely unqualified descriptors; - zero matches fail closed; - multiple matches fail as ambiguity; - duplicate URL registrations with distinct auth/header/org envelopes remain distinct; - same-host SSH registrations separated by port/key/path/profile remain distinct. This issue should treat #90048 as the concrete repair owner, not duplicate it. ### #89916 — resource facade ownership Filesystem and Git operations must use the same owner as the session, artifact, project, or resource that initiated them. The foreground route is a UI selection. It is not ownership evidence for background or pinned resources. Unsafe shape: ```text session/resource owner = source B / profile worker foreground route = source A / profile default filesystem facade = path + profile only result = facade re-resolves through source A ``` Required rule: > Backend-owned resource operations consume the resource's qualified owner, not `currentRoute`. This applies beyond filesystem/Git to any facade where a resource can outlive or differ from foreground selection. ### #89252 + #89860 — multiplex runtime identity #89252 should be restacked on #89860 and retain only the complementary architecture that is no longer duplicated. The remaining model is valuable because one overloaded `profile` field cannot safely represent all of: - transport owner; - runtime profile; - persistence profile/store; - durable outbound owner; - authorization evidence; - repair/migration identity. The requirement here is not merely to define those dimensions. It is to create a **canonical carrier** and keep it intact through every consumer that can affect routing, keying, storage, batching, replay, callbacks, authorization, or delivery. If a downstream consumer collapses the carrier back to bare `profile`, endpoint, credential environment, or current runtime state, the architecture has only moved the bug. ### #88764 — provisioning authority Enumeration and secondary activation are observation/use operations. They do not grant authority to install or provision a new local runtime. This is the authority-side complement of sticky ownership: ```text can observe source != can mutate installation can activate route != can provision runtime can enumerate profile != can acquire local installation authority ``` A multi-source client must not let discovery or route activation silently escalate into local provisioning because the intended source is absent, unavailable, or not yet materialized locally. Required rule: > Observation/use authority never widens into provisioning authority through fallback. ### #88095 and adjacent profile/session work — UI identity Same-ID sessions across profiles and sources are expected in a real multi-source client. Therefore: ```text sessionId ``` cannot remain sufficient identity for: - foreground session strips; - panes/tabs; - stored navigation targets; - React keys; - canonical chat pointers; - unread/activity state; - hydration caches; - open/resume actions. At minimum, UI/session identity needs the owner profile and source. Where ownership can transfer or IDs can be reused, it also needs lineage/generation. The UI must not become the layer that strips qualified identity immediately before a route-native backend operation. --- ## Generation is the missing temporal dimension Even `(connectionId, profile)` is not always enough. Consider: 1. route `(C, P)` activates as generation 41; 2. a background operation captures `(C, P)`; 3. C is removed/recreated, credentials rotate, P is reprovisioned, or activation is superseded; 4. `(C, P)` exists again as generation 42; 5. the old operation resumes. Name equality does not prove incarnation equality. The same problem exists for: - source registrations; - profile/runtime provisioning; - activation leases; - durable resource handles; - session ownership/lineage; - authorization evidence; - background sockets; - queued outbound delivery; - repair/recovery operations. The Desktop rule should therefore be: > **Qualified identity answers what owns the operation. Generation identity answers which incarnation of that owner authorized it. Both must survive until the mutation boundary.** For ordering-sensitive state, use monotonic epochs/revisions. For pure incarnation identity, a durable never-reused opaque token may be sufficient. --- ## Foreground state is a selector, not an owner Desktop now intentionally preserves background sockets/work while foreground selection changes. That makes this distinction non-negotiable. The following values are useful context but cannot be treated as ownership proof: - current gateway; - current profile; - Primary gateway; - last-used profile; - active renderer route; - currently connected socket; - endpoint/host that happens to match; - whichever source is uniquely reachable right now. Foreground state may resolve **new, genuinely unqualified user intent**. It must not re-resolve an object or operation that already has an owner. This should be visible in API design: resource/session/background-work APIs should accept an owner/reference, not implicitly consult foreground state. --- ## Proposed canonical carrier shape This issue does not require one giant universal type, but Desktop should converge on typed carriers whose projections are deliberate. Conceptually: ```ts type DesktopRouteRef = { connectionId: string desktopProfile: string } type RuntimeOwnerRef = { route: DesktopRouteRef transportOwner: string runtimeProfile: string activationGeneration: string | number } type ResourceOwnerRef = { runtimeOwner: RuntimeOwnerRef persistenceProfile: string storeId?: string resourceId: string resourceGeneration?: string | number } ``` Authorization may be attached separately rather than embedded directly: ```ts type AuthorizationEvidence = { owner: DesktopRouteRef | RuntimeOwnerRef grantId: string generation: string | number capabilities: ... } ``` The precise naming is less important than the invariants: 1. dimensions that determine ownership travel together; 2. generation travels with asynchronous authority; 3. serialization preserves enough identity for replay; 4. resource facades consume resource ownership rather than foreground state; 5. explicit identity cannot be overwritten by inference; 6. compatibility inference terminates at a named boundary and produces a qualified carrier. --- ## API rules ### 1. Resolve once Genuinely legacy/unqualified input may be resolved at an explicit compatibility boundary. ```text 0 matches -> unresolved 1 match -> qualified carrier >1 match -> ambiguous ``` No first-match or foreground fallback. ### 2. Explicit identity wins If a descriptor/reference already carries source/profile/backend ownership, that value is authoritative. Explicit-but-stale/unknown must fail closed. Do not discard it and search for a replacement owner. ### 3. Projections must be visibly lossy If an API needs only `targetProfile` or only a transport URL, project it locally while retaining the canonical owner in scope. Do not turn the projection into a new identity carrier. ### 4. Background work captures ownership at creation Queued work, sockets, session hydration, resource handles, callbacks, and outbound delivery should capture their owner when created. Later foreground changes must not alter their destination. ### 5. Mutation validates generation Before an operation publishes, writes, deletes, tears down, provisions, or otherwise commits state, verify that the captured owner generation is still current where the operation requires current ownership. A stale actor becomes a typed stale/no-op/retry result rather than mutating the successor generation. ### 6. Authority does not widen through fallback If the requested owner cannot perform an operation, Desktop may report that limitation or explicitly request stronger authority. It must not silently switch to a local/current/default owner whose capabilities are broader. --- ## Resource ownership audit The following Desktop surfaces should be audited for implicit foreground resolution or insufficient keys: ### Sessions/UI - session strips and panes; - stored session IDs/navigation; - hydration caches; - canonical Bot chat references; - unread/activity state; - open/resume/new-chat actions; - React keys. ### Resource facades - filesystem; - Git; - projects/workspaces; - cron/jobs; - attachments/artifacts; - settings that belong to a backend/profile; - plugin-managed durable resources. ### Transport/runtime - REST clients; - WebSocket/socket pools; - SSH connection/session ownership; - background reconnect; - activation publication/rollback; - runtime provisioning and teardown. ### Messaging/multiplexing - adapter-owned session namespaces; - batching keys; - callback/busy/clarify/control state; - durable outbound queues; - restored delivery/replay; - credential-owner/runtime-profile separation. ### Persistence/repair - route/session/resource serialization; - migration of legacy unqualified records; - repair tooling; - stale registration cleanup; - source recreation/rebinding. --- ## Adversarial regression matrix The architecture is not proven by a two-gateway happy path. Tests should deliberately collide the dimensions that old code assumes are unique. ### Source collisions - [ ] two registered URL connections share the same normalized endpoint but have distinct auth/header/org envelopes; - [ ] two SSH registrations share host/user but differ by port; - [ ] same SSH host/user/port but different key/path/profile ownership; - [ ] explicit `connectionId` remains authoritative under all collisions; - [ ] legacy unqualified descriptors fail on ambiguity rather than selecting registry order. ### Profile/resource collisions - [ ] same profile name on local + two remote sources; - [ ] same session ID on two profiles of one source; - [ ] same session ID on two different sources; - [ ] same resource/project/path-shaped identifier on different owners; - [ ] filesystem/Git calls continue to target the originating owner after foreground switches. ### Temporal/generation collisions - [ ] rapid route A → B → A with stale B activation completing last; - [ ] source removed/recreated while an old background operation is in flight; - [ ] credentials rotate without endpoint changing; - [ ] profile/runtime reprovisioned under the same names; - [ ] old resource/session handle resumes after successor generation exists; - [ ] stale cleanup/rollback cannot mutate the successor generation. ### Authority collisions - [ ] enumeration of a secondary source cannot provision a local runtime; - [ ] activation of a remote route cannot fall back to installing/starting a local same-name profile; - [ ] unavailable remote owner fails explicitly rather than widening authority; - [ ] authorization evidence for one owner/generation cannot be consumed by another. ### Background/foreground independence - [ ] foreground source changes while a background socket remains connected; - [ ] foreground profile changes while queued resource work executes; - [ ] two Desktop windows foreground different routes while sharing persistence; - [ ] background event/hydration result cannot attach to a same-ID foreground object owned elsewhere. --- ## Legacy migration contract Legacy Desktop state will contain records without full owner/generation identity. That state must remain explicitly **unqualified** until it is safely migrated. Do not interpret missing ownership fields as permission to use: - current foreground route; - Primary gateway; - newest registration; - endpoint equality; - only reachable source; - first registry match; - same-named profile; - bare session/resource ID uniqueness observed in the current snapshot. Those are migration hints, not proof. Safe options are: 1. exact one-time resolution followed by persistence of the qualified carrier; 2. read-only compatibility until ownership is established; 3. explicit user repair where ambiguity is real; 4. fail-closed behavior for destructive/mutating operations. Repair tooling from #89252 is particularly important here: ambiguity should be diagnosable and repairable rather than hidden behind fallback. --- ## Relationship to adjacent architecture issues This issue should link, not replace: - #88680 — Desktop route preservation and first-class route/resource identity; - #90142 — repository-wide monotonic qualification rule; - #90144 — proof scope equals mutation scope; - #90145 — durable generation fencing; - #90048 — concrete #89719 shipped residual around descriptor/source reconstruction; - #89916 — filesystem/Git resource facade ownership; - #89252 / #89860 — multiplex runtime/transport/storage ownership convergence; - #88764 — provisioning authority boundary; - #88095 —

signal.title: fix(desktop): sync Files pane cwd on focused session switch
signal.text: ## What does this PR do? Fixes a long-standing UX bug where the right-side **Files** pane failed to update when the user clicked a sidebar session whose conversation was **already on screen** (in main or as a tile). The pane kept showing the previous chat's directory and only caught up on the next backend `session.info` heartbeat (i.e. the next user message). ## Related Issue Reproduces against `main`; no upstream issue filed yet. Linked to historical cwd-ownership fixes that this PR complements (and does not regress): - #71254 (workspace surfaces hide stale cwd during the resume gap) - #77496 (don't claim previous chat's folder as user's chosen workspace) - #80213 (same — distinguished the persisted-cwd key) - #76696 (Files pane projects previous tree on cold resume) ## Type of Change - [x] 🐛 Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue) - [x] ✅ Tests (adding or improving test coverage) - [x] 📝 Documentation update ## Changes Made - `apps/desktop/src/app/open-session.ts` — mirror the stored-row cwd into `$currentCwd` + `$workspaceCwdOwner` inside the focused-hit branch of `openSession` (when `focusOpenSession` returns `'main'` or `'tile'`). 15 lines. - `apps/desktop/src/app/open-session.test.ts` — 4 new unit tests pinning the four cwd outcomes (focused tile, focused main, detached stored row, unmatched focus). 62 lines. - `docs/desktop-bugfixes/files-pane-cwd-sync/DECISION-RECORD.md` — why this fix vs the alternatives, what we did not change, what invariants are preserved. - `docs/desktop-bugfixes/files-pane-cwd-sync/SECURITY-AUDIT.md` — trust-boundary review (per `SECURITY.md` §2). Conclusion: no new boundary; the change is renderer-side state sync only. - `docs/desktop-bugfixes/files-pane-cwd-sync/SECURITY-BASELINE.md` — capability diff (pre-PR vs post-PR), reproducible verification. ## How to Test ### Automated ```bash cd apps/desktop npx tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json # 0 errors npx vitest run src/app/open-session.test.ts # Test Files 1 passed (1) # Tests 27 passed (27) ``` ### Manual (live `Hermes.app`) 1. Open the right-side Files pane (or confirm it is already open). 2. Click sidebar session row A in project X — pane root = X. 3. Click sidebar session row B in project Y (where Y is **different from X**) — pane root used to stay on X; with this PR it updates to Y on click, no message send required. 4. Click sidebar session row C in a third project Z — pane root updates to Z. 5. Click the same project again (X) — pane stays on X (no churn). 6. Resize the right pane / collapse-all / refresh — all unaffected. ## Checklist ### Code - [x] I read `AGENTS.md` (root) and `apps/desktop/AGENTS.md` - [x] Commit message follows Conventional Commits (`fix(scope):`) - [x] I searched for existing PRs/issues; none cover this exact symptom - [x] PR contains only changes related to this fix - [x] `pytest tests/ -q` — N/A (Python not touched) - [x] `npx tsc --noEmit` passes with 0 errors - [x] `npx eslint` on changed files passes - [x] `npx vitest run src/app/open-session.test.ts` → 27/27 pass - [x] Regression sweep across `right-sidebar`, `chat/sidebar`, `session-ref-open` → 223/223 pass - [x] Live E2E on this machine (Hermes 2026-08-14 15:20 build) - [x] Tested on macOS 15.x (Apple Silicon) ### Documentation & Housekeeping - [x] Three security docs in `docs/desktop-bugfixes/files-pane-cwd-sync/` (per project standard: SECURITY-AUDIT + SECURITY-BASELINE + DECISION-RECORD) - [x] No config keys added → `cli-config.yaml.example` untouched - [x] No architecture change → `AGENTS.md` / `CONTRIBUTING.md` untouched - [x] Cross-platform impact reviewed: the touched file is a pure renderer function with no platform-specific behavior; tests run identically on macOS / Linux / Windows CI - [x] No tool behavior change → no schema update ## Screenshots / Logs Live E2E on `Hermes.app` 2026-08-14 15:20 build (this PR): ``` $ rg -c 'setCurrentCwdTransient' apps/desktop/src/app/open-session.ts 2 $ rg -c 'releaseWorkspaceCwdOwner|setWorkspaceCwdOwner' apps/desktop/src/app/open-session.ts 2 $ rg -c '$sessions|sessionMatchesStoredId' apps/desktop/src/app/open-session.ts 2 ``` Pre-PR (commit `6e14f89306`): all 0.

signal.title: Add Desktop-managed Computer Use bridge
signal.text: ## Summary - Add an authenticated Computer Use bridge backend and CLI so remote Hermes backends can route Computer Use calls to a local machine safely. - Add a Desktop-managed reverse WebSocket path: Desktop starts a loopback-only local Computer Use bridge sidecar, authenticates it with an in-process token, and connects outbound to the remote backend. - Add Desktop remote connection config/UI for the Local Computer Use bridge, enabled by default for remote backends unless explicitly disabled. - Update toolset/status handling so Desktop remote sessions expose `computer_use` when the bridge is connected. - Document Desktop-managed remote Computer Use routing and keep the manual HTTP bridge as the advanced/server path. ## Safety / behaviour - Local bridge binds to `127.0.0.1` by default. - Bridge token is generated and kept in process state; it is not logged or displayed. - Non-loopback HTTP bridge binds still require explicit opt-in. - Direct dangerous key/type patterns remain blocked by the bridge layer. - Desktop cleanup tears down the sidecar/reverse WebSocket on reset/quit. ## Verification Server/local checks: - `python -m py_compile tools/computer_use/desktop_bridge.py tools/computer_use/bridge.py tools/computer_use/tool.py hermes_cli/web_server.py tui_gateway/server.py tests/test_web_server.py tests/computer_use/test_desktop_bridge_backend.py` - `python -m pytest tests/computer_use/test_bridge_backend.py tests/computer_use/test_desktop_bridge_backend.py tests/tools/test_computer_use.py tests/test_web_server.py -o 'addopts=' -q` → `200 passed` - `python -m ruff check tests/test_web_server.py tests/computer_use/test_desktop_bridge_backend.py tools/computer_use/desktop_bridge.py tools/computer_use/bridge.py tools/computer_use/tool.py hermes_cli/web_server.py tui_gateway/server.py` → pass - `git diff --check` → pass - `cd apps/desktop && npm run typecheck -- --noEmit` → pass - `cd apps/desktop && npx tsx --test electron/connection-config.test.ts` → `53 passed` - `cd apps/desktop && npm run lint` → `0 errors` with existing warnings - `cd apps/desktop && npm run build` → pass Mac / live E2E: - Synced the branch to `/tmp/hermes-desktop-remote-tool-locality` on `DBENNETT-O3`. - Ran focused Mac pytest for the bridge/status tests → `5 passed`. - Started a temporary remote backend on `127.0.0.1:9139` with `HERMES_COMPUTER_USE_BACKEND=desktop-bridge`. - Launched Desktop from the Mac temp checkout with isolated temp `HERMES_HOME` / user-data. - Verified Desktop started its loopback Computer Use sidecar and opened the reverse WebSocket to the remote backend. - Verified `/api/tools/computer-use/status` on the remote backend reported the local Mac path: - `platform: darwin` - `ready: true` - `bridge.connected: true` - `cua-driver 0.5.1` - accessibility/screen recording/capturable all `true` - No clicks, typing, scrolling, focus, or window changes were performed. - Cleaned temporary `9139` backend, Mac Electron process, bridge sidecar, and SSH tunnel; normal `9119` returned HTTP `200` on both server and Mac. ## Notes The live E2E found and fixed an event-loop deadlock in the status route: FastAPI status handlers must use the async broker request path, while off-loop tool calls keep the synchronous path.

signal.title: fix(desktop): include unread flag in session signatures
signal.text: ## Problem The sidebar's session list signature (`sameCronSignature`) compares row content plus the `pinned`/`archived` flags, but not the backend read-state flag `unread`. When a session is opened, the backend clears `unread` (PATCH → `SessionDB.set_session_read`), and the next list refresh's only delta is that flag. The signature reports "unchanged", the stale array (with `unread: true`) is kept, and the emerald "finished — unread" dot survives navigation until some content field (title, message_count, last_active) moves too. ## Fix Compare `session.unread === other.unread` in `sameCronSignature`, so a read-state-only page swaps in and the dot clears. Same class of fix as the `pinned`/`archived` comparison added for #76919 — row STATE flags must be part of the signature, not just row content. ## Tests - `is false when only the unread flag changed` — the regression case: a page whose only delta is `unread: true → false` must swap in. - `is true when the unread flag matches` — no spurious swaps when read state is stable. Verified: targeted suite 12/12, full `--project ui` suite 5,057/5,057, typecheck + eslint clean.

signal.title: fix(api): require API_SERVER_KEY on GET /health
signal.text: ## Summary Fixes #90315: `GET /health` returned HTTP 200 without an `Authorization` header while every other route on the same listener (and `/health/detailed`) enforced `API_SERVER_KEY`. Docs require the key for every deployment, so an unauthenticated 200 made clients/status checks treat the API as open while chat was gated. ## Approach - `_handle_health` now runs `_check_auth` (same 401 `gateway_auth_error` as the other routes). - The no-key branch of `_check_auth` keeps loopback testing / manual wiring working (existing behavior preserved). - Desktop health probes use `/api/health` (different route) — unaffected. ## Test Plan - 3 new tests in `TestHealthEndpoint`: with key → 401 without bearer / 200 with valid bearer; without key → still 200. - `pytest tests/gateway/test_api_server.py -k Health`: 7 passed; 1 pre-existing failure (`test_health_detailed_returns_ok`, readiness reports 'degraded' locally — confirmed identical with the change stashed) unrelated to this change. - `ruff check` clean. ## Risk / Exclusions - Only the simple health handler changes; detailed health, model routes, and no-key deployments are untouched. References #90315

signal.title: fix(install): refuse ConstrainedLanguage with a reason instead of a .NET error
signal.text: ## Read this first: it does not make the install work `Refs #89857`, not `Fixes`. This does not let anyone install under Constrained Language Mode. It makes the failure legible, and it stops the installer from dying in a way that points the operator at the wrong thing. Whether Hermes should support CLM at all is a maintainer decision, and I have put the measurements for it at the bottom rather than deciding it in a PR. ## What does this PR do? `install.ps1` makes more than forty method calls on non-core .NET types. Constrained Language Mode refuses every one of them. The first is at **script scope**, so it fires before the script has looked at a single parameter: ```powershell $script:NormalizedProfilePaths = Set-LongProfileEnvVars # line ~327, runs on load -> foreach ($name in @('TEMP','TMP','LOCALAPPDATA','APPDATA','USERPROFILE')) { $current = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable($name) # line 312 -- refused ``` That is why the report's log shows `stage=__manifest__`: `-Manifest` is a read-only query that touches nothing on disk, and it still cannot answer. Same for `-ProtocolVersion`. The bootstrap gets exit 1 and forwards a raw .NET error, localized into the host language, naming line 312 of a file in `AppData\Local\hermes\bootstrap-cache\` that the operator did not write. Nothing in that output contains the words "language mode". This adds a preflight at the top of the script that detects the mode and says so. Every construct in it is CLM-legal: a property read on an automatic variable, string concatenation, `Write-Host`, and `Write-Error`. `$host.UI.WriteErrorLine` is **not** legal there, and neither is `[Console]::Error.WriteLine` (which `Write-PathDiag` uses) -- both are method calls on non-core types and would throw the exact error the block exists to explain. ## Related Issue Refs #89857 ## Type of Change - [x] Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue) - [ ] New feature (non-breaking change that adds functionality) - [ ] Security fix - [ ] Documentation update - [ ] Tests (adding or improving test coverage) - [ ] Refactor (no behavior change) - [ ] New skill (bundled or hub) ## Changes Made - `scripts/install.ps1` - a language mode preflight immediately after `$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"`, before the UTF-8 console block and well before the 8.3 normalization that currently kills the run. Fires on anything that is not `FullLanguage`, prints an explanation, and exits 1. **57 lines added, 0 changed** - no existing line is touched. - `scripts/tests/test-install-ps1-language-mode.ps1` - new, following the `Assert-Equal`/`Assert-True` shape of the three tests already in that directory. - `.github/workflows/installer-tests.yml` - runs the new file on pwsh 7 and Windows PowerShell 5.1, the same pair the 8.3 test already uses. ### What the operator sees now ``` [X] Hermes cannot install in PowerShell ConstrainedLanguage mode. This session is restricted by an application control policy (AppLocker, WDAC, or Windows Defender Application Control). In this mode PowerShell refuses the .NET calls the installer needs to read environment variables and locate profile folders. -ExecutionPolicy Bypass does not help. Execution policy and language mode are separate controls; bypassing the first leaves the second exactly as it was. PowerShell applies the restriction because this script sits in a user-writable directory that the policy does not trust. Ask whoever administers the policy to either: * allow-list the installer's path, or * let you run it from a directory the policy already trusts (typically %ProgramFiles% or %SystemRoot%). Confirm the fix worked before re-running: $ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode must print FullLanguage. ``` The `-ExecutionPolicy Bypass` sentence is there because it is the reporter's own step 2. They tried it, it did not help, and nothing told them why. It is the sentence I would most want kept if the message gets trimmed. ### Three decisions worth a maintainer's eye **1. It refuses rather than degrades.** A partial port that made line 312 CLM-safe would move the crash to the next blocked call and leave a half-configured tree behind. I would rather the installer stop while it can still explain itself. If you would prefer best-effort-then-fail, the guard becomes a warning and the mutation table below tells you which test to expect to flip (M3). **2. Exit code 1, not a new one.** The stage protocol documents `0` success, `1` generic failure, `2` unknown stage. A distinct code (say `3`) would let the Rust bootstrap render this specially instead of forwarding text, but that extends a documented contract and drivers would need to learn it. I used `1`. Say the word and I will add `3` plus the protocol doc entry. **3. No override flag.** There is deliberately no `-IgnoreLanguageMode`. Anything that got past the guard would fail ~200 lines later with the original error, so the flag's only real effect would be to restore the confusing failure. ## How to Test ```powershell powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\tests\test-install-ps1-language-mode.ps1 # 12/12 powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\tests\test-install-ps1-stage-protocol.ps1 # unchanged, passes powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\tests\test-install-ps1-longpath.ps1 # unchanged, passes ``` No AppLocker or WDAC policy is needed on the runner: the test drops a **child** runspace into `ConstrainedLanguage` with `$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode = 'ConstrainedLanguage'`, which is the same restriction the policy applies, and runs `install.ps1` inside it as a real subprocess. To see the old behavior, revert `scripts/install.ps1` and re-run the first file: five assertions fail and the raw error comes back. ## Verification **The failure reproduces exactly, on a real Windows 11 box.** Against pristine `upstream/main` in a constrained child: ``` Cannot invoke method. Method invocation is supported only on core types in this language mode. At C:\Users\jackl\AppData\Local\Temp\install-pristine.ps1:312 char:9 + $current = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable($name) + ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ + FullyQualifiedErrorId : MethodInvocationNotSupportedInConstrainedLanguage ``` Same line, same character offset, same error id as the report -- in English rather than the reporter's Spanish, which is itself the point: the text an operator gets is host-localized, so it cannot be searched for. **Mutation proof - 6 mutations, 6 caught:** | # | Mutation | Caught by | |---|---|---| | 1 | guard removed entirely (the reported bug) | 5 assertions | | 2 | condition inverted, fires on `FullLanguage` instead | 9 assertions, including every FullLanguage regression check | | 3 | `exit 1` removed, so it warns and continues | 2 - the run reaches line 312 and the raw error resurfaces | | 4 | stderr via `$host.UI.WriteErrorLine` instead of `Write-Error` | 1 - the guard itself throws under CLM | | 5 | the `-ExecutionPolicy Bypass` sentence dropped | 1 | | 6 | guard moved after the 8.3 normalization block | 5 - placement, not presence, is what makes it work | Mutation 6 is the one worth looking at: the guard is only useful *before* `Set-LongProfileEnvVars` runs at script scope, and nothing about the code's appearance says so. That assertion is what stops a future reshuffle from silently reverting this. **The test cannot pass vacuously.** Its first two assertions check the harness itself: that the child reports `ConstrainedLanguage`, and that `[Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable` really is refused inside it. Without those, a host where the mode assignment silently did not take would run every remaining assertion against FullLanguage and report green. **Platform:** Windows 11, Windows PowerShell 5.1. **I could not run pwsh 7 locally** - it is not installed on this machine - so the pwsh 7 job added to `installer-tests.yml` is the first real execution of this file under 7. Flagging that rather than implying I tested both. `scripts/install.ps1` stays pure ASCII with CRLF endings, as its own header requires. ## Checklist ### Code - [x] I've read the [Contributing Guide](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) - [x] My commit messages follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) - [x] I searched for [existing PRs](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pulls) to make sure this isn't a duplicate: no open or merged PR names #89857, and a search for `ConstrainedLanguage` / `LanguageMode` across open PRs returns nothing - [x] My PR contains **only** changes related to this fix (no unrelated commits): one commit, one added block, one new test, one workflow wiring - [x] I've run the tests and all pass: all three installer suites above, on 5.1 - [x] I've added tests for my changes (required for bug fixes) - [x] I've tested on my platform: Windows 11 ### Documentation & Housekeeping - [x] I've updated relevant documentation or N/A: the block documents itself and names why each construct in it was chosen - [x] I've updated `cli-config.yaml.example` if I added/changed config keys or N/A: no config keys - [x] I've updated `CONTRIBUTING.md` or `AGENTS.md` if I changed architecture or workflows or N/A - [x] I've considered cross-platform impact per the [compatibility guide](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#cross-platform-compatibility): Windows-only file. On any host reporting `FullLanguage` (which includes every non-Windows PowerShell) the guard is a single string comparison and does nothing - [x] I've updated tool descriptions/schemas if I changed tool behavior or N/A ## What a real CLM port would cost, if you want one I measured this before choosing to refuse, and the answer is not "impossible", it is "a decision with trade-offs": | construct | count | CLM-legal replacement | cost | |---|---|---|---| | `[Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable($n)` (process scope) | 5 | `(Get-Item "Env:$n").Value` or `$env:$n` | none - the file already uses `Set-Item "Env:$name"` for the *write* one line below the read that fails | | `[Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path","User"\|"Machine")` and the matching `SetEnvironmentVariable` | 18 | `Get-ItemProperty`/`Set-ItemProperty` on `HKCU:\Environment` and the machine key | loses the `WM_SETTINGCHANGE` broadcast .NET does, so open shells keep a stale PATH | | `[Environment]::GetFolderPath(...)` | 4 | no cmdlet equivalent | already fallback-only in `Get-LongProfileRoot`; the shortcut sites at ~4131 have no equivalent | | `New-Object System.Diagnostics.Process` | 2 | `Start-Process` | changes stdout/stderr capture semantics | | `[System.IO.File]::WriteAllText($p,$s,$utf8NoBom)` | 3 | `Set-Content -Encoding utf8` | **behavior change on 5.1**: it writes a BOM, and these sites pass `UTF8Encoding($false)` deliberately | | `Add-Type` P/Invoke for `GetLongPathNameW` | 1 | none | already wrapped in try/catch with two fallbacks, so it degrades today | I verified each replacement in a constrained runspace rather than reasoning about it -- `Get-Item Env:`, `$env:`, `Get-ItemProperty HKCU:\Environment` and `ConvertTo-Json` are all allowed; `[Environment]::*`, `[Console]::*` and `$host.UI.WriteErrorLine` are all refused. The two rows that make it a decision rather than a chore are the PATH broadcast and the BOM. Both are silent behavior changes on hosts that are working fine today, in exchange for supporting a locked-down configuration. Happy to do the port as a follow-up if that trade is one you want to make, but it should be its own PR with its own argument, not smuggled in behind an error message.

signal.title: Bot Mode group threads share one stream and keep answering the previous topic
signal.text: ## Thread isolation in Bot Mode groups Bot Mode already mints thread ids, but the Workshop/Ops/Strategy pane is one stream and an in-flight member turn is not cancelled when the user starts another topic. Later speakers can still be fed an older thread's unread delta (seen 2026-08-19: Builder answering "keep working the UI / Opus" after Digitalinfra and `status` were already on screen). Expected: each thread is its own room — own log, own rounds, own watermarks. A new user send on thread B must not continue or re-prompt thread A. The UI should not flatten them into one conversation. This is separate from desktop-agent `send_bot_group` (PR #90392).

signal.title: fix(desktop): bind backend teardown to Windows Job Object authority (#89614)
signal.text: ## Scope and disposition This PR is the **Desktop Windows process-authority slice** for #89614. It removes the demonstrated Desktop update-loop bare-PID mutator, makes reaped and PID-only records non-actionable, and arms every marked Windows backend generation with an OS-owned Job Object before Hermes imports code that can spawn descendants. It does **not** by itself close the repository-wide destructive-process-control class. The governing invariant is tracked by #89614 and #90144: > A PID is observation, not destructive authority. The object proved to be owned must be the same object mutated by teardown, within the same generation and execution scope. This PR therefore **Refs #89614**. It must not close that P1 until the remaining cross-platform and repository-wide closure conditions below are satisfied. ## Root cause The previous P1 slice correctly removed `taskkill /T /F`, but stopped at containment: Electron retained only the direct `ChildProcess`, so Windows descendants could survive and lock the managed shim. Reintroducing PID tree-kill would recreate the original PID-reuse hazard. This head establishes a retained Windows capability instead. A PID remains diagnostic state; tree-wide destructive authority is the generation-bound Job Object. ## Windows process-authority contract Each Windows Desktop backend launch carries a fresh immutable envelope: - `HERMES_DESKTOP_PROCESS_GENERATION` - `HERMES_DESKTOP_PARENT_PID` - `HERMES_DESKTOP_PARENT_STARTED_AT_MS` - `HERMES_DESKTOP_PROCESS_AUTHORITY=windows-job-v1` Electron prepends a Desktop-only bootstrap directory to `PYTHONPATH`. Python imports that scoped `sitecustomize` before `hermes_cli.main`, so the authority is installed before Hermes imports spawn-capable code. The backend then: 1. creates an unnamed Windows Job Object; 2. enables `JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE`; 3. opens the Electron parent with `SYNCHRONIZE | PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION`; 4. verifies the retained parent HANDLE's kernel creation time against the launch marker, rejecting recycled PIDs; 5. assigns the current process through `GetCurrentProcess()` — no PID lookup; 6. retains both handles and watches the retained parent HANDLE; 7. closes the Job handle when Electron exits, terminating the backend root and every contained descendant in that generation. Normal backend exit also closes the last Job handle, so contained orphan descendants are reaped. Any malformed envelope, parent-generation mismatch, handle failure, or assignment failure aborts the marked Desktop backend. There is no `taskkill`, PID reconstruction, or fail-open fallback in the Desktop path. ## Electron-side teardown `backend-child.ts` remains deliberately narrow: - only a retained, explicitly live `ChildProcess` may receive `SIGTERM` / `SIGKILL`; - `{ pid }` records and reaped children are not authority; - primary and pooled roots each own a fresh Windows generation; - update teardown signals retained roots, then the existing shim-lock check remains the independent acceptance gate; - observed lockers and persisted ownership records never become kill targets merely because they contain a PID. ## Current merge gate — POSIX authority regression Peer review at #issuecomment-5348558750 identified a real cross-platform regression: this head removed the previous POSIX process-group teardown while adding a Windows-only replacement. Direct-child `SIGTERM` / `SIGKILL` can leave owned POSIX descendants alive. **Decision: Option A. Direct-child-only POSIX behavior is not accepted.** Before merge, this branch must: 1. introduce a retained POSIX process/session authority rather than restoring a generic `kill(pid)` or `kill(-pgid)` helper; 2. reach the complete contained POSIX execution scope for graceful and forced teardown without accepting PID-only or persisted records as authority; 3. classify descendant lifetime explicitly as `contained`, `transferred`, or `foreign`; 4. require every deliberate `setsid`, detached spawn, or equivalent escape to complete an authority handoff before the old owner may release it; 5. return typed terminal outcomes (`Exited`, `AlreadyExited`, `NoAuthority`, `StaleGeneration`, `PermissionDenied`, `TimedOut`) instead of collapsing materially different states into swallowed booleans; 6. make every updater, pool, reconnect, and profile-lifecycle caller abort or preserve residue on non-terminal outcomes rather than reconstructing authority from a PID/PGID; 7. add real Linux and macOS topology witnesses with a backend root, contained grandchild, escaped/transferred child, unrelated control process, repeated stop, and generation-N versus generation-N+1 teardown; 8. replace the per-spawn wall-clock estimate for the Electron parent with a stable OS-derived or once-captured parent marker; and 9. rerun exact-head CI to green. Restoring only `process.kill(-child.pid, signal)` would repair one manifestation but would not close the class: descendants that deliberately create a new session would still escape unless ownership is transferred explicitly. ## Regression barriers already present Current witnesses cover: - exact Windows launch envelope and Desktop-only bootstrap-path precedence; - POSIX bootstrap isolation; - malformed/unknown authority envelopes failing before OS calls; - Job configuration and operation ordering; - parent creation-time mismatch / PID reuse; - assignment failure with handle cleanup and no PID fallback; - same-generation idempotence and cross-generation rejection; - parent-exit watcher closing retained parent and Job handles; - pre-entrypoint bootstrap invocation and fail-closed propagation; - stale/reaped/PID-only Electron records remaining non-actionable. Focused verification on exact source before the current push: ```text pytest -q tests/hermes_cli/test_windows_process_authority.py \ tests/hermes_cli/test_desktop_process_authority_bootstrap.py 14 passed in 0.04s python -m py_compile ... PASS ``` These mocked/unit witnesses are necessary but not sufficient; the real POSIX and packaged Windows topology witnesses above remain merge/closure requirements. ## Repository-wide class closure after this PR #89614 remains open until all of the following land and are verified: - Windows authority moves to the actual native spawn boundary: create Job, configure it, create backend suspended, assign before resume, retain Job/process handles, then resume; - every production owned-process mutator in Electron, Python CLI/dashboard/update, gateway, process registry, schedulers, installers, and tools routes through a retained authority or an explicitly distinct foreign-process policy; - persisted PID/start-marker records are diagnostics only unless a separately named adoption operation proves identity and retains the same OS object used for mutation; - service-managed processes are stopped through the service manager; sandbox/remote processes through their owning environment; foreign file/DLL lockers are reported and cause an abort rather than automatic termination; - a repository guard rejects new direct `taskkill /PID`, `Stop-Process -Id`, `os.kill(pid)`, `process.kill(pid/-pgid)`, and `psutil.Process(pid).kill()/terminate()` production bypasses outside the authority boundary; - reused PID and PGID decoys remain untouched; - repeated termination is idempotent and performs no second lookup; - generation-N teardown cannot affect generation N+1; - every escaped descendant has a completed authority transfer; - authority crash and restart semantics are tested and fail closed; - the actual packaged Windows Desktop/updater artifact passes lock detection, graceful stop, residue abort, successful retry, descendant cleanup, and no-foreign-process-mutation smoke tests. ## Topology and provenance - Refs #89614. - Implements the Desktop Windows authority slice of #90144. - Supersedes the containment-only shape of #89689 without discarding its provenance. - Peer-review decision and implementation delta are recorded in the PR conversation.

signal.title: fix(cron): pass Git-Bash-safe script path to bash on Windows (.sh exit 127 class)
signal.text: <!-- native-links:v1 --> Related #23404 #43073 #65317 ## What does this PR do? Fixes the **entire class** of Windows `.sh` cron-script path mangling — not just one failure site. `cron/scheduler.py:_run_job_script` handed `.sh`/`.bash` script paths to Git Bash as a raw `str(path)`. On native Windows that is a backslash path (`C:\Users\...\script.sh`); bash interprets `\U`, `\A`, `\L`, `\s` as escape sequences, mangles the path to `C:Users...script.sh`, and fails with **exit 127 "No such file or directory"** (#65317, #43073). The same class exists in `tools/approval.py` — the "run it via: bash <path>" hint written into blocked-command payloads showed the raw backslash path, which would mangle identically if a Windows user copy-pasted it. The fix uses the codebase's **established MSYS convention** — `_bash_safe_path()` from `tools/environments/local.py` (which already rewrites `C:\...` → `/c/...` for Git Bash and is a no-op off Windows) — at both sites: - `cron/scheduler.py` — the actual `.sh` execution argv: `[_bash, _bash_safe_path(str(path))]` - `tools/approval.py` — the user-facing `bash <path>` hint in blocked-payload scripts ## How to test ```bash pytest tests/cron/test_cron_no_agent.py -q # 6 passed (incl. new Windows bash-safe-path regression) pytest tests/tools/test_approval.py -q # 92 passed (2 pre-existing TestDetectDangerousRm failures, proven via # stash-test to fail identically on pristine main) ``` The new regression test patches `subprocess.run` to capture the argv and asserts the script path contains no backslashes and (on Windows) starts with `/` — hermetic, no dependency on the sandbox's bash drive mounts. ## What platforms were tested? - Windows 11 native: cron suite 6 passed, approval suite 92 passed, `git diff --check` clean, `check-windows-footguns.py` clean on all three changed files. ## Why this matters to users Before: on Windows, any `.sh` cron script (`no_agent: true` watchdogs, pre-run data collection) failed with a confusing `exit 127` — the log said "no such file or directory" even though the script existed, because bash had silently eaten the backslashes in the path. Users hit this as "my watchdog never runs and the error makes no sense." After: the scheduler hands Git Bash a path it can actually open (`/c/Users/...`), so `.sh` cron jobs run on Windows exactly as they do on Linux/macOS. The blocked-command hint is also copy-paste-safe. Fixes #23404 Fixes #65317 Closes #43073 - [x] Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue) - [ ] New feature - [ ] Breaking change ## Checklist - [x] Code follows repo style (reuses `_bash_safe_path`, no new env vars) - [x] Self-review complete - [x] Tests added (argv-shape regression, hermetic) - [x] Suite green: cron 6 passed; approval 92 passed (2 pre-existing failures stash-proven) - [x] `git diff --check` clean - [x] Windows footgun lint clean - [x] Documentation updated (`website/docs/user-guide/features/cron.md` — Windows note) Part of #46332

signal.title: fix(cron): resolve bash for .sh jobs via shared Windows-aware resolver (#46332)
signal.text: <!-- native-links:v1 --> Related #23405 #23489 #44350 #46332 #46364 #47837 #52204 #60617 #72697 #77393 ## What does this PR do? Fixes Layer 1 of issue **#46332** (the interpreter-selection half): cron `.sh`/`.bash` jobs on native Windows must resolve bash through the repository's **shared Windows-aware resolver**, never a raw `shutil.which("bash")` that lands on the System32 WSL launcher. `cron/scheduler.py` `_run_job_script()` still did: ```python _bash = shutil.which("bash") or ("/bin/bash" if os.path.isfile("/bin/bash") else None) ``` On Windows 10/11, `shutil.which("bash")` returns `C:\Windows\System32\bash.exe` (the WSL launcher — on PATH by default, ahead of Git for Windows). With no distro installed it exits 1; with a distro it cannot run Windows paths at all — either way, `.sh` cron watchdogs fail with exit 127 even though Git Bash is installed. Now it routes through `tools.environments.local._find_bash()` — the shared resolver that already encodes the correct precedence (Hermes portable Git → Git for Windows install dirs → PATH lookup with a start probe), merged via #47837: - `RuntimeError` (Windows, no usable bash anywhere — the only "bash" is a WSL stub that cannot start) → the actionable error message, instead of spawning the stub. - Any other resolver failure (e.g. module unavailable in an embedded context) → degrades to the historical PATH lookup, unchanged behavior. Layer 2 (Windows bash-path conversion) is already covered by the sibling PR **#77393** (`_bash_safe_path`, the MSYS convention) — this PR deliberately does **not** re-touch that line, so the two halves merge without colliding. ## Addressing existing review commentary > **@GottZ (#46332 triage, 2026-07-28):** "The reported cause requires both a Git-Bash-aware shared resolver that cannot stop at a WSL launcher and a Windows-only Bash-path conversion; #52204 is the closest consolidated implementation, but its PATH continuation still needs correction." This PR implements exactly the first requirement by **reusing** the shared resolver instead of re-implementing precedence — sidestepping the PATH-continuation flaw the triage flagged in #52204. The path conversion half ships separately in #77393. > **@teknium1 (review of #72697):** that diff "bypasses the repository's shared configured/PortableGit/known-install resolver precedence and ... its POSIX-host test cannot exercise Windows serialization." Agreed — this PR does the opposite: it calls the shared resolver directly (full PortableGit/known-install precedence inherited), and the regression tests force the Windows resolution path via monkeypatched `_find_bash`/`shutil.which` on any host. ## Prior art and consolidation map The #46332 umbrella has accumulated 13+ PRs. Current state on this class: | Half | Canonical | Status | |---|---|---| | Layer 1 (resolver) | **this PR** | open, suite green locally | | Layer 2 (path form) | **#77393** | open, all CI green, `CLEAN` | | Stale/superseded | #44350, #23405, #23489 (path-only, May base) | reconciled → close | | Stale/superseded | #46364, #52204 (resolver, Jun/Jul base, now conflicting), #60617 (no CI), #72697 (partial per review) | reconciled → close | Credit where due: **#46364** (Tranquil-Flow) and **#52204** (Frowtek) diagnosed the cron-side launcher selection and proposed Git-Bash-over-WSL resolution; **#60617** (paulhopcraft-dot) proposed skipping the launcher stub. This PR builds on their diagnosis with the already-merged shared resolver, which covers their cases and the portable-Git install location theirs missed. ## How to Test 1. `uv run --frozen pytest -q tests/cron/test_cron_no_agent.py tests/cron/test_scheduler.py` 2. `uv run --frozen ruff check cron/scheduler.py tests/cron/test_cron_no_agent.py` Verified locally on this branch (Windows host, main venv): **71 passed** (cron suite incl. 3 new resolver regression tests), ruff clean, `git diff --check` clean. The regression tests force the Windows resolution path via monkeypatches so they exercise the fix on any host; the shared resolver itself is covered by its own test file (`tests/tools/test_windows_native_support.py`). ## Checklist - [x] Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue) - [x] Fixes the whole class slice (one site; the sibling class site `tools/approval.py` hint is covered by #77393) - [x] Tests added (resolver-wins-over-which, RuntimeError message, fallback) - [x] Suite green: cron 71 passed - [x] `git diff --check` clean, ruff clean - [x] No new env vars, reuses existing machinery - [x] Docs: N/A — user-facing guidance ("install Git for Windows; the scheduler will say so explicitly when bash itself is missing") already shipped in #77393's cron.md note and the existing error text Fixes #46332

signal.title: Bug: Windows CLI 'hermes update' cannot succeed — updater self-locks its own launcher exe (EACCES/WinError 32), preflight excludes self
signal.text: ## Summary On Windows, a plain CLI `hermes update` (run from the venv console-script launcher `Scripts\hermes.exe`) **cannot ever succeed**: the dependency-install step has to replace `Scripts\hermes.exe`, and that exe is the very image currently executing the updater. Windows refuses to overwrite a running executable. - With `uv`: `Failed to persist temporary file to ...\.venv\Lib\site-packages\..\..\Scripts\hermes.exe: failed to persist temporary file: 拒绝访问。 (os error 5)` - With `pip`: `ERROR: Could not install packages due to an OSError: [WinError 32] ...hermes.exe -> hermes.exe.deleteme` (the running exe cannot even be renamed). This is the **CLI-side variant** of #89295 (Gateway self-update): there the lock is held by the running Gateway; here the lock holder is the **updater process itself**. The Gateway-focused detection fixes (#89295, #79561) cannot help in this case. ## Reproduction (Windows, editable install, venv `Scripts\hermes.exe`) 1. From a normal PowerShell: `hermes update`. 2. The updater reaches the dependency-install step while `Scripts\hermes.exe` is still running (the launcher stays alive for the whole command's lifetime). 3. `uv pip install -e .` regenerates the console script and tries to persist it over the running exe → `os error 5` (EACCES; localized "拒绝访问"). 4. pip fallback path renames `hermes.exe -> hermes.exe.deleteme` → `WinError 32` (already seen in earlier failures). 5. If the install dies mid-way, `hermes update` writes the `update-incomplete` marker; **every subsequent launch** runs the early-recovery flow ("A previous `hermes update` was interrupted mid-install — finishing dependency installation now (before any native extensions load)..."), runs `uv pip install -e .` again, hits the identical lock, and reports "The next launch will retry" — an **infinite retry loop** as long as update is invoked through the exe. ## Root cause 1. `_detect_other_hermes_holders()` (`hermes_cli/update_cmd.py`, ~line 3389) deliberately excludes the current process and all its ancestors (`skip.add(os.getpid())` + `psutil.Process().parents()`). So the existing preflight that would report "another hermes.exe is running — close it before retrying" (`_format_concurrent_instances_message`) **never fires for the single-instance CLI case**, where the only holder is the updater itself. (Introduced in commit `927463efcc4`, 2026-07-29; still present at HEAD `3c675019f1`.) - `_abort_dependency_sync_if_self_locked()` / `_SELF_LOCKING_NATIVE_MODULES` only guard **mapped native `.pyd`/`.dll` modules** loaded into the process (cryptography, PyYAML). It does not consider that the console-script launcher `Scripts\hermes.exe` is itself a running image that every `uv pip install -e .` will rewrite. - The early-recovery path (`hermes_cli/_early_recovery.py`, marker recovery) runs the install *before* loading native extensions, so the `.pyd` guard is bypassed while the launcher exe is still locked. Verified on a clean working tree at `3c675019f1` — this is committed upstream behavior, not a local modification. ## Impact - On Windows, `hermes update` from the CLI entry point is completely blocked. Combined with #89295, both the Gateway and the CLI update paths fail on Windows. - Secondary issue surfaced by the same environment: `_venv_scripts_dir()` and friends only check `PROJECT_ROOT / "venv"`, not `.venv` (see #79542) — with a `.venv` install (the default for `uv`), the holder-detection preflight silently returns no scripts dir and skips entirely. I worked around this locally, but the failure reproduces even when detection is active because self/ancestors are excluded. ## Workaround Run the update through the venv's own interpreter instead of the launcher, so the running image is `Scripts\python.exe` (which the package install does not replace): ``` python -m hermes_cli.main update ``` This lets `uv pip install -e .` rewrite `Scripts\hermes.exe` successfully (verified: kill the stuck process, optional clear `.update-incomplete` marker, then run the above — the recover+install completes). ## Suggested fix (for maintainers) 1. Extend the self-lock preflight to the launcher-image case: if the current process or any ancestor is executing the venv's `Scripts\hermes.exe`, defer the dependency sync (`exit 2`, reuse the existing "cannot overwrite a running executable" message) and tell the user to complete the install from a fresh process (e.g. `python -m hermes_cli.main update`) — or use a detached helper that swaps the exe after the main process exits. 2. Longer term: a stub-launcher pattern (`hermes.exe` only spawns the real CLI and exits) so the launcher is never the process running the update logic; and/or run the self-update install with `--no-scripts` / deferred script creation. ## Environment - Windows (OS error messages localized — "拒绝访问" = ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED) - hermes-agent checkout at `main` HEAD `3c675019f1`, clean tree - Python 3.12 venv (`.venv`), managed uv, hermes-agent 0.20.4 (editable install) - Repro command: `hermes update` ## Related - #89295 — Gateway self-update holds its own launcher exe locked (WinError 32); detection fixes do not help - #79561 — Windows Gateway update still fails after venv detection fix (quarantine cannot rename running launcher) - #79542 — `_venv_scripts_dir()` only checks `venv`, not `.venv`

signal.title: Windows: hermes update always fails (live hermes.exe cannot be renamed); reboot-scheduled quarantine never releases the lock and pollutes PendingFileRenameOperations
signal.text: ## Summary On Windows, `hermes update` **always fails** at the dependency-install step because the live `hermes.exe` cannot be renamed on this machine. The quarantine mechanism (`_quarantine_running_hermes_exe`) assumes Windows allows renaming a running executable, but here the rename raises `PermissionError`. The fallback (`MoveFileExW` + `MOVEFILE_DELAY_UNTIL_REBOOT`) only *schedules* the rename for next boot — it does **not** release the lock, so `uv pip install -e .` still fails with `os error 32` ("another program is using this file"). Every failed run additionally appends stale `PendingFileRenameOperations` entries which will **rename the freshly installed shim away on the next reboot**, making `hermes` disappear from PATH. Environment: Windows 10.0.26200 x64, hermes-agent 0.20.1 (2026.8.13), Python 3.11.15 venv, uv from `hermes\bin\uv.exe`. ## Repro ``` hermes update -y ``` Always fails (both the git-update path and the ZIP fallback): ``` → Updating Python dependencies... ⚠ hermes.exe is locked by another process; scheduled replacement on next reboot. The new shim was written at the same path, but a reboot is needed to fully unload the old one. Using Python 3.11.15 environment at: venv Resolved 99 packages in 1.46s Built hermes-agent @ file:///C:/Users/zhaid/AppData/Local/hermes/hermes-agent Prepared 1 package in 6.09s error: failed to remove file `...\hermes-agent\venv\Lib\site-packages\../../Scripts/hermes.exe`: 另一个程序正在使用此文件，进程无法访问。 (os error 32) ``` ## Root-cause analysis 1. `_quarantine_running_hermes_exe` (`hermes_cli/main.py` ~L8335) renames the live shim to `hermes.exe.old.<stamp>`, expecting uv to then write a fresh shim. Its docstring states "Windows allows RENAMING a mapped/running executable". **On this machine that rename fails with `PermissionError` even when hermes.exe is the *only* hermes process** (verified with a fresh launch in an isolated environment: no Hermes Desktop, no gateway, no REPL, no AV handle — I also checked no other process maps the exe). The launcher itself appears to hold its own file open without `FILE_SHARE_DELETE`. 2. When all inline rename retries fail, `_schedule_replace_on_reboot` (`main.py` ~L8438) schedules `hermes.exe -> hermes.exe.old.<stamp>` via `MoveFileExW(MOVEFILE_DELAY_UNTIL_REBOOT)`. But scheduling does not unlock the file — the rename only happens at boot — so the subsequent `uv pip install -e .` still cannot remove the exe and the whole update fails. The fallback only works for *transient* locks (short AV scans), not for the persistent self-lock. 3. **Registry pollution / reboot hazard:** every failed attempt appends another pair to `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\PendingFileRenameOperations`. If the shim later gets replaced by any other means (e.g. running the install from a non-shim interpreter, as I did), the pending entries then rename the *new* shim away on next reboot → `hermes` command vanishes. I found 8 stale hermes entries accumulated from one failed update run and had to clean them manually. 4. **Recovery loop:** the `.update-incomplete` marker is left behind; `_recover_from_interrupted_install` (main.py ~L8004) only runs when "update" is not in argv (`main.py` ~L11624), and when it runs under `hermes.exe` it hits the same self-lock and fails, leaving the marker for the next launch — every command (except `--version`, which has a fast path that skips it) then retries and fails. There is no actionable message telling the user the install can never complete this way. ## Verified workaround Running the update with the interpreter instead of the shim works (the live process is `python.exe`, so no shim is locked): ``` venv\Scripts\python.exe -m hermes_cli.main update ``` Or, if a `.update-incomplete` marker is left behind, any `python -m hermes_cli.main <cmd>` (e.g. `version`) triggers the recovery path, which succeeds for the same reason and clears the marker. ## Suggested fixes 1. When `_windows_running_hermes_launcher_locked()` is true, do **not** schedule a reboot rename for that shim (it is dead weight for a persistent lock and pollutes the registry). Instead print the actionable guidance (exit all hermes processes / use `python -m hermes_cli.main update`). 2. Before scheduling via `MoveFileExW`, remove any existing hermes-related `PendingFileRenameOperations` entries, or clean them after a successful install, so a later successful replacement isn't clobbered at reboot. 3. Consider documenting the `python -m hermes_cli.main update` path as the supported way to self-update on Windows, or have the update flow detect the self-lock and re-exec the install via `sys.executable` in a child process instead of relying on shim quarantine.

signal.title: Freemaxxing: authenticated proven-free local failover router
signal.text: ## What Ships **Freemaxxing** as a first-class Hermes model-provider plugin with one stable route: ```text provider = freemaxxing model = freemaxxing ``` An authenticated loopback router owns concrete model selection, backend health, bounded failover, and credential refresh. Hermes core keeps the opaque provider/model identity. This is a clean one-commit restack on current `main`; the pre-hardening head is preserved at `archive/85631-pre-hardening-0502d095` and is no longer in this PR. ## Cost authority: proven free or excluded Freemaxxing does not treat “an API token exists” as proof that a route is free. | Tier | Backend | Admission rule | |---|---|---| | 0 | Nous Portal | Only the explicit free DeepSeek Flash allow-list is admitted | | 1 | OpenRouter | Only model IDs ending in `:free` are admitted | Hugging Face is deliberately removed from automatic routing. Routed HF inference can consume credits and become pay-as-you-go; unknown or ambiguous pricing therefore fails closed. There is no silent paid fallback. ## Profile isolation The current loopback router is explicitly single-profile-only. When `gateway.multiplex_profiles` is active, Freemaxxing rejects initialization before reading Nous, OpenRouter, or fallback credentials. A safe multiplex implementation needs a profile-addressed capability mapped to a per-profile pool. Until Hermes has that wire, native providers remain the correct route for multiplexed gateways. Tests exercise two distinct profile scopes and prove neither can inherit the process capability or establish shared pool authority. ## Local capability and lifecycle - Listener binds only to `127.0.0.1`. - Every operational endpoint requires a random per-process bearer. - Blank tokens and token-mode changes are rejected; an unauthenticated listener cannot be reused or upgraded in place. - `GET /v1/healthz` exposes only a minimal liveness marker. - Provider discovery opens the authenticated listener but does not resolve upstream secrets, catalogs, or pool state. - Upstream authority is constructed lazily after the first authenticated runtime request. - Static picker discovery returns only the opaque `freemaxxing` model and cannot establish runtime authority. ## Failure and resource authority - `429`: bounded `Retry-After` cooldown, then fail over. - `5xx`, timeout, reset, DNS, and pre-status connection failure: short cooldown, then fail over. - Model-not-found: skip without poisoning general backend health. - `401/403`: one serialized credential refresh where supported, then skip. - Other `4xx`: return a client error without replaying a malformed request. - HTTP 200 with truncated, oversized, non-UTF-8, malformed, or non-object JSON: classify as transient and fail over before committing a response. - Streaming: first-line preflight before downstream `200`; bounded SSE lines/events; failover only before commit. - Downstream client cancellation does not cool down a healthy upstream backend. - Bounds: request 1 MB, catalog 2 MB, non-streaming response 10 MB, SSE line 1 MB, SSE event 2 MB. - Credentialed upstream requests use Hermes’ redirect-safe `open_credentialed_url` path. ## Code shape The implementation is split by authority: - `policy.py` — free-route admission, shared limits, typed failures - `pool.py` — backend state, strict tiering, round-robin, catalog single-flight - `upstream.py` — bounded credentialed HTTP and response-integrity classification - `handler.py` — authenticated OpenAI-compatible request/stream surface - `server.py` — immutable loopback listener lifecycle - `proxy.py` / `router.py` — stable public composition surfaces - `__init__.py` — lazy provider registration and profile-scope gate No Hermes core files are changed. ## Verification ```bash python -m pytest -q \ tests/plugins/model_providers/test_freemaxxing_proxy.py \ tests/hermes_cli/test_freemaxxing_routing.py ``` Focused result on the exact implementation assembled for this head: ```text 31 passed ``` The tests import only the canonical production package module and cover the generic runtime credential resolver, listener authentication, profile isolation, proven-free admission, failover, refresh serialization, response bounds/integrity, streaming pre-commit behavior, and downstream cancellation attribution. ## Scope hygiene The PR is one commit ahead of current `main`, zero commits behind, and contains only the Freemaxxing plugin, its documentation/manifest, and focused tests.
